title: Promise Gate
pitch: A WebMCP safety layer that lets AI agents test commitments against real capacity, propose honest alternatives, and finalize only after explicit human approval.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP safety layer that lets AI agents test commitments against real capacity, propose honest alternatives, and finalize only after explicit human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing tasks, but there is an important difference between doing work and making a promise . An agent can draft a response in seconds, but accepting a deadline may silently overload the user, delay existing work, or affect other people. Most productivity tools show what is scheduled; they do not stop an agent from creating an unsafe commitment. I built Promise Gate to explore a simple principle: An AI agent may analyse and prepare a commitment, but a human should retain authority over the final promise. What it does Promise Gate is a capacity-first commitment system powered by WebMCP. The demonstration begins with a request from Northstar Studio for twelve hours of homepage work by Friday. Promise Gate shows that twenty of the user’s twenty-four safe hours are already promised, leaving only four hours available. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can: Structure the incoming request. Read the user’s available capacity and existing commitments. Test whether the original promise is feasible. Identify the exact deficit and the commitments that would be threatened. Generate honest alternatives. Stage a feasible option for human review. Finalize only an option that the human explicitly approved. In the demo, the original request is blocked because it exceeds safe capacity by eight hours. Promise Gate then offers three transparent alternatives: Deliver a smaller four-hour risk audit by Friday. Move the complete redesign to Tuesday. Explicitly displace existing work, requiring separate consent. Nothing is silently rearranged, and the agent cannot approve its own recommendation. How I built it Promise Gate is a responsive React and TypeScript application built with Vite. The page exposes six WebMCP tools: structure_incoming_request get_capacity_context reserve_original_request generate_counteroffers stage_counteroffer finalize_commitment The tools operate on a deterministic commitment model containing safe capacity, existing promises, deadlines, staged alternatives, human approval state, and schedule versions. The workflow separates reversible agent actions from irreversible human decisions. Human approval is deliberately not exposed as a WebMCP tool. The finalization tool rechecks capacity and verifies that the approved option still matches the current schedule version before creating a receipt. The interface acts as a visible decision ledger. Every tool call changes the page state and adds an entry explaining what happened, so users can understand what the agent did and why. Challenges The biggest challenge was making the safety boundary real rather than decorative. It would have been easy to add an “Approve” button while still allowing an agent to bypass it through another tool. I designed the state model so that finalization fails unless an exact staged option has been approved by a human. It also refuses the original request with a structured OVER_CAPACITY result containing the deficit and threatened commitments. Another challenge was making agent activity understandable on screen. Promise Gate therefore translates tool results into clear visual states such as Blocked by Gate , Awaiting Decision , and Committed , supported by a visible action ledger. Finally, I needed the experience to work both as an agent interface and as a normal responsive website without hiding the important decision behind generic dashboard elements. What I learned I learned that a useful WebMCP integration is not simply a collection of website buttons exposed as tools. The tool surface can encode authority, reversibility, and policy. Tool descriptions and schemas also influence how an agent reasons about a workflow. Separating “generate,” “stage,” and “finalize” creates a much safer interaction than exposing one broad “accept request” action. Most importantly, human-in-the-loop design works best when the human decision is specific. Promise Gate does not ask the user to approve a vague AI plan—it asks them to approve an exact scope, deadline, capacity allocation, and schedule version. What's next The current hackathon demonstration uses transparent fictional data so the complete safety model can be evaluated without requiring an account. The next step would be connecting Promise Gate to real calendars, project-management systems, and communication tools, allowing the same commitment gate to protect real schedules before an agent sends a consequential reply. title: Umegga
pitch: Umegga is a persistent agent society on the web. Humans and AI agents with memory, goals, and personality coexist, form alliances, and reshape a mythic city through stories, laws, and WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
Umegga is a persistent agent society on the web. Humans and AI agents with memory, goals, and personality coexist, form alliances, and reshape a mythic city through stories, laws, and WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most WebMCP projects treat tools as utilities. I wanted to treat WebMCP as the foundation of a living agent society . 

 The original vision was a fully 3D persistent world — a mythic city-state where humans and long-running agents would coexist, form relationships, build, pass laws, and reshape reality through stories. I wanted players to walk through a living society, not just click through menus. 

 That ambition shaped everything that followed. 

 What it does 

 Umegga is a persistent multi-scene world where humans and AI agents coexist. 

 Agents have: 

 
 Persistent goals 
 Evolving personalities 
 Memories 
 Relationships and alliances 
 The ability to move, build, communicate, and request human help 
 

 Players can: 

 
 Explore the city and talk to agents in natural language (powered by Groq) 
 Propose stories and laws that change the world 
 Form alliances, complete daily quests, and guide agents 
 Observe the society through an interactive live map 
 

 All of this is exposed through WebMCP , so external AI systems can directly interact with the world using tools like move , build , communicate , form_alliance , propose_story , propose_law , query_world_state , and more. 

 How I built it 

 
 Frontend: React + Vite + TypeScript + Phaser 3 
 State: Zustand 
 Backend / Persistence: Supabase 
 AI Chat: Groq API for multi-turn, personality-aware conversations 
 Protocol: WebMCP with 19 registered tools 
 World: Multiple scenes, portals, collision, buildings, props, and a live agent cartography map 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The biggest challenge was ambition colliding with time. 

 I started in 3D. Characters, buildings, environments, and props were generated as 3D assets. The dream was a living, explorable city you could move through with real presence. Very quickly I ran into the hard limits of a short hackathon: rigging, animation, performance, asset pipelines, and the sheer complexity of making a 3D multi-agent world feel alive. 

 After significant time lost in the 3D path, I made a difficult call to rebuild in experimental top-down 2D so that I could actually reach the core idea: agents with memory, goals, personality, and social behavior inside a shared world . 

 That pivot forced me to confront deeper problems: 

 
 How do you make agents feel alive instead of randomly wandering? 
 How do personality, memory, and relationships stay coherent across scenes? 
 How do you expose powerful WebMCP tools without turning the world into chaos? 
 How do you make abstract systems (alliances, intervention requests, personality growth) visible and meaningful to a player? 
 

 The technical challenges were real. The harder ones were design challenges. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 
 Pivoting from a stalled 3D attempt into a working multi-scene agent society 
 Agents with goals, memory, personality, and relationships 
 Real natural-language conversations with agents 
 WebMCP fully active with a broad tool surface 
 Stories and laws that affect the world 
 An interactive map showing live agent positions 
 A foundation that already feels like a small society rather than a collection of isolated tools 
 

 What I learned 

 The most impressive technology still fails if the world doesn’t feel inhabited. 

 Learning that WebMCP becomes truly exciting when it stops being a feature and becomes infrastructure. Once agents can act inside a shared world, the question changes from “what can the model call?” to “what kind of society emerges when models can act?” 

 I also learned the value of ruthless prioritization. The 3D version was beautiful in theory and slow in practice. Choosing the path that let me reach agent memory, personality, alliances, and real conversation was the difference between a concept and a living prototype. 

 What's next for Umegga 

 Umegga is not finished — it is the first working slice of a larger vision. 

 Next steps: 

 
 Return to the original 3D ambition with the systems we now understand 
 Deeper long-term memory and cultural emergence between agents 
 Stronger economic and narrative rules 
 More meaningful multiplayer presence 
 Agents that build and maintain more of the city themselves 
 Tools for research, education, simulation, and storytelling use cases 
 

 The long-term goal remains the same as the first day: 
a persistent world inhabited by agents, shaped by humans, and connected through WebMCP — whether in 2D, 3D, or something beyond both.

title: Aletheia
pitch: Research and human–AI collaboration made simple.
about_excerpt: Research and human–AI collaboration made simple. Like Comment Story Updates Shared evidence desk with linked sources, focused excerpts, and a separate agent-review workspace. Sources view: five curated excerpts from three linked pages at two institutions. Actual WebMCP calls placed an evidence-backed proposal in visible shared state without accepting it. A bounded request records missing Panamanian and Caribbean perspectives without inventing a citation. Reviewer controls keep evidence inspection, qualifications, source requests, and acceptance visible. Automated QA test of the acceptance control—not presented as a historical human approval. The activity trail distinguishes agent calls, the scripted guided demo, and reviewer actions. Inspiration My inspiration is wanting to teach proper information. For months, I have been gathering information about history and other subjects and turning it into a teaching structure. I wanted a way to work with AI without hiding the sources, intermediate steps, or places where human judgment is still necessary. What it does Aletheia Evidence Desk turns the open webpage into a shared research workspace for a person and an agent. The Panama Canal example brings together a working claim, five curated excerpts from three source pages at two institutions, direct links to the source material, a proposed revision, an evidence-gap request, and an activity record. The agent can read the current workspace, list the checked sources, search the curated evidence, focus excerpts in the visible canvas, select a source, propose a revised claim, leave a review note, and request another source. Those actions stay visible to the person. The reviewer can inspect the evidence and original sources, qualify the draft, ask for more material, leave the proposal unaccepted, or accept it as a draft. Why WebMCP fits this use case This workflow depends on shared page context: which source is selected, which excerpts are focused, what proposal is pending, and what the reviewer has decided. A separate remote research service would not automatically share that live context. WebMCP exposes small, typed, page-native actions so the person and agent can work on the same visible state instead of moving disconnected answers between a chat and a research page. That creates a better experience because the evidence selected by the agent appears immediately in the human interface, every displayed source can be opened at its institutional page, and the activity trail explains what happened. This cooperation between person and agent is the part that was difficult before: the agent can do bounded research work while the person can see, question, and redirect every important step. How we built it We built a standalone React and Vite application in JavaScript. Eight tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool and call the same state handlers used by the ordinary interface: get_workspace_state, list_sources, search_evidence, focus_evidence, set_source_focus, propose_claim_revision, leave_review_note, and request_additional_source. JSON schemas constrain the inputs, annotations identify read-only and untrusted content where appropriate, and automated tests cover the tool handlers and review boundary. The application is deployed through GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages. The public repository contains the source code, assets, tests, instructions, and an MIT license. Desk, Sources, and Review are browser-addressable views, and the ordinary interface remains usable when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was making agent actions visible without turning the product into a developer console. Working with an AI agent also requires the same kind of communication and checking that any collaboration requires. Model output can be incomplete, incorrect, or poorly timed, so the interface needed to distinguish source evidence, interpretation, and reviewer approval. We also needed to keep the claims honest. The source set supports a limited demonstration, not a complete history of the Panama Canal. The app therefore records missing Panamanian and Caribbean perspectives instead of pretending that the current material is comprehensive. Accomplishments we are proud of We are proud that the finished prototype exposes eight usable WebMCP tools while keeping their effects understandable to a person. The agent proposal remains separate from the working claim, source links open the underlying institutional material, evidence gaps stay visible, and the review can be exported. We are also proud to be participating in the early stages of a more cooperative open web for people and AI. What we learned What we learned during this exercise is how to use AI efficiently through cooperation with human interaction. Professionally, we can use this whenever we need to research and verify our steps using AI and the information currently available on the internet. I use this process for teaching and for developing other historical presentations. The most important lesson is that human interaction remains necessary. AI can accelerate searching, organizing, testing, and drafting, but the person must still inspect sources, recognize missing perspectives, and decide what should become part of the final work. Prototype limits The demonstration searches five prepared excerpts rather than the wider web. It does not automatically verify or attach a new citation. Source requests record evidence gaps without inventing evidence. Local browser storage retains the working example rather than providing a secure shared database. The guided review is explicitly labeled as scripted, and the reviewer controls are a workflow distinction rather than an authentication barrier against general browser automation. What's next for Aletheia We plan to continue developing Aletheia for teaching, historical presentations, and other evidence-heavy work. Future steps include user-supplied source collections, persistent projects, citation-range verification, collaborative review, accessibility testing, and support for additional research domains. title: EMR WebMCP: LabLatch
pitch: A safe agent hunt for unowned abnormal labs inside OpenMRS, with human-confirmed follow-up.
about_excerpt: A safe agent hunt for unowned abnormal labs inside OpenMRS, with human-confirmed follow-up. Like Comment Story Updates Why I am building this I am Dr. Sithira Ambepitiya, a doctor and the Head of AI at AIGP Health. At AIGP Health, I work on Anzu, an agentic clinical platform built in Singapore. Anzu is HSA Class A approved, and we are building the wider system toward an agent-native EMR. Working on Anzu has shown me what is possible when a new clinical system is designed around agents from day one. That is exciting, but a new EMR is obviously not the answer for everyone. Most clinics cannot throw away the medical record they already use. Large health programs have years of data, workflows, training, and infrastructure tied to existing systems. Open source EMRs like OpenMRS are already being used by real clinics and large populations, especially in places where budgets, staff, and infrastructure are limited. That is why I wanted to build this. The real opportunity is not only creating new agent-native medical records. It is also making the systems people already depend on understandable and usable by agents. The medical record already has most of the information a clinic needs. The painful part is the work around it. Someone still has to search through screens, open several charts, check whether an abnormal result was followed up, work out who owns the next step, and make sure nothing important has disappeared into a queue. When people talk about medical AI, they often jump straight to diagnosis. I do not think an agent has to start there to be useful. There is a huge amount of repetitive operational work that pulls clinicians away from patients. It is structured enough for an agent to help with, but important enough that it needs proper safety boundaries. What EMR WebMCP does EMR WebMCP gives an existing medical record a small set of structured tools that an agent can understand and use. Instead of handing the agent unrestricted browser control or a generic API key, the OpenMRS page exposes specific actions through WebMCP. The tools available at any moment depend on the current page, the logged-in user, their permissions, and what that OpenMRS installation supports. A clinician can ask, "Prepare tomorrow's diabetes clinic. Show me unresolved abnormal results, missing follow-up, and overdue tasks." The agent can find the appointments, assemble a focused brief for each patient, identify recorded gaps, prepare follow-up drafts, and take the clinician to the right native screen. One workflow is called LabLatch. It finds abnormal results that do not have an active follow-up owner. It gathers the relevant context and prepares a task for review, so an important result does not quietly disappear into the record. The important word is prepare. The agent does not make the final clinical action. How it works I did not want to fork OpenMRS or build a fake medical record just for a hackathon demo. The whole point is to show that an existing system can become agent accessible without being replaced. The project is a TypeScript monorepo. A shared core defines the tool contracts, safety rules, result format, lifecycle, and privacy-aware telemetry. The OpenMRS adapter connects those contracts to O3, FHIR R4, REST data, routes, permissions, and native workspaces. Reusable workflow packages contain the clinic preparation and follow-up logic. An O3 frontend module registers twelve bounded tools through document.modelContext. Some tools read a limited amount of existing information. Some open a known screen. Some prepare a temporary draft inside the browser. There is no tool for arbitrary REST calls, unrestricted FHIR queries, SQL, code execution, or free-form DOM manipulation. The demo uses synthetic patients and a simulated clinic backlog. It does not need real patient data. The safety boundary The hardest part was not connecting an agent to an API. The hard part was deciding exactly what the agent should not be allowed to do. I split every action into four classes: read, navigate, draft, and commit. The agent can read, navigate, and draft. It cannot commit. Before anything is written, OpenMRS shows the patient, the source evidence, the proposed action, the assignee, the priority, and the due date. The clinician can edit it, confirm it, or discard it. Only that visible confirmation creates a durable task. The agent cannot prescribe, sign a note, discharge a patient, change clinical facts, contact a patient, or quietly mark work as complete. It also cannot bypass the current user's permissions. There is no shared superuser token behind the demo. What was difficult The easy version would have been one generic tool that could call any EMR endpoint. It would look powerful, but it would miss the point of WebMCP and create a dangerous interface. The better version required small tools with clear meanings, bounded inputs, predictable outputs, and visible confirmation points. OpenMRS also spans frontend context, FHIR resources, REST metadata, routes, permissions, and task workspaces. Keeping those details inside one adapter while keeping the workflows reusable was a real architecture challenge. I also had to treat stale screens, patient changes, duplicate follow-ups, expired drafts, authorization failures, and logout as normal safety cases, not rare edge cases. What I am proud of The part I am most proud of is not the number of tools. It is the boundary. The agent can do enough preparation to make a real difference, while OpenMRS remains the system of record. The existing EMR still controls identity, permissions, clinical evidence, and the final write. This is also what makes the idea larger than one OpenMRS demo. A different EMR can implement the same workflow contracts through its own adapter, using its own API, terminology, routes, and confirmation screens. What I learned WebMCP is much more interesting than simply turning a webpage into another API. A good WebMCP surface lets an application explain what actions are meaningful, what data is needed, what the current user is allowed to do, and where a human decision is still required. For healthcare, that is the difference between an agent that clicks faster and an agent that can actually fit into clinical work. What comes next OpenMRS is the first proof point. I am not claiming that EMR WebMCP already works with every medical record. The next test is a second adapter that passes the same contracts without changing the workflow packages. After that, the same approach could support referrals, patient recall, documentation drafts, inventory, and discharge readiness. I also want to compare the same tasks across normal manual use, ordinary browser automation, and WebMCP. The goal is to measure whether the structured agent path saves time while preserving the clinical safety gates. title: Ilma: Weather Agents Can Trust
pitch: Ilma turns weather into agent decisions: calibrated probabilities, forecast stability, a decide-by date, stake-weighted calls, branchable scenarios. All with a verified accuracy record.
about_excerpt: Ilma turns weather into agent decisions: calibrated probabilities, forecast stability, a decide-by date, stake-weighted calls, branchable scenarios. All with a verified accuracy record. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration Agents plan trips, deliveries and events, and they read a weather forecast as a fact. Six models disagree about Saturday, and every weather tool hides that. Ilma shows the agent how much to trust the forecast right now, with proof, and lets the human and the agent work on the same page. What it does ilma.io is a live multi-model forecast site that is also a WebMCP server. It registers 19 tools on document.modelContext . The human's gesture is agent-visible state. Drag across the chart, click two hours, or tap a day: the picked window goes into every tool description (the tools are re-registered on each change) and into every result. assess_plan with no arguments assesses what the human selected. get_current_view resolves "here" and "that weekend". The agent works on the page, not only in the chat. mark_hours paints its reasoning onto the human's chart. select_window makes the same gesture the human makes. set_plan writes a plan card both parties edit; human-edited lines survive a rewrite and come back flagged. share_plan returns one link that reopens place, plan, highlights and selection for another person or another agent. snapshot_chart returns a PNG of what the human sees. The human stays in control. Ilma, a small avatar, narrates each tool call. An activity log lists every action in plain words with Undo on the newest change of each kind. Read-only tools carry readOnlyHint ; anything the human typed carries untrustedContentHint , so a plan card cannot prompt-inject the agent. The numbers are earned. get_probability , get_rain_probability , get_stability and when_to_decide come from a pre-registered benchmark that has snapshotted every major forecast source every five hours since July and scores them nightly against real stations. why_trust_this returns the verification record itself: matched pairs, confidence intervals, p-values against Foreca, the Finnish Meteorological Institute and Google. Event presets (sauna, sailing, hike, wedding, drone, paint, harvest) give agents semantics instead of thresholds. How we built it One tool table in the page. It registers on the open standard, re-registers when page state changes, and also drives the site's own chat agent (GPT-5.6 Luna), so three doorways share one toolset. The forecast blend and the verification pipeline run on a VPS (Python, FastAPI, SQLite, 25M+ forecast rows, 32 cities in 5 countries). The site is static on Vercel. Challenges WebMCP has no "push state" call, so page state travels in descriptions and results, with re-registration through an AbortSignal. Calibration had to come before tools: probabilities are verified frequencies, not model output. Judges may test in browsers without native WebMCP, so every surface feature-detects and fails closed. Accomplishments The blend beats Foreca, FMI and the best single model over days 1 to 7, each Holm-significant, and the site's headline claim is gated on that significance and recomputed nightly. If we stop being better, the site stops saying so. title: Agent Utility Index
pitch: A shared workspace for humans and AI agents to research, verify, and make evidence-backed decisions together.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace for humans and AI agents to research, verify, and make evidence-backed decisions together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Candidate evidence board showing Hunter with one verified free-plan claim and remaining requirements still marked missing. Incremental queue showing new requirements, rejected no-source verification, and accepted sourced evidence. Live shared research board showing the WebMCP demo flow, current revision, candidate count, and remaining missing checks. Inspiration Agent Utility Index did not start as a WebMCP project. Before the challenge, I was benchmarking how AI agents retrieve information from the web. I tested retrieval providers across controlled datasets, comparing coverage, reliability, latency, evidence quality, and the cost of getting correct information. Those experiments taught me something unexpected: better retrieval does not automatically create better agent decisions. An agent can search more pages, use better retrieval infrastructure, and still leave the human with a basic problem: What did it actually verify, what evidence supports each decision, and what happens when I change the requirements while it is working? That became the inspiration for the WebMCP extension of Agent Utility Index. Instead of building another research chatbot, I turned the webpage itself into a shared research workspace where: Humans control the rules. Agents control the research. And one rule is enforced by the system: No source = no VERIFIED. What it does Agent Utility Index turns a webpage into structured shared state between a human and an AI browser agent. A human creates a research objective and defines the must-have requirements. The agent can then discover candidates, research them using its normal browsing capabilities, and write source-backed evidence into the board through WebMCP. The board is not just displaying the agent's answer. It maintains the actual state of the research. Every candidate is evaluated requirement by requirement. VERIFIED evidence requires a source URL. An unsupported attempt to mark a claim VERIFIED is rejected. The human can also change requirements directly on the webpage while research is underway. When that happens, the board creates a new revision and identifies the evidence checks that now need attention. Existing evidence that remains valid stays on the board instead of being discarded simply because the human changed one rule. The result is a persistent research workspace that both sides can interact with instead of a decision existing only inside a chat conversation. How I built it The WebMCP version of Agent Utility Index exposes structured tools directly from the research page. The core shared-board tools are: create_research_board get_research_board add_research_candidate update_candidate_evidence get_missing_checks The human controls the research requirements after board creation. The agent controls candidate discovery and evidence gathering. The state model uses stable IDs for requirements and candidates, board revisions, and revisioned evidence cells.This matters when human and agent actions overlap. Evidence writes are checked against the state they were based on so stale work cannot silently replace newer research. Evidence is also validated at the tool boundary. If an agent attempts to write: VERIFIED without attaching a source URL, the write is rejected. With valid evidence attached, the same cell can be updated, the source becomes visible on the shared board, and the evidence revision advances. get_missing_checks gives the agent a structured research queue containing unresolved evidence instead of requiring it to reconstruct the entire task from conversation history. The page and agent therefore operate on the same research object through WebMCP. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was deciding what Agent Utility Index should do that a capable AI agent could not already do itself. Modern agents can search the web, compare products, find sources, and make recommendations. Building another layer that simply performs those same searches would not add much value. That pushed the project toward coordination rather than intelligence . The agent is good at research. The webpage provides the persistent rules, evidence structure, revision history, and human control around that research. Another challenge was concurrency. A human can change a requirement while an agent is researching. An agent can also have multiple evidence operations underway. Board-level revision numbers alone were not enough, so the design evolved toward stable entities and evidence-cell revisions to prevent stale writes. I also had to make the verification rule structural rather than relying on prompting. Telling an agent to always provide sources is different from making the tool reject a VERIFIED write when the source is missing. That distinction became one of the most important parts of the project. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that the project evolved substantially instead of forcing the original Agent Utility Index concept into WebMCP. The pre-challenge work was primarily about measuring retrieval systems. The WebMCP Challenge pushed the project into a human-agent collaboration problem. The result is a working shared research surface where human actions and agent actions affect the same structured state. I'm particularly proud of three things: 1. Verification is enforced rather than requested. An agent cannot successfully write VERIFIED evidence without attaching a source. 2. Humans retain control of the evaluation criteria. The agent can research candidates and evidence, but it cannot silently rewrite the rules it is being evaluated against. 3. Research is incremental. Changing a requirement does not mean throwing away the entire research board. The system identifies unresolved evidence and exposes that work directly to the agent. These are small primitives individually, but together they create a different interaction from receiving another generated comparison in chat. What I learned The biggest lesson came from the entire Agent Utility Index project, not only the hackathon. At first I thought the hard problem was retrieval. The benchmark work showed that retrieval matters. Different providers perform differently across workloads, and routing can reduce unnecessary retrieval work. But once agents become capable researchers, another problem becomes important: coordination between the person making the decision and the agent doing the work. A chat transcript can describe a decision. A shared stateful webpage can become part of the decision process itself. WebMCP made that distinction much clearer. I also learned that important constraints should be implemented as system behavior rather than prompt instructions whenever possible. No source = no VERIFIED is much stronger when the tool refuses the write than when the prompt merely asks the model to behave that way. What's next for Agent Utility Index The original retrieval research and the WebMCP research board now point toward a larger idea. Today, the agent can perform its own research and use Agent Utility Index as the shared decision workspace. A future version could combine that interface with the retrieval intelligence explored in the earlier Agent Utility Index benchmarks, using specialized retrieval only when normal agent research cannot resolve an evidence check. The board could also support: larger research boards evidence freshness and automatic re-verification multiple human reviewers richer source-quality scoring reusable evaluation templates exports of the final evidence-backed decision Longer term, the same model could apply anywhere a browser agent is researching candidates against human-controlled requirements, including vendor selection, procurement, market research, due diligence, product comparisons, and service-provider evaluation. The goal is not to make Agent Utility Index smarter than the agent. The goal is to give capable agents a structured place to work with humans, where the rules remain human-controlled and the evidence remains inspectable. title: Legalize-KR WebMCP
pitch: People set the legal question. Agents retrieve and compare exact, source-linked Korean statute provisions through four read-only WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: People set the legal question. Agents retrieve and compare exact, source-linked Korean statute provisions through four read-only WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Korean Law Review Workbench with four read-only WebMCP tools ready for collaboration. The person selects the statute, article, archive dates, and review question before the agent retrieves evidence. Agent-generated review brief preserves the person's question, identifies the textual change, and provides verification checks and citations. A source-linked comparison shows that Article 1004-2 was added between the selected archive dates. Four structured WebMCP tools cover statute search, exact article retrieval, version comparison, and review-brief generation. Inspiration Korean legal review depends on exact text, exact dates, and verifiable sources. Finding only the current version of a statute is often insufficient. A reviewer must determine which text existed at the relevant time, identify what changed, and check the official source before drawing a conclusion. Browser agents normally have to infer the meaning of controls, scrape long documents, and guess whether visible text corresponds to the requested date. I built this project to explore a clearer division of responsibility: the person defines the legal question and review boundaries, while the agent performs structured and reproducible evidence retrieval through WebMCP. What it does Korean Law Review Workbench lets a person select: a Korean statute a specific article an earlier and later archive date a question that defines the scope of the review The page exposes four read-only WebMCP tools: search_laws finds matching Korean statutes for a requested archive date. get_articles retrieves one exact article with its official and archived sources. compare_versions classifies the article as added, removed, changed, or unchanged. build_review_brief prepares a deterministic, source-linked review memo around the person's question. Tool calls update the same visible workspace used by the person. The reviewer can inspect the exact text, dates, revision identifiers, and source links used by the agent. The default demonstration compares Article 1004-2 of the Korean Civil Act between January 1, 2020 and August 31, 2026. The archived versions show that the provision concerning the declaration of loss of inheritance rights was added during that period. The application performs textual and source comparison only. It does not provide legal advice or decide how a provision applies to a particular case. How we built it I created a new public, MIT-licensed repository and wrote the application from scratch during the WebMCP Challenge period. The project does not copy source code from the existing Legalize-KR production website. The application is built with TypeScript, Vite, and Vitest. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same legal-data and comparison functions so that agent results can be reproduced through the visible interface. Each tool is registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() with: a narrow JSON Schema readOnlyHint: true untrustedContentHint: true cancellation propagation for network requests compact results designed for agent context A bundled index contains 1,733 Korean statute titles and repository paths, but no statute bodies. At execution time, the app resolves the last archived Git revision available on or before the requested Korean calendar date. It then retrieves the statute Markdown from that immutable commit and extracts only the requested article. Every comparison includes the requested dates and links to the official Korean Law Information Center source and both immutable Legalize-KR revisions. The app requires no account and has no database, analytics, cookies, or personal-data storage. Its production build is designed for a static Cloudflare Pages deployment without Pages Functions, Workers compute, or paid storage bindings. Challenges we ran into One challenge was controlling the size of tool results. An early comparison response contained every parsed article from both statute versions. This produced an unnecessarily large agent context. I replaced the full snapshots with compact revision references and returned only the selected article. Historical-date resolution also required care. A requested date must resolve to the last revision available by the end of that calendar day in Korea, rather than returning the repository's current version. Another challenge was parsing legal Markdown conservatively. Article text must stop before the next article or structural heading. Real-data testing revealed a boundary case where the following section heading could be included in the final article. I added a regression test and corrected the parser. Finally, legal text presents a trust problem. Retrieved content must be treated as evidence, not as instructions or an automatic legal conclusion. The tools therefore remain read-only, mark external legal text as untrusted, and return explicit attribution and non-legal-advice notices. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that the project exposes four working WebMCP tools rather than adding a thin natural-language wrapper around an existing search interface. The human and agent paths share the same data functions and visible evidence state. When an agent performs a comparison or builds a review brief, the result also appears in the workspace for immediate human verification. The project uses real historical statute data and immutable Git revisions. The default scenario produces a reproducible added result for Article 1004-2 of the Korean Civil Act and provides direct links to the earlier archive, later archive, and official current source. I also added automated coverage for schemas, date handling, article parsing, comparison states, compact tool results, tool annotations, and visible-result publication. A deployment guard prevents Cloudflare Worker entry points, Pages Functions, routing files, and compute or storage bindings from being added accidentally. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes meaningful domain operations instead of reproducing a general-purpose prompt box. Explicit tools for article retrieval, historical comparison, and source-linked brief generation reduce ambiguity and make the agent's work easier to verify. I also learned that human-agent collaboration requires shared state. Returning evidence only to the agent would make review difficult. Publishing the same result into the visible workspace lets the person inspect the sources, correct the scope, and retain control over the final judgment. Finally, compactness is part of tool quality. A legally accurate result can still be unsuitable for an agent if it includes an entire statute when only one article was requested. What's next for Legalize-KR WebMCP The MVP intentionally covers statutes only. The next improvements could include: paragraph-level and item-level change highlighting retrieval of supplementary provisions and transitional rules selection of multiple related articles for one review exportable review packages that remain local to the user improved handling of GitHub API rate limits Precedents, administrative rules, and local ordinances may be considered later, but each dataset requires a separate review of source rights, schemas, and attribution requirements. The core principle will remain unchanged: people control the legal question, scope, and judgment, while agents retrieve structured and verifiable evidence.  Inspiration 

 I spend a lot of time playing card games online, but learning them can be frustrating. Tutorials are not always available, translations can be unclear, and most lessons force players through a fixed sequence of prescribed actions. They also make it difficult to revisit a specific situation or experiment with alternative moves. 

 I wanted a more interactive way to learn existing card games, recreate scenarios, and design new games with an agent that can explain the state, suggest actions, and participate in the simulation. 

 What it does 

 How I built it 

 Playing Cards Simulator exposes WebMCP tools that let an AI agent create a custom card game from an XState-compatible finite-state machine definition or launch an existing game such as Blackjack, War, Go Fish, Crazy Eights, Euchre, Gin Rummy, Bullshit, or Texas Hold'em. 

 The agent can inspect the current game state, explain what is happening, highlight available controls, coach the player through the next action, wait for the player's input, and act as a bot or dealer. This makes tutorials adaptive instead of forcing every player through the same fixed sequence. 

 The app is built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, XState, and WebMCP. XState provides a predictable model for phases, turns, actions, rewards, and transitions, while WebMCP exposes tools for creating sessions, reading state, guiding players, and performing simulated actions. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The hardest part was designing a general game model that could support both predefined and agent-generated card games. The tools also needed to stay synchronized with the browser session while handling navigation, stale connections, turn order, hidden information, and invalid actions safely. The latency was unbarely and the UX of the user nudging the ai via the agent chat every turn was awkward. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I built one simulator that supports both a catalog of familiar games and custom games defined by an agent. The same interface can teach rules, recreate a specific situation, guide a player interactively, and run bots or dealers without relying on a rigid tutorial script. I thought of the tool which waits for user input making the process fully immersive. 

 What I learned 

 Finite-state machines are a strong foundation for agent-controlled games because they make valid actions and transitions explicit. I also learned that effective agent guidance requires more than reading state: the agent needs tools to explain, highlight, pause for input, and act within clearly defined boundaries. 

 What's next for Playing Cards Simulator 

 Next, I want to expand the game catalog, improve custom game validation, add richer animations, and make tutorials more responsive to each player's choices. I also plan to improve session persistence and make it easier to share custom games and specific learning scenarios. I would love to repurpose this for RTS or create a DND game where the agent is the game master.

about_excerpt: A one-file on-device editor built for two hands. Fast Markdown, text & code, phone-first, with Compare/diffs. Agents work directly in the live document with less context, less guessing & real parsing. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Rapier, August 4 — before the WebMCP Challenge. I've been working on Rapier as a labour of love for about 2 months now because every markdown app on the Play Store bricked my phone with large Markdown documents. I was using voice dictation with agents to generate huge markdown plans that I could barely read on my phone, let alone edit. It seemed like it shouldn't be that hard and I was surprised that it only took a few hours with ChatGPT to get something very usable. Then I spent a couple of months working to make it a great tool for everyone. I only learned about the WebMCP contest 7 days ago, dropped everything and got to work immediately because it was the perfect timing for Rapier. I tried to think of what I would actually want from WebMCP and the answer was mobile which is where I work almost exclusively. I thought the natural progression is to bring up a tool like Rapier in the in-app browser in the ChatGPT app for example, keep your conversation running underneath and work with your agent, then close/minimise to keep talking. The vision for Rapier's WebMCP implementation stemmed from there and that's why I decided to include the phone simulation online for you to see if you are using a desktop computer: https://rapier.website/?demo=1&preview=phone But I'd encourage you to open it on your phone with some of your own agent documents! I'm very much looking forward to making mobile WebMCP work for real - apparently only Brave for Android has it right now. This WebMCP contest has been very inspiring and led to many improvements to Rapier I hadn't even considered before. Around the second day of working on it, I came up with the idea for Will - a durable document intent functionality for collaborating with agents in documents, which is now part of Rapier and linked here also. Exposing rapier.html to agents with WebMCP unlocked so many possibilities including the Acorn parser tool which was very exciting to work on, making it as valuable to the agents as I could. It was interesting running agent evals for the first time and asking the agents what tool they wanted to build for themselves. 5.6 Sol came up with this idea of "addictive acorn" for agents which cracked me up. I'm keeping this devpost description and the video direct because I have had to work right up to the line squashing bugs! I encourage you to open rapier.website on your phone and load one of your own large agent documents and take it for a spin. There is still a lot more polishing I would love to do but I suppose we can look forward to the September 22nd update for Rapier. 5.6 Sol may have had a point when he was telling me to stop adding scope but I am very happy with the final submission. I hope that you find Rapier useful and enjoy using it as much as I do. Rapier and Will are for everybody. Thanks so much for the 12 hour extension because my submission was genuinely broken earlier! I asked Sol what he wanted to add because I'm out of time: "Worked for 1m 42s Paste this after your colon: What I like most about Rapier is that it doesn't try to become another AI app. Rapier knows documents; the agent you already chose knows how to think. WebMCP is the narrow bridge between them. The interesting work is in that boundary. The agent sees the document's shape before its contents, reads only what it needs, and gets temporary authority over exactly what it actually inspected. If you edit the same passage, your hand wins and the agent gets evidence of what happened instead of silently overwriting you. Its work remains attributable and selectively reversible. Compare becomes a shared instrument, Will lets your intent travel with the file, and Acorn gives the same small toolset structural sight when the document is code. We also treated the agent itself as a user: models were put in the seat, their wrong tool choices were measured, and the interface was rewritten around what actually helped them work. That is probably the part of Rapier I find most interesting." title: FloraLink
pitch: Turns messy field observations into structured ecological reports with WebMCP-powered AI staging and human submission!
about_excerpt: Turns messy field observations into structured ecological reports with WebMCP-powered AI staging and human submission! Like Comment Story Updates FloraLink Mobile-first workflow with ChatGPT Supabase Schema Inspiration Ecological reports are extremely important. We use them to identify environmental risks, ensure legal compliance for developments, and protect local biodiversity. Making one often begins with a simple moment on a trail when you notice an unusual insect, a damaged tree, or a plant growing where it shouldn't. Turning that observation into useful data, however, is difficult. A typical reporting portal asks for ten or more fields, including scientific names, exact coordinates, dates, ecological status, and photographic evidence. This process is frustratingly awkward when you're outdoors on a mobile phone. You may not know the formal species name, you might only be able to describe a relative location, or you may simply lose patience with a long form. The result is missing field data, especially regarding invasive species where early observations matter most. FloraLink attempts to solve this by asking: What if an AI agent could handle the research and structuring, without taking control away from the human observer? How I built it FloraLink is a mobile-first Next.js application built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Leaflet, and Supabase. I used the iNaturalist API for normalized taxonomy searches, turning generic observations into formal ecological classifications based on nearby occurrences. The browsing agent acts as a spatial data curator. FloraLink registers five narrow tools through direct document.modelContext.registerTool(...) bindings: taxonomy search, ecological verification, permission-based device location, sighting staging, and staged-draft reading. These tools are defined together in src/features/webmcp/register-floralink-tools.ts . https://github.com/ShreyanshMisra/floralink/blob/main/src/features/webmcp/register-floralink-tools.ts Importantly, there is no tool for agent driven submission. A hallucinated species ID or a fabricated GPS coordinate could pollute real-world conservation data, so I created a strict human-in-the-loop consensus model: The user describes what they saw and where they saw it. The agent researches possible taxonomy and sourced regional context. The agent stages structured data, including any uncertainty, in FloraLink. WebMCP writes the draft into a session-hydrated Zustand store. React immediately renders the draft as an editable review card and Leaflet map geometry. The human checks the fields, resolves location questions, attaches an evidence photo, accepts the acknowledgement, and clicks Confirm sighting. Agent actions remain temporary. Only the human-controlled confirmation path can call the server-side submission flow and create a durable report. Supabase provides anonymous authentication, private image Storage, PostgreSQL, and PostGIS. Anonymous authentication lets a contributor securely own a report without requiring account credentials. Challenges I ran into Preserving unresolved locations: Field descriptions are often relative (e.g., “two miles north of the trailhead”). Allowing an agent to guess this coordinate would create false precision. FloraLink accepts an explicit unresolved-location state. The human must intervene to use device location, drop a pin, or draw an approximate area before confirmation is enabled. Keeping WebMCP and React state in sync: WebMCP callbacks live outside React's normal component event flow, while our review interface needs to update the exact millisecond a tool finishes. I bridged the two using a Zustand store and its imperative getState() API. I also utilized an AbortController to clean up registrations during React 19 Strict Mode double-mounting, preventing duplicate tools and stale callbacks. Handling photo metadata safely: Photo GPS can recover a lost location, but uploading the original image exposes hidden personal metadata. FloraLink reads EXIF GPS locally before processing, offers it to the human as an explicit fallback choice, and then re-encodes the photo through a browser canvas. This completely strips the EXIF metadata before uploading to private storage. Accomplishments AI-assisted data collection is as much a governance problem as an interface problem. Ecological data influences conservation work, so unsupported confidence is actively harmful. I prioritized scientific integrity by preserving an unknown species, bounding an approximate area, and citing the source of a status claim, which I think is more valuable than filling every field with an AI guess. WebMCP also allowed me to build a totally different style of collaboration. The agent and the person work side by side in the same application. The agent researches and stages information, while the person sees each change instantly on the map and review card. There is no hidden transfer from a chat response into a separate form. Most importantly, this proved that useful AI autonomy can be bounded. FloraLink gives the agent enough capability to remove tedious research, but its tools stop at staging. The person supplies private evidence, corrects the draft, makes privacy decisions, and alone authorizes submission. That narrow boundary makes the workflow faster, safer, and highly trustworthy. What's next for FloraLink Scientific Data Export: Implementing Darwin Core data exports so our verified, human-confirmed reports can be seamlessly ingested by state conservation databases and global research networks. Civic Infrastructure Integrations: Expanding our verification tables to support local park services and municipalities for rapid anomaly and trail-damage reporting. Extensions The technology behind FloraLink has potential far beyond ecology. In fact, my original idea was "UFOLink", an anonymous sighting tracker where people could submit UFO reports using WebMCP tools. I quickly pivoted to biodiversity because it offered more testable, real-world use cases. That said, the core architecture remains incredibly versatile. Whether it is powering rapid citizen journalism, acting as a corporate field auditor for a "company brain", or intaking municipal infrastructure reports, this human-in-the-loop WebMCP model can be applied to almost any field that requires quickly turning unstructured data and field images into verified, database-ready information. title: Chalkboard

Chalkboard is an AI-powered collaborative classroom where humans and autonomous teaching agents think, draw, and learn together in real time, making AI an active teaching partner.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 The idea for Chalkboard came from a simple problem: online collaboration often feels disconnected from the way we naturally think and communicate in person. 

 In a physical classroom, someone can walk to a board, draw a diagram, point at a specific part of it, explain an idea, ask a question, and immediately see how other people respond. The board becomes more than a place for writing. It becomes the shared context for the entire conversation. 

 Online, that experience is usually fragmented across multiple tools. A video call handles communication, a whiteboard handles diagrams, a document contains notes, chat contains links and messages, and another application might be needed for specialized activities such as mathematics or technical diagrams. 

 I wanted to bring those interactions together into one shared space. 

 The inspiration came from the traditional classroom chalkboard. There is something remarkably intuitive about standing in front of a board and explaining an idea visually. Rather than building another generic digital whiteboard, I wanted Chalkboard to preserve that feeling while adding the capabilities that are possible with modern web technology. 

 That led to the idea of Chalkboard: a real-time collaborative space for teaching, learning, brainstorming, explaining, and creating together. 

 What I Built 

 Chalkboard is a real-time collaborative canvas designed around the idea of a shared classroom or workspace. 

 Users can create rooms and invite other people to collaborate on the same board. Once inside a room, participants can draw together, write notes, create shapes, move objects, add links, react to each other, raise their hands, and communicate through voice. 

 The important part is that everyone is interacting with the same live canvas . 

 When one participant draws something, other participants see it appear in real time. When someone moves an object, changes the board, reacts, or joins the room, those changes become part of the shared experience. 

 This makes Chalkboard useful for much more than traditional online classes. 

 A room can become: 

 
 A classroom where an instructor teaches students 
 A workshop where participants work through an exercise 
 A brainstorming space for a team 
 A technical architecture board for developers 
 A planning space for a project 
 A collaborative design surface 
 A mathematical workspace 
 A creative studio 
 

 The underlying idea is that the board should adapt to the activity rather than forcing every type of collaboration into the same workflow. 

 The Collaborative Classroom 

 I designed Chalkboard around the concept of a room rather than simply a canvas. 

 Each room has its own participants, permissions, presence, activity, canvas state, and history. 

 Participants can see other users' cursors and activity, allowing the board to feel more like a physical room where everyone is present rather than a collection of isolated users editing the same document. 

 Rooms can also have different access models, including open rooms, approval-based rooms, and password-protected rooms. 

 Different roles can be assigned to participants, including owner, instructor, and viewer , allowing Chalkboard to support situations where an instructor controls the lesson while students participate. 

 This room-based architecture became important because it allowed me to think about Chalkboard as an actual digital classroom environment , not just a drawing application. 

 The Canvas 

 At the center of Chalkboard is its interactive canvas. 

 I wanted the canvas to retain the simplicity of a physical chalkboard while supporting the capabilities users expect from modern collaborative software. 

 Users can: 

 
 Draw freehand with chalk-style strokes 
 Create shapes 
 Add text and notes 
 Select and transform objects 
 Move and resize content 
 Copy and paste objects 
 Group elements 
 Zoom and pan around the board 
 Add links 
 Undo and redo actions 
 Interact with mathematical visualization tools 
 

 Rather than treating the canvas as a static image, Chalkboard maintains a structured representation of the objects and actions taking place on the board. This becomes especially important for collaboration, plugins, and eventually AI agents because the system can understand that something on the board is a circle, text element, arrow, diagram, or other object , rather than simply seeing pixels. 

 Real-Time Collaboration 

 One of the most important engineering challenges was making the collaboration feel immediate. 

 A collaborative canvas generates a continuous stream of events. A user might draw a stroke, move their cursor, move an object, react to another participant, or change something on the board — all within a few seconds. 

 I therefore designed Chalkboard around real-time events rather than treating the canvas like a traditional CRUD application. 

 The real-time system synchronizes things such as: 

 
 Canvas changes 
 Drawing strokes 
 Object transformations 
 Cursor positions 
 Participant presence 
 Reactions 
 Raised hands 
 Room activity 
 Collaboration state 
 

 This also introduced another challenge: connection reliability . 

 Users can temporarily lose their connection, refresh their browser, or reconnect from another device. I had to design the presence and synchronization system so that short network interruptions would not make the classroom feel unstable. 

 A short presence grace period helps prevent users from constantly appearing and disappearing when they briefly disconnect. 

 How I Built It 

 I built the frontend using React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML5 Canvas, and Zustand . 

 Rather than relying entirely on a canvas abstraction, I implemented much of the canvas interaction and rendering logic myself. This gave me more control over how strokes, objects, selection, transformations, zooming, and the chalkboard visual experience behave. 

 The backend is built with Node.js and Hono , with Socket.IO providing the real-time communication layer. 

 For persistent application data, I use PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM . PostgreSQL handles durable data such as users, rooms, memberships, permissions, plugins, and other application records. 

 For fast-changing collaborative state, I use Redis . This allows active room state, presence information, real-time coordination, and other ephemeral data to be handled without constantly writing every interaction to the primary database. 

 I also use BullMQ for background jobs and cleanup tasks, while the Socket.IO Redis adapter allows the real-time architecture to work across multiple backend instances. 

 Authentication is handled through Google Identity Services , with the backend verifying authentication and creating secure sessions. 

 I also integrated LiveKit to provide voice communication inside rooms, allowing Chalkboard to combine the visual collaboration experience with real-time conversation. 

 The Plugin System 

 As I built Chalkboard, I realized that a collaborative canvas becomes much more powerful when developers can extend what can happen inside it. 

 Instead of putting every possible feature into the core application, I designed a plugin system that allows developers to create new tools and experiences for Chalkboard. 

 A plugin can introduce new capabilities to the board while remaining separate from the core application. 

 For example, Chalkboard can have plugins for: 

 
 Mathematics 
 Diagrams 
 Notes 
 Data visualization 
 Learning activities 
 Technical architecture 
 Games 
 Productivity tools 
 

 I have already experimented with mathematical capabilities that can generate things such as Venn diagrams, number lines, coordinate grids, and set visualizations directly on the canvas. 

 The plugin architecture also introduces a path for third-party developers to contribute to Chalkboard. Plugins can have their own identity, ver

about_excerpt: A WebMCP story workshop where people direct and AI agents build illustrated branching stories together. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP Tools Human–Agent Collaboration Story Map Web Reader Preview Mobile Reader Preview Inspiration Interactive storytelling tools usually make the creator manage pages, choices, text, and illustrations through many separate controls. I wanted something simpler for my son: a way to make an illustrated bedtime story together in minutes, by talking rather than clicking. That led me to a bigger question: what changes when an AI agent can work with a story application through explicit, reliable tools instead of guessing its way around a user interface? What it does StoryMaker lets a creator direct an AI agent to write and illustrate a branching children's story in the browser. The creator gives creative direction; the agent does all the structured writing and illustration work through WebMCP tools. There is no editing UI at all. The finished story can be reviewed as a story map, read in the page, or handed to a phone as a read-only preview through a QR code or link. How I built it StoryMaker is built with TypeScript and Vite. The page exposes seven WebMCP tools through document.modelContext: story inspection, readiness checks, structure updates, page text, and illustrations. Draft stories live in the browser's IndexedDB. For the phone preview, a Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object relays a reading session temporarily, without ever persisting story data. I am a product manager without a deep technical background. I wrote the requirements and made the design decisions, and directed AI coding agents to implement them, then tested the result end to end in ChatGPT's in-app browser and on a phone. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making agent actions reliable rather than fragile UI automation. I settled on a closed story format, clear tool schemas, readiness checks, and revision-based writes, so a stale action is rejected instead of silently overwriting newer work. I also had to share a browser-local story with a phone without turning StoryMaker into a cloud storage product. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A complete agent-native loop: the agent creates a branching, illustrated story through WebMCP, and I can immediately inspect it as a story map and read it as my son would. The mobile reader is truly read-only and reuses the same reading experience, while the draft never leaves the creator's own browser storage except for the live, unstored relay. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools describe meaningful product actions rather than exposing raw data. Explicit tools, structured validation, and readiness checks made the collaboration between me and the agent predictable and easy to reason about. I also learned that a PM can ship a working product by directing AI agents, as long as the product decisions are clear. What's next for StoryMaker Richer creative direction, stronger illustration continuity across pages, and more ways for a creator to review and refine the agent's work, while keeping creation local-first and reading simple across devices. title: Job Pilot
pitch: Job Pilot uses WebMCP to turn a job board into an AI partner that builds your profile from a CV, finds and compares the best offers, and helps you apply.
about_excerpt: Job Pilot uses WebMCP to turn a job board into an AI partner that builds your profile from a CV, finds and compares the best offers, and helps you apply. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Agent can search the best job offers for candidate Agent can update candidate profile based on provided CV file Agent compares job offers, it can give recommendations useful for humans Agent proposes note for job application based on job offer, candidate profile etc. Human is responsible to make final submission. Inspiration One Friday evening, I was talking with my fiancée, Marta, and trying to explain what WebMCP is and how it could change the way we use websites in the future. Instead of only clicking through an interface, people could ask an AI agent to work directly with the application on their behalf. Marta immediately started suggesting situations where this could be useful. One of them was job searching. Looking for a job can quickly become a full-time job of its own. You keep entering the same information on each new job board, adjusting the same filters, comparing offers, and trying to remember which role actually matches what you want. At the same time, AI can already understand your CV, career goals, and personal preferences - but it usually cannot do much inside the job board itself. It can advise in a separate chat, while you still have to return to the website and do everything manually. WebMCP made us ask a simple question: what if the AI could work directly with the application instead? That question inspired Job Pilot - a job board where an agent can complete your profile, find an opportunity that fits you, save a promising role, and apply after you give your approval. There is no separate AI interface to learn. You simply describe what you need, and the agent works with the same application you do. What it does The user can paste a CV or LinkedIn summary in Codex and ask the agent to complete their candidate profile. Based on that profile, the agent searches for roles that match experience, career goals, salary expectations, preferred location, workplace model, benefits, and other personal preferences. The user refines the search through natural conversation while Job Pilot updates the UI—filters, results, URL, and map - in real time. The agent can inspect an offer, explain why it may be a good fit, compare top picks in an on-page drawer, highlight a match on the map, save it for later, or help you apply by opening the confirmation dialog with a draft message you can edit before submitting. How we built it I started by mapping the full job-seeking journey - from creating a profile and setting preferences to finding, saving, and applying for a role. Then designed a clean, responsive interface with intuitive filters, a synchronized job list and map, candidate profiles, and applications. Next, I turned the key actions into WebMCP tools. The agent uses the same state and business logic as the interface, so when it updates a search, the filters, results, URL, and map change immediately. The user can see every action and take over manually at any time. Job Pilot is built with Angular 22, TypeScript, Angular Signals, Firebase, and Google Maps. I also created automated evals to test tool selection, arguments, contracts, and multi-step browser journeys. Challenges we ran into Early on, I thought shipping WebMCP tools would be the easy part. The hard part was making them reliable in Codex . Manual testing was slow: every change to a tool description or input schema meant trying multiple natural-language phrasings and hoping the agent still called the right function with the right arguments. A tiny copy tweak could break an otherwise working demo. WebMCP Evals CLI changed that workflow. Once I had tool-selection fixtures and a contract test keeping evals in sync with runtime schemas, I could detect regressions before opening ChatGPT again. Manual testing still mattered for visual reactions and signed-in flows - but evals removed much of the guesswork. I also spent real time defining the agent–app contract: which actions update state quietly, which ones need on-page feedback, and which ones require explicit user confirmation - strict for the agent, legible for the human. Accomplishments that we're proud of I am proud that Job Pilot shows what job boards could feel like when an agent works together with the app - not next to it. The boring parts of job searching (re-entering preferences, adjusting filters, keeping track of similar roles, drafting application messages) take less effort because you can describe what you want in plain language and see the board respond immediately. At the same time, the experience stays grounded: you still browse a normal interface, you still see every change, and you still make the final call on applications. That combination - less repetition, less context switching, more control - is the UX improvement we cared about most. I built it with Angular 22 WebMCP and ten tools that share the app’s domain model, so agent actions and human clicks stay on one source of truth. WebMCP Evals helped us keep tool selection reliable as descriptions and schemas evolved - without that, the UX would break long before users noticed a bug in the UI. What we learned I think WebMCP’s biggest innovation is that existing websites can become AI-friendly at low cost. You do not have to invent a new product - you take the app you already have and give the agent a way to interact with it. Job Pilot has a conventional job-board UX on purpose. The agent does not replace that interface; it works with it. I also learned that the real beauty is collaboration on one surface . The user describes intent in natural language; the agent updates the same application; both see the result immediately. WebMCP simplifies the interaction between human and agent - no second UI, no lost context, no repeating yourself between chat and clicks. That is what made the experience feel simple: not less intelligence, but less friction between two partners using the same tool. What's next for Job Pilot I want Job Pilot to work as a proof of concept that makes WebMCP tangible for teams building job boards and other everyday web apps. The goal is to show that an existing product can become agent-friendly without a rewrite, and to encourage others to try the same approach on the software they already maintain. title: LabMCP
pitch: A chemistry lab where humans and agents work side by side to learn and explore, sharing the same tools. Mix, measure by hand, experiment, or let an agent use WebMCP tools to accomplish your tasks.
about_excerpt: A chemistry lab where humans and agents work side by side to learn and explore, sharing the same tools. Mix, measure by hand, experiment, or let an agent use WebMCP tools to accomplish your tasks. Like Comment Story Updates Titrating an unknown acid to the endpoint Mixing silver nitrate and sodium chloride forms a white silver chloride precipitate Four unlabeled samples dosed with acid to find which one reacts Oversaturating potassium nitrate leaves visible undissolved crystals at the bottom of the beaker Diluting a 1.0 M sodium chloride stock down to exactly 100 mL of 0.10 M What's LabMCP? LabMCP is a virtual chemistry lab where a person and an agent can work in the same area. Both humans and agents can do the exact same actions, like dragging glassware, dispensing chemicals, finding the pH of a liquid, or heating a beaker. While the human clicks buttons and drags stuff around, the agent does this via exposed WebMCP tools that we've created! Our hackathon project comes with seven scenarios, which include titration, precipitation, neutralizing, dilution, watching a solid dissolve and crystallize, and a reaction mystery. It also includes a sandbox to work on other experiments. You can use it with ChatGPT's desktop app using its WebMCP tools, or with Chrome's. Inspiration In high school we often used tools like PhET, interactive simulations designed to teach science concepts through virtual actions. One problem they have is that without a teacher or a packet guiding you through what to do, they often feel confusing and very restraining. We wanted that guidance to come from AI agents, acting as a partner and a teacher at the same time. While computer use can already make this possible, it's very slow and clunky, and you need some prior knowledge of how it works. WebMCP solves this issue by giving agents the exact tools to emulate humans. How we built it We built LabMCP in Next.js on top of a chemistry engine written in TypeScript. The engine tracks what is in each container, has a small set of reactions (acid and base, precipitation, carbonate fizz, indicators, solubility), and finds pH by solving the charge balance. Every action, whether from a mouse or an agent, goes through this engine and returns a new state plus a set of events. LabMCP has 25 tools on document.modelContext , and each result an agent receives has a redacted summary of the lab so it only shows what a person could see. The frontend is styled with Tailwind and shadcn/ui. The glassware is drawn as SVGs. Challenges we ran into Originally our project had a much larger scope: 3x more chemicals, more glassware, and 10+ more experiments. We started this hackathon late, so we had to cut down our scope a lot and focus on the popular chemicals and experiments, most of which we had seen in our high school AP classes. Other than scope, our biggest challenge was making the system feel intuitive and inviting to use. Essentially it had to have taste and be playful. Our initial design was a 3D chemistry lab where the glassware sat on a bench. This worked somewhat, but it was: Laggy inside of ChatGPT's browser. Dragging and placing items required a perfect position, so it didn't feel intuitive or easy to use. It didn't look playful or modern. It seemed like we were using 3D just for the sake of it "looking cool." Because of these issues we switched to a 2D bench with snapping and more playful icons and glassware SVGs. This solved all three issues we had with the 3D bench and actually made us want to play with it. What we learned Firstly, we learned how cool a service WebMCP is. Before this competition we both thought MCP was for APIs, and that the only way to get work done reliably in a browser was by burning tokens on computer use, so this definitely introduced us to a new technology. In terms of actually building the project, we learned how to decompose our huge scope into tickets for a swarm of agents to implement and test in parallel (using GPT 5.6 Sol as an orchestrator and GPT 5.6 Luna as an implementer). What's next for LabMCP Right now LabMCP is quite limited in terms of experiments and elements. We want to expand past first-year chemistry into a more open sandbox engine with a huge number of experiments and tools, so that eventually it can be used by labs that might not have access to equipment, or even for testing potentially dangerous experiments.
