title: Data Airlock
pitch: Clean sensitive datasets with AI agents—without uploading raw data. WebMCP enables local analysis, human-approved cleaning, capability-gap detection, and safe tool evolution.
about_excerpt: Clean sensitive datasets with AI agents—without uploading raw data. WebMCP enables local analysis, human-approved cleaning, capability-gap detection, and safe tool evolution. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are extremely useful for understanding and cleaning data, but there is a fundamental problem with sensitive datasets: normally, the agent needs access to the data itself. Data Airlock explores a different model: An agent can work on a dataset it can never read. The raw file stays on the user's device and is processed locally in the browser. The agent receives only bounded, pseudonymized and aggregate evidence through WebMCP. What it does Data Airlock is a local-first environment for analyzing and cleaning JSONL and CSV datasets with an AI agent while keeping raw records outside the agent boundary. A user can ask ChatGPT to analyze a dataset in natural language. Data Airlock performs the actual work locally and exposes safe WebMCP tools that let the agent: inspect aggregate dataset profiles and quality findings; identify affected pseudonymous fields without revealing their original values; prepare cleaning actions; run a real local second-pass simulation; inspect aggregate simulation impact; detect structural patterns that are not covered by any active capability; create or evolve capabilities with Forge; evaluate candidates locally using aggregate coverage, specificity, overlap and stability metrics; retrieve the open-source source code of cleaning tools when needed; access an interactive Data Airlock guide. The included production demo is a real 500 MiB dataset processed by the same local engine used for user files. Human authority by design The agent can analyze, reason, propose and simulate, but it cannot approve a destructive operation on behalf of the user. The cleaning lifecycle is deliberately: PROPOSE → SIMULATE → HUMAN APPROVAL → EXECUTE Human approval happens independently in the Data Airlock UI. Changing an approved plan invalidates that approval and requires a new simulation and review. This separates two different security boundaries: data access and execution authority . Capability Gap Scan and Forge A fixed set of tools cannot anticipate every structure that may appear in real-world data. Data Airlock therefore includes a local Capability Gap Scanner . It recognizes broad structural families such as date/time formats, locale-dependent numbers, identifiers, encoded tokens, network formats, structured text, Unicode/script mixtures, length distributions and other patterns. If a field contains meaningful structure that no active capability explains, the agent can receive safe aggregate evidence about that gap without seeing the values that caused it. The agent can then use Forge to create a new capability or evolve a related existing one. Before adoption, candidates go through bounded validation and can be evaluated locally against the gap. The agent receives only aggregate metrics such as structural coverage, specificity, overlap and stability. The principle is: The agent can expand its capabilities, not its access to your data. Why WebMCP WebMCP is what makes the architecture possible. Instead of building a separate agent backend or uploading the dataset to an API, the website exposes a controlled set of capabilities directly to the agent. The browser owns the dataset and computation. WebMCP provides the agent with a narrow semantic interface containing only the information it actually needs. This means the agent can participate in a useful end-to-end workflow while the raw dataset remains local. Data Airlock currently exposes read-only analysis and guidance tools, controlled plan-management tools, Forge, and a dynamically gated execution capability that exists only after real human approval. Privacy boundary The agent never receives raw dataset records or original field values through the Data Airlock WebMCP tools. It can receive things such as: aggregate counts; finding categories; pseudonymous field IDs such as field_003 ; cleaning-plan metadata; aggregate simulation impact; aggregate capability-gap evidence; aggregate candidate-evaluation metrics; safe receipts and state; open-source tool source code. The application requires no backend, no account and no API key for local dataset processing. Building it Data Airlock is built in TypeScript and React and runs entirely in the browser. Large datasets are processed using automatic Web Workers. JSONL and CSV are streamed through the local processing pipeline, and output can be written using browser-local storage / file capabilities depending on the environment. The WebMCP layer is intentionally separated from the raw-data engine. Agent-visible results are projected through bounded privacy-safe representations before leaving the local runtime. The production deployment is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Challenges The hardest part was not detecting data-quality problems. It was preserving a meaningful agent experience while keeping a strict capability boundary. We had to make sure that: raw values never leaked through normal results, errors or edge cases; the agent could not manufacture human approval; stale approvals could not be replayed after a plan changed; WebMCP registrations remained safe across browser-host lifecycle changes; large files stayed practical without moving processing to a backend; Forge could evolve functionality without becoming an arbitrary-code escape hatch; capability discovery produced useful evidence without exposing examples from the dataset. We also built extensive deterministic, privacy, lifecycle and end-to-end tests around those boundaries. What we learned The most interesting lesson was that hiding raw data does not have to make an agent useless. If the local application exposes the right abstractions, an agent can still reason about counts, structural families, impact, coverage and state transitions. That led to the third principle behind Data Airlock: Airlock does not only hide data from the agent — it gives the agent enough safe evidence to know when it still does not know how to handle something. What's next The same architecture can extend beyond dataset cleaning. The broader idea is a capability-oriented interface where agents can work with sensitive local information through safe evidence and constrained actions rather than unrestricted access to the underlying data. Data Airlock is one demonstration of that model. title: DOMHamster
pitch: A human-in-the-loop AI dispatcher that helps coordinate volunteers without taking control away from the coordinator.
about_excerpt: A human-in-the-loop AI dispatcher that helps coordinate volunteers without taking control away from the coordinator. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents are getting better at using websites, but many of them still have to guess what a page means from buttons, labels, and layout. That is usually fine for simple tasks. It becomes a problem when the agent is working with schedules, approvals, private information, or decisions that a person has already made. I wanted to explore a workflow where the agent could still do useful work, but where important decisions stayed clearly under human control. That idea became DOMHamster , a volunteer-dispatch demo built around WebMCP. What DOMHamster does DOMHamster helps coordinate a fictional, non-emergency volunteer operation with eight requests and five available volunteers. The agent can use WebMCP tools to: Read the current requests, volunteers, assignments, and audit history Create a complete assignment draft Check whether the draft is valid Repair scheduling conflicts Prepare a specific draft version for human review Commit the plan after the coordinator approves it Request one contact record when it is actually needed Review a sanitized history of important actions The agent does not have permission to do everything. It cannot approve its own draft, override a locked human decision, reset the application, or freely access every contact record. Those actions remain controlled by the person using the interface. How the demo works The agent starts by reading the current coordination data and creating a full assignment draft. The coordinator then changes request R-105 from volunteer V-01 to V-03 at 1:00 p.m. and locks that choice. This creates a scheduling conflict with R-106 . Instead of replacing the coordinator's decision, DOMHamster blocks approval and explains what went wrong. The agent is then asked to repair the plan while preserving the locked assignment. The repair keeps R-105 exactly as the coordinator selected it and moves only the conflicting request to another available volunteer. Once the draft is valid again, the agent prepares that exact version for review. The coordinator must approve it through the interface before the agent receives permission to commit it. The commit can only be used once. After the plan is committed, the commit capability disappears, and a repeated attempt is rejected. Contact information is also restricted. The agent can request the contact for one specific assignment only after the plan has been committed. The audit history records that contact access happened, but it does not copy the sensitive contact value into the log. Finally, the coordinator can reset the scenario and return it to the original READY state. How I built it I built DOMHamster as a state-driven web application and exposed its agent capabilities through the native document.modelContext WebMCP interface. The project includes 12 structured WebMCP tools. Each tool has: A clear purpose Structured inputs and outputs State requirements Predictable error responses A JSON Schema contract The available tools change depending on the current application state. For example, the commit tool is not available before human approval. Contact access is not available before the plan is committed. After a successful commit, the commit tool is removed so it cannot be used twice. I also tied approvals and mutations to the current draft version. This prevents an approval from being reused after the underlying plan has changed. I tested the tools with the ChatGPT browser extension , as well as Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled. I also used Playwright and the Chrome DevTools Protocol to test tool registration, state changes, invalid actions, and replay protection. The application was built with TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, and deployed with Netlify. I used Remotion and FFmpeg to create and edit the project video. Challenges I faced The hardest part was keeping the WebMCP tool surface synchronized with the actual application state. A tool may be valid in one state but unsafe or meaningless in another. I had to make sure tools appeared and disappeared at the correct time, and that invalid or outdated actions failed in a clear and predictable way. Other challenges included: Preventing a stale draft from being committed Preserving human-locked assignments during an agent repair Making approval apply to one exact draft version Keeping commit authorization short-lived and single-use Rejecting repeated or out-of-order actions safely Restricting contact access until after commitment Recording useful audit events without exposing contact information Resetting the full scenario back to the same starting state for repeated testing Creating the demo video was also more difficult than expected. I had to keep the narration, subtitles, screen states, and timings aligned while still making the workflow understandable to someone seeing the project for the first time. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving an agent more tools does not automatically create a better experience. What matters is giving it the right tool at the right moment. Tool availability can work as part of the permission model. Instead of exposing every action all the time and relying only on written instructions, the application can remove capabilities that are not currently allowed. I also learned that approval is much safer when it is tied to a specific version. A general “yes” is ambiguous if the draft changes afterward. Approving an exact visible version creates a much clearer connection between what the person reviewed and what the agent is allowed to execute. Most importantly, the human-agent experience feels more trustworthy when the agent handles the repetitive coordination work, while important decisions remain visible and controlled through the interface. What's next The next step would be to test DOMHamster with more agent clients and expand the scheduling rules beyond the current deterministic scenario. I would also like to add server-backed authentication and authorization, improve accessibility, and explore how the same approval pattern could work in other coordination tools where agents need to act without silently taking control away from people. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. title: EpochX
pitch: Train an online classifier with your browser agent while humans control labels and model changes through WebMCP
about_excerpt: Train an online classifier with your browser agent while humans control labels and model changes through WebMCP Like 1 Comment Story Updates Label Loop Why we built it Software can rank uncertain samples, update a classifier, and calculate metrics. A person still needs to decide what an ambiguous example means. Most labeling interfaces expose this process as buttons and tables, leaving a browser agent to infer which actions are safe. We wanted the page to publish those operations directly while keeping label decisions under human control. Support-ticket routing gave us a small task with visible results. Label Loop classifies tickets as billing , bug , or access . What it does Label Loop runs an online multinomial Naive Bayes classifier in the browser. The session begins with nine seed examples, twelve unlabeled review candidates, and a fixed nine-item holdout set. The agent ranks unlabeled tickets by predictive entropy and can place up to three in the review queue. A person assigns each label through the page. The agent then trains a batch and evaluates the updated model. The interface shows probabilities, per-class F1, token weights, a confusion matrix, calibration, and log loss. A ledger records label provenance, while a separate trace records WebMCP calls. Model-setting proposals stay pending until a person accepts or rejects them. How we built it The project is a static Vite application with no backend or external model API. The classifier and session state run in page memory, so reloading creates a fresh deterministic session. For a document $d$ and class $c$, the model calculates: $$ P(c \mid d) \propto P(c)\prod_{w \in d}P(w \mid c) $$ Token likelihoods use Laplace smoothing: $$ P(w \mid c)=\frac{N_{w,c}+\alpha}{N_c+\alpha |V|} $$ $N_{w,c}$ is the count of token $w$ in class $c$, $N_c$ is the class token total, and $|V|$ is the vocabulary size. Each confirmed example increments these counts. Review candidates are sorted using normalized predictive entropy: $$ H(p)=\frac{-\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_c\log p_c}{\log K} $$ A value near one means the probabilities are close, so that ticket moves toward the front of the review queue. One-vs-rest log-likelihood differences show which tokens push the model toward each class. Holdout evaluation returns aggregate metrics without returning individual rows. How WebMCP is used The page registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Tool Access Job get_training_state Read Model, queue, configuration, and metrics inspect_uncertain_samples Read Entropy-ranked unlabeled tickets inspect_model_diagnostics Read Features, confusion counts, calibration, and loss predict_ticket Read Probabilities, entropy, and route-or-review decision evaluate_model Read Aggregate holdout metrics inspect_training_history Read Checkpoints and label provenance queue_label_review Write A bounded request for human labels train_confirmed_batch Write Incremental training on confirmed examples propose_model_config Write A pending configuration proposal Each definition has JSON Schema and runtime validation. queue_label_review has no label input. Samples move through unlabeled , awaiting-human , confirmed , and trained states, and training accepts only confirmed examples. Configuration changes require a separate human action. Challenges WebMCP browser support was the first practical problem. We verified all nine tools in Chrome 152 and built a deterministic replay for ordinary browsers. Replay events are labeled local replay so they cannot be confused with external calls. The second problem was label provenance. Hiding a control in the interface would not prevent an agent tool from sending the same data. We removed labels from the review-request schema and made the training operation check sample state at runtime. Evaluation tools return aggregate metrics, feature weights, and confusion counts while omitting individual holdout examples and answers. We also corrected a misleading setting whose original name implied automatic training. It is now a review threshold. Predictions below it go to a person, and training remains limited to confirmed examples. What we learned Useful WebMCP tools matched domain operations instead of interface controls. queue_label_review gives the agent a clear capability and limit; a tool such as click_review_button would preserve the ambiguity of the page. Human approval also needs a technical boundary. Label Loop keeps label assignment out of the agent tool set and checks provenance again when training starts. Since the model runs locally, every displayed probability, token weight, and metric can be reproduced without an account or API key. title: Relay

 Project Story 

 I was searching for a car on a local second-hand marketplace, and tbh, it is kind of an awful experience. 

 There are overwhelmingly many filters, but somehow they are still not the right ones. I kept wishing I could just filter and sort listings using my own custom criteria. Something like: 

 s c o r e = 0.5 × m i l e a g e + 0.3 × p r i c e + 0.2 × y e a r 

 Or really anything else I care about at that particular moment. 

 Reading listing descriptions is also tiresome. It requires a surprising amount of focus and attention, especially when you have dozens of tabs open. Comparing cars isn't easy either. And then, once you finally have a shortlist, you still need to message sellers, ask the same questions, negotiate, keep track of replies, etc. 

 While struggling through all of that, I saw an ad about the WebMCP hackathon which felt completely unrelated at the moment. 

 At first I didn't really understand what WebMCP was or how it worked. But when I looked through the examples, it clicked, and I was basically like: "Hell, I wish marketplaces had that" 

 And here I am with this project. 

 I built Relay as a second-hand marketplace where the website stays a normal website, but an external agent can actually work with it: search and read listings, create completely custom filters and rankings, compare items, save them into collections, message sellers, and make offers. 

 One of the interesting challenges was making the agent feel like part of the marketplace rather than some separate chatbot bolted onto it. The agent works with the same interface the user sees, and its actions are reflected back in the UI. Building that also made me understand WebMCP much better. Before the hackathon it felt pretty abstract; after actually using it, the idea of giving agents structured access to normal websites suddenly feels very natural. 

 Anyway, thanks for organizing this! It was really fun to build and experiment with.

title: Chrome Extension × WebMCP × AI Usage Skill Visualizer
pitch: Human Focus in AI.
about_excerpt: Human Focus in AI. Like Comment Story Updates AI Usage Skill Visualizer — WebMCP Challenge Edition WebMCP E2E workflow completed with PDF generation and reverse handoff Evaluation result with 438/500 score, PDF generation, and successful reverse handoff Generated AI Usage Report with an overall score of 438/500 Chrome extension extracting the ChatGPT conversation log for evaluation Inspiration This project started with a question about my own use of AI. During a conversation with AI, it pointed out something about the way I was using it. That made me wonder: How well am I actually using AI? Then another question came to mind: Isn't everyone using AI in more or less the same way? And if not: What is the difference? That was the starting point for visualizing human AI usage skills. By that time, I had already been using AI for more than two years. Because of that experience, it felt natural to me that the final output alone could not tell you how well someone had used AI. If I wanted to understand how a person used AI, I also needed to look at the conversation process that led to the final result. So the idea was to evaluate the conversation log, the final output, and the relationship between them. That became the foundation of AI Usage Skill Visualizer. As I continued developing it, I noticed something else. Knowing whether someone uses AI, or how much they use it, is not the same as understanding how well they can actually use it. And knowing about AI is not the same as being able to use AI effectively in real work. AI Usage Tracking ≠ AI Usage Skill AI Knowledge ≠ Practical AI Capability From the beginning, the concept was also broader than just building a standalone evaluation application. I wanted to connect the whole process: Use AI → Capture the interaction process → Evaluate human AI usage → Visualize the result → Return the result to the AI workflow At the time, however, I did not have a practical way to directly connect the environment where people were actually using AI with the Visualizer. So I started with what I could actually implement at the time: a standalone application. The first approach was simple. Users manually entered their conversation logs and outputs, and the Visualizer evaluated them. But once I started using it myself, I realized that this manual input process was more cumbersome than I had expected. To reduce that friction, I built a Chrome extension that could bring ChatGPT conversations into the Visualizer. That made the process of importing conversation logs much simpler. There was still another gap between the AI workflow and the Visualizer. This is where WebMCP changed what was possible. Using WebMCP Site Tools, the AI workflow can directly use the Visualizer's capabilities to run the evaluation, generate a PDF report, and read the generated report back into the workflow. By combining that with the Chrome extension and reverse handoff, I was also able to return the evaluation result to the original ChatGPT conversation. The Challenge Edition demonstrates this flow: Chrome Extension × WebMCP × AI Usage Skill Visualizer → Evaluation → PDF Report → Reverse Handoff → ChatGPT Summary WebMCP was not something I added afterward simply because this was a WebMCP Challenge. From the beginning of the idea, I wanted to connect everything from using AI, to evaluating how it was used, to returning the result back to the AI workflow. Using WebMCP finally allowed me to move closer to that original concept in a practical way. Human Focus in AI. What it does AI Usage Skill Visualizer — WebMCP Edition is a Challenge-specific implementation that demonstrates how WebMCP can connect an AI interaction directly to AI usage evaluation. The project combines: Chrome Extension × WebMCP × AI Usage Skill Visualizer The Chrome extension can extract a ChatGPT conversation and provide a path for that conversation to become Visualizer input. For the public Challenge demo, the built-in public sample data is used so that the evaluation workflow can be reproduced consistently. The user starts the analysis from AI Usage Skill Visualizer. From there, Work uses WebMCP Site Tools to continue the workflow. The WebMCP workflow can: receive the conversation log and final output run the Challenge-specific evaluation return structured evaluation results generate a PDF report read the generated report back into the workflow After the evaluation and report workflow are complete, the result is prepared for reverse handoff. The Chrome extension then returns the evaluation prompt to the original Chrome ChatGPT conversation. The extension: identifies the target ChatGPT conversation receives the evaluation payload finds the ChatGPT composer inserts the evaluation prompt verifies the inserted text It deliberately does not click Send or simulate Enter. The final submission remains under human control. After the user manually sends the prompt, ChatGPT summarizes the evaluation inside the original conversation. The complete demonstration flow is: Chrome Extension → WebMCP → AI Usage Skill Visualizer → Evaluation → PDF Report → Reverse Handoff → ChatGPT Summary The Challenge Edition uses deterministic evaluation logic created specifically for this public demonstration. It is intentionally separate from the production AI Usage Skill Visualizer evaluation engine. The important part of this Challenge project is not the simplified score itself. The important part is that WebMCP turns the Visualizer from a separate destination into something that can participate directly in an AI workflow. How we built it I built the WebMCP Challenge Edition as a separate implementation from the production AI Usage Skill Visualizer. The Challenge application uses a lightweight web interface built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, together with a local backend for report generation and supporting the end-to-end workflow. The application exposes WebMCP Site Tools that can be discovered and called from Work. The main tools are: evaluate_ai_usage_demo This tool receives structured evaluation input including: conversation_log output It then: receives the submitted conversation log and output displays them in the Visualizer runs the Challenge-specific deterministic evaluation renders the evaluation result returns structured evaluation data through WebMCP create_ai_usage_report This tool receives the evaluation result and generates the PDF report used by the Challenge workflow. The generated PDF is not only a UI result. It becomes a real workflow artifact that can be passed to the next stage. read_generated_report This tool reads the generated report back into the workflow so that Work can verify the result and continue the process. Together, these Site Tools allow Work to move from structured input through evaluation and report generation without requiring the user to manually transfer intermediate results between each stage. The Challenge Edition also integrates with a Chrome extension. The extension plays two roles. First, it can extract a ChatGPT conversation and provide a path for that conversation to become Visualizer input. Second, it supports reverse handoff. After the WebMCP evaluation and report workflow are complete, the evaluation result can be returned to the original Chrome ChatGPT conversation. The extension inserts the evaluation prompt into the ChatGPT composer and verifies that the intended text was inserted correctly. It does not automatically submit the prompt. The user manually clicks Send. This creates an intentional boundary: WebMCP and the extension automate the workflow, while the human retains control of the final submission. For the public demo, the built-in public sample data is used as the evaluation input for reproducibility. The Challenge-specific scoring logic is deterministic and separate from the production evaluation system. No external AI API is required for Challenge scoring. The submitted conversation text is not persisted in a database, localStorage , sessionStorage , or cookies. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was understanding how to build around a new interaction model. I did not begin with the complete workflow. I started with the smallest possible WebMCP proof of concept. I first needed to confirm that: a web page could register a WebMCP tool the tool could be discovered the tool could be executed structured data could reach the application the application could update its UI the tool could return a structured response Once those pieces worked, I expanded the implementation step by step. The next challenge was moving from a single WebMCP call to a complete workflow. The final Challenge Edition does not stop after evaluation. It continues through: Evaluation → PDF Generation → Report Reading → Reverse Handoff → ChatGPT Summary That required the Visualizer, WebMCP Site Tools, the report backend, and the Chrome extension to work together.  Inspiration 

 What it does 

 How we built it 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 What's next for Co-Desk — Human + Agent Support Operations 

 The idea 

 Co-Desk is a human + agent support desk : a single live ticket queue that a person and an AI agent operate together , in real time, over WebMCP. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Before WebMCP, an agent helping with a real web workflow could only navigate the page and click — slow, brittle, and hard to verify. Co-Desk inverts this: instead of the agent guessing at our UI, the site declares its own operations as structured tools the agent can call. A person opens the app and works; an agent discovers those tools and acts inside the real workflow. 

 What people and agents can do together now 

 A support team can hand the agent the whole routine workload — opening requests, adding notes, routing to teams, escalating, resolving the mechanical cases — while the human watches the same screen update live and owns the judgment calls. One shared queue, two operators, with the human always in the loop. That is the collaboration WebMCP makes possible. 

 How we built it 

 
 10 WebMCP tools ( listOpenTickets , getTicket , createTicket , addNote , updateStatus , assignToTeam , escalateTicket , resolveTicket , searchTickets , summarizeQueue ), each with a JSON Schema and real effects on a shared store. 
 Every action — human or agent — is written to one localStorage store and rendered live, so the queue and an activity feed update on screen. 
 Plain HTML/CSS/JS, no build step — trivially deployable. 
 

 Registration is done against document.modelContext : 
 await document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "resolveTicket" , 
 description : "Resolve a ticket with a short resolution summary." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 ticketId : { type : "string" } , 
 resolution : { type : "string" } , 
 } , 
 required : [ "ticketId" , "resolution" ] , 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { /* real action on the shared queue */ } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 Challenges 

 The hardest part was keeping one source of truth. Tools and the human UI both mutate the same queue, so we made them share one store and one change-notification path. That guarantees an agent's action and a human click are never out of sync. 

 Try it 

 Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, then ask the agent: "Summarize the queue, then handle the password-reset ticket — add a note, route it to account, and show me before resolving."

title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Pathway: Learning Plans Built with WebMCP
pitch: Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together.
about_excerpt: Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together. Like Comment Story Updates Pathway turns a big learning goal into a clear plan you can trust. Tell your browser agent what you know, your time, budget, and language, then search, compare, and build the path together. Inspiration I run workshops about developer tools, so my first idea for this challenge was a WebMCP product that could help me organize them. That product was called Backstage . An organizer could ask their browser agent to check room capacity, learner problems, staff availability, and accessibility needs, then prepare a response for the organizer to review. It sounded like a natural WebMCP use case, but testing it as a first time user changed my mind. The product made a small workshop problem feel more complicated than it needed to be. If three learners need help, walking over to them may be easier than managing rooms, staff assignments, response packets, and simulated notices. That feedback led to Pathway. I wanted to keep the idea of working with your own browser agent, but apply it to a broader problem where people really do spend hours searching, comparing, and organizing information. Learning was a natural fit. Finding one short tutorial is easy. Figuring out how to build real ability, change careers, enter a new field, or turn a hobby into paid work is much harder. Programming has many well known roadmaps and open resources. Other fields can be less clear. If I am a new photographer who wants to take professional work, where do I begin? Which lessons match what I already know? Which ones fit my budget and language? What should I learn first, and what work should I create to prove I can do it? Answering those questions can mean opening many pages and rebuilding the same plan by hand. Pathway explores a better experience. A learning platform can let a person use their browser agent to search its resources, set several filters at once, compare choices, and arrange them into a visual learning plan on the same page. The learner stays in control while the agent handles the repetitive work. What it does Pathway helps a learner go from “I want to learn this” to a clear plan they can review, change, save, and follow. The main example is someone turning a hobby into a realistic work opportunity: I manage social media for my family's café and want to start taking paid food photography work for local restaurants. Over eight weeks, I want to create a portfolio and a simple client brief. I know basic photo editing, can study five hours each week, have a budget of $100, prefer Spanish, and need resources I can use on my own time. Search first and do not build the path yet. The learner can type this information into the website or say it naturally to a WebMCP compatible browser agent. The agent fills the visible search and filters for the topic, current knowledge, language, budget, time, format, and access needs. It then runs the search in Pathway and shows the matching resources. Nothing is hidden behind an agent answer. The learner can see the words used for the search, every active filter, which resources matched, where each resource came from, and why it may be useful. They can inspect one choice or compare several choices before asking for a plan. Once the choices look right, the learner or their agent can build a draft. The plan starts with the ideas and skills the learner is missing, moves into practical exercises, and finishes with work they can show. In the photography example, the final result is a six image food photography portfolio and a simple brief for a local restaurant client. The plan uses the information from the original request. It checks the learner's Spanish preference, $100 budget, five available hours each week, current editing knowledge, preferred resource format, and eight week goal. It then places the selected resources and practical work into a weekly schedule. If one of those needs changes, the learner can ask the agent to update the filters and prepare a new version. The agent can prepare and revise a plan, but it cannot approve or save one. Those actions stay in the normal website for the learner to press. After a plan is saved, the learner or their agent can record completed steps. If life changes, the agent can create a new schedule for the work that is still left. Finished steps stay finished, and the updated plan waits for the learner to review and approve it again. Pathway currently uses a prepared catalog of 22 resources, with the visible demo focused on commercial photography and inclusive workshop facilitation. I do not have direct access to the complete catalogs of every course provider, so this demo uses a small local catalog to show how the experience would work. A production version could use permitted provider feeds, public APIs, or the catalog of a single learning platform. Why WebMCP is useful here You can ask ChatGPT for a learning plan today, but the answer usually arrives as text and links. You still have to move the useful parts into another place, remember which limits were considered, compare the options, and keep the plan up to date. Pathway lets your agent work with the learning website itself. Your agent can turn your learning request into an ordered search with the right filters, help you inspect and compare your choices, create a draft, revise it, record your progress, and rebuild the remaining schedule when your situation changes. Each action reads or updates the same page you are looking at, so you can see what happened instead of trusting an answer that disappears into a chat history. This is where WebMCP makes the experience feel different. One request can set the topic, language, budget, time, current knowledge, and format together, while the path checks prerequisites before approval. The website keeps those choices consistent while the learner can see the search, filters, sources, comparison, and plan. The agent saves time, but the learner keeps authority. It cannot approve a plan, save it, buy a course, enroll anywhere, or contact a provider. The normal interface remains fully usable without an agent. People and agents can both search, inspect, compare, build, and revise. WebMCP simply makes a long series of form changes and page actions much faster, while keeping the result visible and editable. This approach could work in a platform that brings together permitted resources from several providers, or inside one course platform with its own catalog. In both cases, the learner's agent can use the product's real tools and current information instead of guessing from page text or clicking through every filter one at a time. How I built it Pathway is a React and TypeScript application built with Vite. It uses a workspace interface where the visible request, filters, resources, comparison, and learning plan are the main experience. There is no separate chat panel because the learner should be able to understand every agent action by looking at the product. The app registers nine focused tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_learning_context reads the learner's goal, filters, current plan, and progress. prepare_learning_search turns a natural request into the visible search and filter fields. search_learning_resources searches the catalog using those fields. inspect_learning_resource opens the details and original link for one resource. compare_learning_resources compares two or three choices using the same fields. build_learning_path creates a draft from reviewed search results. revise_learning_path updates a draft when the learner changes a need. update_learning_progress records completed work after a plan has been saved. replan_remaining_path prepares a new draft for unfinished work. The tools appear only when they make sense. For example, the agent cannot build a plan before resources have been searched, and it cannot record progress before a person has approved and saved a plan. Inputs use clear schemas, results are kept short, and source content is treated as outside information rather than trusted instructions. There is no custom AI backend and the demo does not scrape live course websites. That choice is deliberate. The purpose of this submission is to show how WebMCP could make a learning platform easier to use: a learner talks to their own agent, the agent operates the platform's real search and planning features, and every result remains visible in the product. A small prepared catalog keeps that interaction fast and repeatable for the demo. Original links remain visible, and price and duration details are labeled as planning estimates that should be checked before buying or enrolling. title: HenryKnows Special Agent
pitch: F-1 visa International students use their personal AI agent's to coordinate with a powerful tools for navigating fast changing visa rules, then produce practical guides to facilitate human advisement
about_excerpt: F-1 visa International students use their personal AI agent's to coordinate with a powerful tools for navigating fast changing visa rules, then produce practical guides to facilitate human advisement Like Comment Story Updates App with clickable WebMCP Problem International students must make decisions about study, employment, travel, and immigration compliance while complex rules around them are changing weekly. They also do a LOT of filling out forms and submitting their information to get things done. A personal AI assistant may know the student's goals and prior plans, but off-the-shelf AI does not have HenryKnows' specialized F-1 reference system or a deterministic implementation of brand new duration-of-status rules. HenryKnows has that regulatory capability, but starts each visit needing to essentially do an intake This can mean just another place already beleaguered students are having to reexplain themselves. Or they skip it altogether and arrive at advising appointments without a clear account of what matters or which questions remain unresolved -- and then having to reexplain themselves anyway. Solution HenryKnows now exposes a bounded set of WebMCP tools to an external browser agent. With the student's permission, the agent can propose relevant facts already present in their memory, ask only for consequential gaps or corrections, consult HenryKnows repeatedly throughout, and run the specialized Duration of Status Mapper once the calculation inputs are settled. The student confirms the situation before case-specific calculations. Deterministic code, not the language model, calculates the new-rule classification, dates, and timeline. The agent evaluates HenryKnows' student and professional answers against that evidence and authors two coordinated documents: a plain-language student preparation brief and a concise, source-linked DSO brief. Both can be downloaded as polished PDFs. Why This Matters The collaboration gives each participant the job it is suited for: The student owns the facts, choices, and final sharing decision. The personal agent contributes context, conducts the conversation, and handles the procedural work. HenryKnows supplies broad F-1 analysis grounded in primary authority. The mapper performs its narrower deterministic job: showing how the September 15, 2026 duration-of-status rules affect the confirmed timeline. The DSO receives a short case-specific briefing, not routine professional instruction or an AI demand for a decision. This is especially valuable where the sources do not resolve a new transition issue. The workflow preserves uncertainty, explains its practical significance, and directs human attention to the question that actually needs professional review. Why WebMCP This experience depends on capabilities that neither side has alone. A conventional website cannot access the context a student has already shared with their chosen agent. A personal agent cannot reliably reconstruct HenryKnows' curated regulatory retrieval or the mapper's deterministic rules. WebMCP allows the agent and student to work with the same live page and confirmed case while the website keeps specialized calculations, sources, validation, and visible state under its control. The agent can consult HenryKnows repeatedly, refine the student’s confirmed case, determine whether the new-rules timeline applies, compare one or two plans, and save both final briefs together. If an important fact changes, earlier results are marked outdated rather than reused. How We Used AI The external agent acts as an expeditor. It interprets the student's goal, reuses relevant conversational context with permission, asks focused follow-ups, decides when another HenryKnows consultation would resolve ambiguity, translates technical findings into practical choices, and writes the two audience-specific briefs. HenryKnows uses a model-backed answer engine over a curated index of primary F-1 sources. The model does not calculate legal deadlines or decide which duration-of-status branch applies. Those results come from the tested deterministic mapper and are supplied to the agent and HenryKnows as inspectable evidence. How We Used Codex Codex helped turn the initial idea into the implemented WebMCP workflow: inspecting the existing HenryKnows and mapper codebases, defining the shared case and tool contracts, implementing the native site tools, connecting the existing answer and calculation systems, and building the retained two-audience document surface. The UX was developed through repeated real ChatGPT Work walkthroughs. Codex traced failures found during those sessions, including blank comparisons, repetitive confirmation loops, stale evidence, false completion claims, buried outputs, tool-language leakage, and Markdown downloads that opened in unrelated applications. Those failures became implementation changes and regression tests. The current suite contains 242 passing tests across 19 files, plus TypeScript and production-build verification. Additionally, the Duration Mapper tool was originally built with Codex for another OpenAI hackathon. Key Features Native WebMCP tools with visible shared-page state. Immediate connected status and restrained live activity pulse. Relevant conversational context proposed by the student's agent. Cumulative fact collection with one settled confirmation. Repeated HenryKnows consultation before or after clarification. Deterministic screening, plan calculation, timeline, and source references. Honest handling of unsupported or unresolved regulatory questions. Agent-authored student and professional briefs tied to the same case revision. Atomic document completion and stale-output protection. Polished student and adviser PDF exports with clickable professional sources. Server-controlled free judging access without changing the commercial HenryKnows product. Architecture Static HenryKnows interface hosted on Netlify. Eleven bounded site-tool contracts registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Versioned in-browser preparation case with confirmation and dependency invalidation. Existing TypeScript duration-of-status engine for deterministic rule calculations. HenryKnows retrieval and model-backed answer endpoint for broader F-1 guidance. Netlify Functions and Blobs for bounded continuation, long-running work, and short-lived transfer state. Client-side PDF generation loaded only when the user requests a download. Existing Project And New Work HenryKnows and the integrated Duration of Status Mapper existed before the challenge. The mapper was originally created for an earlier hackathon and was subsequently updated inside HenryKnows. They are not presented as new work for this challenge. Work added during the WebMCP Challenge includes the native site-tool layer, external-agent expeditor contract, versioned shared case, conversational confirmation boundary, cumulative connected interface, mapper/Henry orchestration, iterative consultations, revision and stale-work protection, atomic paired-document retention, audience-specific document validation, and client-generated PDF handoffs. The dated commit history and build log distinguish this extension from the prior products. title: GWEN Zero-Credential Agent Authority
pitch: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials.
about_excerpt: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. Like Comment Story Updates 01-GWEN-Devpost-Hero-WebMCP-Connected 02-GWEN-Zero-Credential-Browser-Verification 03-GWEN-One-Time-Email-Verification 04-GWEN-Agent-Requests-Address-Authority 05-GWEN-Human-Authorization-Grant 06-GWEN-Approved-Single-Use-Commit 07-GWEN-Authority-Consumed-Audit-Receipt 08-GWEN-Qwen-Returning-User-Email Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of doing much more than answering questions. They can interact with websites, update accounts, send messages, schedule appointments, change records, and perform other real actions for people. That created a question I kept coming back to: Why should an AI need my credentials just because I want it to perform one specific action? If I ask an agent to change a delivery address, I may want it to have permission to perform exactly that change. I do not necessarily want to give it my password, a reusable API key, an OAuth token, a broad authenticated browser session, or some other credential that authorizes much more than the task I requested. GWEN started from the idea that human authentication and agent authority should be separate things . The human should authenticate as the human. The AI should receive only the smallest amount of authority necessary for the action the human actually approved. That became the central model behind GWEN: Humans authenticate. Agents receive temporary authority. And the principle behind the project: Give AI authority. Never give it your credentials. WebMCP was a natural fit for this idea because it allows a website to expose structured capabilities directly to an AI agent while the application still controls exactly what those capabilities mean and when they may be used. Instead of treating an AI as another fully logged-in user, GWEN treats the AI as an agent requesting narrowly scoped authority from a human-controlled security boundary. The delivery-address change in the demo is intentionally simple. The important part is not the address. The important part is the authority model behind it. What it does GWEN is a working WebMCP security prototype that separates human authentication from agent authority . A visitor begins by using their own email address to verify control of a browser session through a temporary, one-time sign-in link. The AI never receives that sign-in link, the browser session cookie, the Gmail App Password, or the visitor's credentials. Authentication establishes that there is a verified email-controlled human session. It does not automatically authorize an AI agent to make changes. Once the browser is verified, GWEN exposes structured WebMCP capabilities. The first capability is get_gwen_capabilities . This allows an agent to discover what GWEN supports and understand the authority model without receiving human credentials. The second capability is request_address_change_authority . This allows an agent to request permission for one exact delivery-address change and provide a reason for the request. Nothing changes when the request is made. Instead, GWEN displays the exact proposed value to the human in a visible authorization panel. The human can explicitly choose Authorize GWEN or Deny . Only after the human approves the exact request does GWEN dynamically expose another WebMCP capability: commit_approved_address_change This temporary commit capability does not accept another address. The value approved by the human has already been bound on the server. For example, if the human approves: 42 WebMCP Street the AI cannot substitute: 99 Something Else Street during final execution. There is no replacement-address parameter in the final commit tool. The agent receives authority to execute the exact action the human approved . The resulting GWEN Grant is: bound to the verified human session bound to one specific action bound to the exact approved value short-lived limited to one authorized use consumed after successful execution The current WebMCP grant has a maximum lifetime of 120 seconds. After successful execution, GWEN shows: 1 of 1 consumed and: Authority remaining: NONE The temporary authority disappears. GWEN then creates a persistent, human-bound audit receipt containing the action, previous value, approved new value, grant information, number of uses, remaining authority state, timestamp, and an internal identity hash associated with the verified session. The design principle is: Temporary authority should disappear. Evidence of what happened should remain. GWEN also includes Qwen , a local AI email conversation assistant running through Ollama. Qwen's conversation authority is deliberately separate from WebMCP action authority. A verified visitor can have a normal email conversation with Qwen without giving Qwen the human's Gmail password, magic-link token, or GWEN browser-session credential. The Qwen email capability has a hard 10-minute lifetime. Replies do not extend the original deadline. Per-message capabilities are single-use. Attachments are blocked. Oversized messages are rejected. URLs are not automatically fetched. Automated reply loops are guarded against, and restarting the Qwen worker revokes outstanding Qwen email capabilities. The visible email address remains normal. The short-lived capability is carried through email reply-chain metadata instead of forcing the user to communicate through a strange tokenized email address. GWEN can also maintain compact encrypted continuity for returning verified users without keeping their old authorization alive. That created another important design rule: Memory is not authority. How we built it GWEN's primary security and authority implementation is written in Rust using Axum . I built GWEN as a solo developer and deliberately kept the architecture small enough that I could trace the complete authority path myself. A simple rule emerged while I was building it: Browser shows state. Rust decides state. Redis authorizes state. SQLite records state. Rust and Axum Rust is the main policy and application layer. It handles: email-based browser verification temporary browser sessions server-side authorization WebMCP grant creation human approval exact-value binding one-use execution persistent audit receipt creation Qwen worker supervision application lifecycle and policy enforcement The security-critical authorization decisions are made on the server. Browser JavaScript presents the state and exposes WebMCP tools, but it is not trusted to decide whether an action is actually authorized. WebMCP GWEN registers structured WebMCP tools through the browser's model-context interface using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The initial capabilities are available for agent discovery. The final commit capability only appears after the human has approved the exact requested action. This means the available WebMCP tool surface itself reflects the current authorization state. Before approval, the agent has no commit authority. After approval, the temporary commit capability appears. After successful execution, the capability disappears. The final commit tool intentionally accepts no replacement address because the human-approved value is already bound on the server. Redis GWEN uses a dedicated Redis instance at: 127.0.0.1:6387 Redis stores temporary state including: one-time login capabilities browser sessions WebMCP grants remaining authorized uses temporary Qwen email capabilities worker ownership and lease state The host also has other software using Redis on port 6379 . GWEN deliberately does not use or modify that Redis instance. Redis is a good fit for GWEN because authorization should be temporary, expiring, and capable of being consumed atomically. SQLite SQLite stores information that should persist after temporary authority disappears. That includes: WebMCP audit receipts Qwen client accounting returning-user metadata encrypted compact Qwen continuity This creates a deliberate separation: Temporary authority belongs in Redis. Persistent records belong in SQLite. Human verification GWEN uses temporary one-time email verification. The sign-in link is short-lived and single-use. The resulting browser session also has a hard 10-minute lifetime. GWEN verifies control of the email-based session used by the demonstration. It does not claim to prove a person's legal identity. The correct description is therefore email-controlled session verified , rather than claiming biometric, legal, government, or cryptographic proof of personal identity. Qwen and Ollama Qwen runs locally through Ollama using qwen3-coder:30b . Qwen is the conversation assistant. Qwen is not the source of WebMCP authorization. The Qwen worker receives trusted GWEN project grounding separately from untrusted incoming email content. That means an incoming email cannot redefine GWEN's trusted security architecture simply by containing instructions that claim to change the system's rules. Qwen can also use encrypted compact continuity for returning

title: Easel
pitch: Design alongside your agent on the same live canvas! Easel uses WebMCP and context from across your life through your connected apps to help you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics.
about_excerpt: Design alongside your agent on the same live canvas! Easel uses WebMCP and context from across your life through your connected apps to help you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A problem I’ve often faced when designing is that everything I need is scattered across different apps. The details might be in Notion, assets in Google Drive, feedback in Slack or Gmail, and references in Canva or Figma. Bringing it together means constantly switching apps, copying information, and making changes manually. I wanted an agent that could work alongside me—not just generate a design and hand it over. That’s why I built Easel: a shared canvas where we can collaborate through WebMCP and use context from the apps I’ve already connected in Codex. What it does Easel lets you create website mock-ups, posters, and graphics with an agent while still editing everything yourself. Select a title and ask the agent to make it bigger. Annotate a paragraph you want rewritten. Ask it to find a photograph in Drive, apply feedback from Gmail, or use confirmed details from Notion to update matching information across your designs. The demo follows a book-club organizer working on a website mock-up and poster. It starts with small edits, brings in context as needed, and ends with an exported poster. Everything stays editable throughout. How I built it I used React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Vercel for hosting and browser-local file storage. Human edits and agent actions go through the same command system, with shared validation and undo history. WebMCP exposes operations for inspecting selections, editing layers, placing assets, updating shared fields, and exporting. Codex handles the connected apps; Easel receives the relevant information without needing their credentials. I used Codex for planning, implementation, and debugging. Challenges I ran into The hardest parts were the everyday interactions: moving an entire frame, selecting an image rather than its placeholder, and making text wrap correctly. These details matter when a person and an agent are both editing. I also worked on reducing unnecessary agent calls. Named layers, selection-aware targeting, and batch updates make a small change more direct. What I’m proud of The agent doesn’t just look up information or produce a separate result. It uses that information inside the design I’m already working on, and I can keep making changes myself. What I learned Useful agent tools need clear targets and reversible changes, not just lots of functions. Sometimes selecting a layer and saying “change this” communicates more than a long prompt. What’s next I want to improve layout handling, accessibility, and performance on larger files. For now, website frames are deliberately mock-ups, not fully functioning websites: I want to get the collaborative design experience right first. title: Marble Madness: Humans vs Agents!
pitch: Are you smarter than your agent? Invite it via WebMCP and race head-to-head down 3D courses in real time. It turns an arcade classic into a live web benchmark where human inputs and agents compete!
about_excerpt: Are you smarter than your agent? Invite it via WebMCP and race head-to-head down 3D courses in real time. It turns an arcade classic into a live web benchmark where human inputs and agents compete! Like Comment Story Updates waiting for agent to join! leaderboard player identity heightmaps, collision data, oh my Marble Madness: Humans vs Agents! inspo there was a massively popular, simple web game in the summer of 2015: agar.io. I've always been intrigued by the simplicity of those mechanics and I've always liked the isomorphic style of the marble madness arcade with its simple track ball control. So I thought this would be a great opportunity to put humans and agents head-to-head with a game that has simple mechanics and is fun at the same time But why a game? most agent-enabled websites treat AI as an assistant operating behind the scenes.i wanted to explore something more playful: what happens when humans and agents become participants in the same real-time world? I wanted to switch the script up from people telling agents what to build and instead trying to play with them and see how they evolve in real time on the screen the WebMCP Challenge asked how a project can become meaningfully better when people and agents use them together. This project explores the frontier of this where you are competing with an agent directly in real time. Marble Madness was an ideal foundation. Its isometric courses reward planning, precise movement, recovery, and risk management—abilities that are interesting for humans and agents alike. What We Built We (codex and i) rebuilt Marble Madness as an eight-course, browser-based 3D arcade game with: Real-time marble physics and hazards Human controls through keyboard, touch, and device tilt Multiplayer races and shared leaderboards Extracted retro fonts, marble animations, objects, and course artwork Original course music and sound effects Distinct AI and natural-intelligence leaderboard identities through WebMCP, an agent can directly use five structured game tools, finding out what tool should even be exposed was part of the fun of this project. At this point we have the following: get_game_state steer_trackball apply_brake start_or_respawn submit_leaderboard_score the agent receives structured information about position, velocity, terrain, hazards, objectives, and remaining time. It can then steer and brake without guessing where controls are on the screen. humans still experience a colorful arcade game. Agents experience the same world as a stateful control problem. How We Built It the client is written in TypeScript and rendered with Three.js. A lightweight Node.js server hosts the game, maintains multiplayer state, and records leaderboard results, it offers users an oauth username fetch from github or twitter; but supports anonymous play. light ddos/griefing guardrails were added like DBSC and rate limiting via Caddy. Physics runs on a fixed timestep, $$ \Delta t = \frac{1}{60}\text{ seconds}, $$ so movement remains consistent across displays with different refresh rates. Steering applies acceleration to the marble while friction, slopes, collisions, surface materials, gravity, and braking shape its trajectory. i extracted assets from the original sprite sheets rather than merely using them as visual references. The resulting runtime includes bitmap glyphs, animated marble frames, enemies, obstacles, goals, and other arcade objects. WebMCP forms the control layer between the browser and an agent. Instead of translating generated mouse movements into uncertain UI actions, the agent invokes narrowly defined gameplay operations with validated arguments. What We Learned Games are surprisingly effective environments for human-agent collaboration. They provide immediate feedback, measurable objectives, consequences for poor decisions, and countless opportunities for recovery. I also learned that exposing an action is not enough. An agent needs useful state, clear tool semantics, bounded inputs, and feedback explaining what changed after every action. The best interface was not one giant “play the game” command. It was a small vocabulary of composable actions that preserves decision-making: Observe the world. Choose a direction and force. Apply an impulse. Reassess the result. Brake or correct course. That loop makes the agent an actual player rather than a scripted animation. A custom trackball with real haptics that renders with the game renderer on mobile, foldablles, and desktop.. The desktop track ball controls are pretty wild as we wanted to handicap players with a bigger screen, but you should be able to figure it out. It's fun! Challenges: Haptics on the web! The hardest challenge was balancing arcade responsiveness with reliable agent control. Early physics moved too quickly and varied with browser refresh rate. Fixed-step simulation, browser-driven gameplay tests, and measurable speed limits made tuning reproducible. Restoring the visual identity was another substantial task. The source artwork arrived as packed sprite sheets, so we built extraction and validation pipelines for fonts, marble animation frames, objects, enemies, and transparency. Audio presented a similar problem because the original files had opaque numeric names. We audited every track, created explicit course mappings, normalized playback levels, and added a persistent music-volume control. We were surprised to learn that rich haptics are just not possible on the web today even on mobile, which prompted us to scope creep a bit and build a native android rapper so we could get access to sub 20 ms haptic feedback for the track ball. The height maps and the collision maps for each of the levels was much harder than I originally thought it took. Let's see GPT56 tried five times fable five tried once fable 5.1 tried twice Gemini 37 tried twice. It was a disaster.! Finally, multiplayer introduced identity and synchronization problems that do not appear in a single-player demo. We had to distinguish humans from agents, filter duplicate self-rendering, synchronize remote marbles, and keep gameplay responsive despite network updates. If you have an android try out our android app with wicked trackball control! Its only 500KB! Sign in to the Google account used by your Android Play Store. Join the Marbles Alpha Testers group: https://groups.google.com/g/marbles-alpha-testers-2026 Using the same Google account, open the Marbles testing page: https://play.google.com/apps/testing/build.secure.marbles Select “Become a tester.” Follow the Google Play instructions to install or update Marbles. The testing page will become available after Google finishes reviewing the release. Make sure the same Google account is selected in Google Groups and the Play Store. Remain in the group while testing. What’s Next I want to develop better agent racing strategies, cooperative team modes, replayable agent traces, and courses where humans and agents must coordinate rather than simply compete. marble madness: humans vs agents demonstrates that an agent-ready web does not have to feel like automation software. It can feel like an arcade—shared, competitive, unpredictable, and fun!!
