title: Outcome Network
pitch: WebMCP turns business websites into capabilities agents can safely compose. Outcome Network coordinates providers, checks constraints, requires human approval, and uses reversible holds.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns business websites into capabilities agents can safely compose. Outcome Network coordinates providers, checks constraints, requires human approval, and uses reversible holds. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most web agents still interact with websites indirectly: read the page, inspect controls, then infer what action to take. WebMCP provides a cleaner model. A site can expose structured capabilities while still owning its UI, state, permissions, and business rules. Outcome Network explores what that looks like for a real multi-provider business workflow. What it does The demo coordinates opening a 15-person Toronto office with two constraints: CAD 12,000 maximum budget Everything ready by Friday Three providers supply furniture, networking, and facilities services. Through WebMCP, ChatGPT can search offerings, check inventory and availability, and create temporary resource holds after the user approves the plan. Those holds are reversible. ChatGPT can release them and restore provider availability without changing the approved plan. Every action is recorded in a visible audit trail with the capability, provider, result, and whether it came from WebMCP or the human workspace. How we built it The app uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vercel, and the native document.modelContext WebMCP API. The production workflow exposes six tools, including: search_products check_inventory check_service_availability reserve_outcome_resources release_outcome_reservations WebMCP calls use the same domain logic and state as the UI rather than separate mock handlers. The production path uses same-origin WebMCP for reliability. I also built an experimental cross-origin implementation using allow="tools" , explicit exposedTo origins, and getTools({ fromOrigins }) . Challenges we ran into The main challenge was working with an emerging browser API. WebMCP support behaved differently across local Chrome, public HTTPS, and ChatGPT's in-app browser. Rather than hiding those differences behind a polyfill, I added runtime diagnostics and kept the reliable production path separate from the experimental cross-origin path. The other challenge was authority and failure handling. Approval is tied to the current plan, so changing the plan invalidates stale approval. Multi-provider reservation failures also trigger compensating releases so partial holds are not left behind. Accomplishments that we're proud of The WebMCP integration is part of the application rather than a demo wrapper. In the deployed app, ChatGPT can: invoke real provider capabilities mutate the same state shown in the UI create six temporary holds across three providers release those holds and restore availability leave a visible WebMCP audit trail The project also supports deterministic supplier failure, replanning, and rollback after partial reservation failure. What we learned Tool discovery is only the beginning. Once agents can change application state, the harder questions are around authority, stale approvals, partial failure, reversibility, and auditability. That led to explicit approval boundaries, typed schemas, shared state, reversible operations, and compensating rollback. What's next for Outcome Network The next step is connecting the same model to real independent WebMCP-enabled businesses across different origins. The goal is not to build another marketplace. Businesses should be able to keep their own applications and rules, expose the capabilities they choose, and let agents coordinate those capabilities into useful outcomes. title: Sân Chơi
pitch: AI-hosted Vietnamese folk playground: Ô ăn quan, Bầu cua, Múa rối nước, Gióng's Iron Garage & Rồng rắn lên mây — 5 games, 21 hang-proof WebMCP tools. sanchoi.app
about_excerpt: AI-hosted Vietnamese folk playground: Ô ăn quan, Bầu cua, Múa rối nước, Gióng's Iron Garage & Rồng rắn lên mây — 5 games, 21 hang-proof WebMCP tools. sanchoi.app Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My 3-year-old nephew loves hearing Vietnamese folk tales and watching water puppet shows during Tết. But these centuries-old traditions — Ô ăn quan (Mancala), Múa rối nước (water puppet theatre), Rồng rắn lên mây (dragon snake chase), Bầu cua tôm cá (Lunar New Year dice), and the legend of Thánh Gióng riding an iron horse — are vanishing from children's daily lives. I wanted to build a digital "sân chơi" (playground) where an AI agent acts as the Game Master (Người Xướng Trò), hosting these folk games for kids, in Vietnamese, with full cultural authenticity. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge was the perfect catalyst: what if the AI doesn't just talk about folk games, but actually runs them — managing game boards, rolling dice, directing puppet shows, chanting call-and-response, and feeding Gióng's iron horse? How I built it Tech stack: Vite + TypeScript, Three.js (3D water puppet stage), GSAP (animations), Web Audio API (synthesized Đàn Bầu, festive drums, gongs), zero backend — fully client-side with localStorage persistence. Architecture: Each game follows a strict split: rules.ts (pure deterministic game logic, no DOM) and scene.ts (Three.js/GSAP visuals). Agent tools live in tools.ts and call rules directly, returning JSON state instantly — animations fire as fire-and-forget side effects. The WebMCP integration registers 32 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool following the standard JSON Schema spec with inputSchema , annotations, and AbortController -based cleanup. A fallback mode exposes tools at window.__debugTools for DevTools testing outside ChatGPT. For audio, I synthesized traditional folk instrument sounds using the Web Audio API — no external audio files needed for the core experience, just procedural Đàn Bầu melodies and percussion. Challenges 1. The hang bug. The first version of Ô ăn quan awaited GSAP animations inside agent tool handlers. In headless/backgrounded browser contexts, requestAnimationFrame is throttled, so the agent hung forever waiting for an animation that never fires. The fix: agent-facing tools ( isAgent: true ) return game state immediately; animations run as void animate().catch(...) fire-and-forget promises. This pattern was then retrofitted to all 5 games. 2. Bầu cua's async dice. The dice-roll scene awaited animateDiceRoll before resolving bets. Same class of hang. Refactored to split roll logic from animation, applied the fire-and-forget pattern. 3. Zero-backend persistence. With no server, game state survives refreshes through localStorage — but only the last active game is saved. I built a save_progress tool and a "flustered game master" easter egg: if the agent does 5+ actions without saving, Chú Tễu pops up with "Người xướng trò bị rối!" (The Game Master is flustered!). 4. Cultural authenticity in code. Every game had to feel Vietnamese , not just reskinned Western games. Ô ăn quan uses relay-sowing rules unique to Vietnam (when your last seed lands in a small pit with >1 seed, you scoop and keep sowing). Water puppetry required understanding the 11th-century thủy đình stage and iconic tales like Cóc kiện trời (The Toad Sued Heaven). Gióng's Iron Garage is rooted in the legend of Thánh Gióng — a folk hero who grew instantly, rode an iron horse, and defeated invaders. What I learned Building agent-native web apps requires a fundamentally different mental model from human-facing UIs. The agent needs instant, structured feedback — it can't "see" animations. This means: Game logic must be pure and synchronous. The DOM is for humans; JSON is for agents. Tool descriptions must be precise enough for an LLM to understand the game's mechanics and cultural context without ever seeing the screen. Easter eggs and "funny hooks" keep the experience playful even when the agent is driving: zero-capture moves in Ô ăn quan make the pit shake indignantly, matching dice in Bầu cua trigger a "XỐC! BA CON!" celebration, and the water puppet applause meter rewards dramatic timing. The result is a new kind of interactive cultural preservation — not a video about Vietnamese folk games, but an AI that can host them. title: DuckStudio
pitch: DuckStudio is a agent-native data app. Datasets stay on your machine. DuckDB-WASM runs queries in a Web Worker inside the browser tab.
about_excerpt: DuckStudio is a agent-native data app. Datasets stay on your machine. DuckDB-WASM runs queries in a Web Worker inside the browser tab. Like Comment Story Updates DuckStudio idle state prior to dataset selection, displaying upload controls on the left and an empty workspace placeholder. Default workspace screen showing no active tasks and prompting dataset activation from available presets or CSV upload. DuckStudio SQL & Lineage tab displaying the generated aggregation query, execution metadata (92.5 ms over 250k rows). DuckStudio displaying a DATASET_UNAVAILABLE error notification after attempting analysis without an activated dataset. DuckStudio Charts dashboard displaying summary KPI cards and an "accounts by tickets" distribution scatter plot completed in 92.5 ms. DuckStudio Charts view showing re-run or alternate query execution completed in 127.4 ms across 250,000 scanned records. Inspiration Analysts in healthcare and finance face strict data protection agreements (DPAs) and egress bans: data cannot leave the tab, but cloud LLMs cannot query browser memory. WebMCP bridges this actuation gap by giving an agent browser-level tools. However, browser agents can observe both tool outputs and the rendered DOM. Sanitizing tool payloads is ineffective if the UI renders raw sensitive rows where the model can inspect them. DuckStudio solves this through custody with controlled release : the agent steers the analysis and inspects safe aggregates, but raw records never cross into tool envelopes or the rendered canvas. What it does DuckStudio is a privacy-first, agent native analytical app where a human and an AI agent operate the same local DuckDB-WASM engine. Data remains in the client tab. WebMCP registers four imperative tools: duckdb_get_context — Returns capabilities, revision, schema digests, budgets, and permitted next actions. duckdb_activate_dataset — Switches datasets using optimistic concurrency through expectedRevision and idempotency keys. duckdb_execute_sql_to_canvas — Validates read-only SQL before execution, runs it locally, creates an immutable artifact with lineage, infers an aggregate KPI or chart specification, and pins it to the canvas. It returns an artifact handle and safe summary—never raw rows. duckdb_verify_zero_egress — Returns scoped evidence covering uploads, release decisions, network interceptors, and artifact lineage. Core Invariants: › Policy follows the dataset. : saas_churn (250,000 synthetic rows) runs under public_synthetic permitting bounded row display. healthcare_pii (100,000 rows with MRN and diagnosis) runs under sensitive_aggregate_only , suppressing raw grids entirely and rejecting cohorts smaller than 10 patients ($k \ge 10$). SQL is gated before execution : Permits only single, parameterized SELECT or WITH queries. Blocks DDL, DML, ATTACH , COPY , remote URLs, and extensions before DuckDB receives them. Deterministic state : Monotonic revisions and idempotency keys prevent race conditions, stale writes, and hallucinated retries. How we built it Stack : Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, lazy-loaded ECharts, and self-hosted @duckdb/duckdb-wasm in a dedicated Web Worker. Edge deployment & isolation : Deployed statically to Cloudflare Pages with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp . DuckDB-WASM binaries ( eh bundle) and fonts are self-hosted in /public to avoid third-party CDN failure under strict COEP. One command path : Human controls, prompt chips, the built-in simulator, and the 4 WebMCP tools all dispatch the exact same 6 domain commands through revisioned-workspace . Honest metrics : The initial workspace is empty—there are no pre-baked artifacts. SaaS metrics such as 14.2% churn and $182,400 impacted MRR are computed live by DuckDB from in- memory row generators and verified by CI contract tests Challenges we ran into DOM as an exfiltration surface : Because agents can scrape rendered elements, we implemented a single custody boundary across tool payloads and React rendering. If a requested view violates policy, it is rejected outright ("deny-over-strip") rather than partially rendered. Eradicating ambient state : Agents fail when tracking implicit context like "the last query." We eliminated ambient state entirely: every canvas view and query refinement references an immutable artifact ID containing a cryptographic SQL hash and parent lineage. Wasm limits & worker lifecycles : Single-threaded DuckDB-WASM ( eh bundle) runs under a browser wasm memory ceiling, clamped to a 5,000 ms execution budget and a 10,000-row cursor. Query cancellation requires terminating and respawning the Web Worker to prevent memory corruption without leaving orphaned partial artifacts. Evidence must be scoped honestly : The custody badge reads 0 Bytes of Dataset Uploaded . Interceptors audit fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon , WebSocket , and WebTransport to separate analytical data from application bundle traffic, avoiding unsupported zero-knowledge claims. Accomplishments that we're proud of Sub-second analytical queries over 250,000 rows executed entirely in client wasm with 0 bytes of dataset egress. Agents receive compact envelopes containing KPIs, chart dimensions, and artifact handles instead of raw row dumps. Self-healing recovery: queries that fail validation or custody rules return structured error codes and actionable recovery steps, allowing models to self-correct autonomously. What we learned WebMCP is most reliable as an explicit, revisioned state machine. Providing schema digests and monotonic revisions prevents model hallucination far better than generic prompt engineering. Local execution is not sufficient for privacy. If an agent has DOM access, data custody must be enforced at the UI projection layer as strictly as the network layer. What's next for DuckStudio Interactive virtualized Data Grid : High-performance, keyboard-accessible table with range selection and clipboard support for public datasets. OPFS streaming export subsystem : Stream CSV/Parquet outputs directly to the Origin Private File System to bypass wasm memory ceilings during large exports. SQL editor deep links : URL-addressable analysis states to share reproducible artifact lineage graphs. * In-tab AI chat panel * : BYO-LLM and WebLLM support with explicit, user-gated PII consent boundaries. Multi-threaded execution : Transition to DuckDB-WASM's coi bundle once cross-browser WebAssembly threading ergonomics and worker isolation stabilize. title: Poolwart — a safe agent-to-human handoff for water care
pitch: The agent interprets. Poolwart calculates. You verify.
about_excerpt: The agent interprets. Poolwart calculates. You verify. Like Comment Story Updates Poolwart turns an agent request into a visible, editable and safety-aware water-care calculation. Inspiration Pool and hot-tub owners often have three disconnected pieces of information: a water volume, a test result, and an active-chlorine percentage printed somewhere on a product label. Translating those values into a dose is tedious, and a generic assistant should not improvise safety-sensitive water-care arithmetic in chat. The useful division of work is different: an agent is good at understanding the messy request and extracting the inputs; a specialist site is good at deterministic, tested calculation; the owner must remain the person who verifies and acts. What it does Poolwart exposes two imperative WebMCP tools: calculate_chlor_topup calculates a dry-granule top-up from a measured free-chlorine value to the target range of the currently open Poolwart segment. calculate_chlor_shock calculates Poolwart's fixed +10 mg/l dry-granule shock increase. Calling a tool does not leave the answer trapped in an invisible tool response. It switches the visible calculator to the right mode, fills every input, and renders the normal dose, warnings, provenance, re-entry guidance, and disclaimer. The person can inspect or change every value and recalculate through the form. Poolwart calculates only. It never controls equipment, purchases a product, or physically doses water. How we built it The site uses imperative top-level registration through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema with numeric limits and additionalProperties: false , followed by defensive runtime validation. Both the manual form and WebMCP call one shared typed adapter, which delegates the actual arithmetic to the existing, tested @poolwart/wasser package. WebMCP is registered only after client mount and receives an AbortSignal , so tools are removed when the component unmounts or the page changes. Unsupported browsers keep the complete ordinary calculator. The challenge extension adds focused tests for calculation parity, boundaries, schemas, registration, lifecycle signals, result size, invalid inputs, unusually large volumes, and above-target measurements. How WebMCP improves the experience Without WebMCP, a user or browser agent must choose a form mode and transcribe each value. An assistant may instead calculate in chat, losing the specialist formula, segment-specific targets, warnings, and an editable verification surface. With WebMCP, the agent invokes a named capability on the page. Poolwart validates and calculates, then makes the handoff visible to the human. This is a genuine shared workspace: the agent can prepare the calculation, the site can prove what it used, and the person stays in control. What existed before the challenge Poolwart, the manual calculator, its deterministic water-care package, target ranges, safety copy, and server-rendered result pages existed before 2026-08-25. The two imperative WebMCP registrations, English tool contracts, shared form/tool adapter, structured outputs, agent provenance UI, lifecycle cleanup, and their tests were created for this challenge. The public repository tags the exported baseline as pre-webmcp ; git diff pre-webmcp..HEAD isolates the new work. See the complete challenge boundary and change log in CHALLENGE.md . Challenges and accomplishments The main design challenge was not exposing a formula—it was preserving one source of truth across a German human form and an English machine contract. Extracting the typed adapter removed the risk of the two paths drifting. An adversarial review also found that the pre-existing form treated any value above the lower target threshold as “in target,” including excessive readings. The challenge work now distinguishes above_target , shows a visible warning, and returns re-entry guidance and unusual-volume status to the agent. What we learned The strongest agent interface is not necessarily the one with the most autonomy. For safety-sensitive calculations, a narrow tool contract and an explicit human handoff are more valuable than an opaque answer. WebMCP can make the website the shared, inspectable source of truth instead of reducing it to a hidden backend. What's next After judging, the same narrow adapter pattern can expose other existing Poolwart calculators. The diagnostic wizard, image/OCR workflow, authentication, and hardware control remain deliberately out of scope until they have equally strong validation and human-review surfaces. Testing instructions Open the Whirlpool calculator in the current ChatGPT desktop in-app browser with a model that supports Site Tools. Ask: “My 1,000 litre hot tub reads 0.4 mg/l free chlorine. The label says 56% active chlorine. Calculate the top-up with Poolwart and show me the result there.” Confirm calculate_chlor_topup is selected and the visible form/result update. Ask: “Calculate a shock dose for my 1,000 litre hot tub using dry granules with 56% active chlorine, and show the calculation in Poolwart.” Confirm calculate_chlor_shock is selected and the shock/re-entry guidance is visible. Chrome alternative: use Chrome 149+, enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , restart, then inspect Application → WebMCP. No login or environment variables are required. title: oa::Network - WebMCP for native Vulkan applications
pitch: Safe, typed WebMCP tools for native C++ Vulkan, ML, and 3D applications.
about_excerpt: Safe, typed WebMCP tools for native C++ Vulkan, ML, and 3D applications. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can operate websites, while serious compute, ML, media, and 3D applications still live behind native C++ runtimes and GPU APIs. Existing browser automation often forces agents to guess through pixels and UI controls, while conventional MCP servers operate separately from the live page the user is viewing. OA already provides a native Vulkan compute and ML runtime, a bounded MCP implementation, training sessions, rendering, video, and experimental prompt-to-motion generation. We wanted to connect those capabilities directly to WebMCP so a person and an agent can safely operate the same live native application—with OA remaining the execution engine rather than moving the workload into JavaScript or a hosted service. What it does oa::Network - WebMCP exposes validated OA application actions as page-local WebMCP tools. A native C++ OA process owns the Vulkan device, compute graphs, models, rendering resources, synchronization, and application state. A small TypeScript adapter discovers its registered tools, exposes them through WebMCP, and forwards calls to the same typed commands used by the human interface. The project is designed around two demonstrations: A tiny-language-model workspace for selecting a model and tokenizer, starting or pausing training, inspecting bounded metrics, evaluating, checkpointing, and generating text on a local Vulkan GPU. A prompt-to-motion workspace using OA’s experimental ALM stack, native rendering, timeline state, and deterministic motion-editing tools. Large tensors, model weights, video frames, and GPU handles never travel through WebMCP. The browser carries only bounded commands, status, metrics, identifiers, and verifiable results. How we built it The native implementation is built in C++20 as part of OA Network. oa::McpServer owns the immutable tool registry, JSON schemas, validation, bounded parsing, and application handlers. The WebMCP bridge composes that server through an explicitly owned network gateway rather than creating a second tool implementation. The browser integration is a small TypeScript layer that: discovers compatible OA tools; registers them with document.modelContext.registerTool ; maps WebMCP annotations and JSON schemas; forwards validated calls to the native process; preserves cancellation, revisions, and ordered results; updates the same React interface used by the human operator. OA’s Vulkan engine performs the actual ML, rendering, and media work. The browser remains a control and presentation surface. Generic interface components come from our existing Realm UI package, while application state and WebMCP registrations remain owned by the OA SDK demonstration. Challenges we ran into MCP and WebMCP are related but have different ownership and lifecycle models. An MCP server can operate independently, while WebMCP tools belong to an open browser page and disappear when that page closes or navigates away. Sharing tool semantics without accidentally creating two canonical execution paths required a careful composition boundary. Native GPU work is asynchronous and stateful. A WebMCP call being accepted does not mean a training mutation, checkpoint, render, or generation request has already completed. We needed explicit accepted, applied, completed, rejected, cancelled, and failed states. Security was another central challenge. The bridge must reject oversized or malformed input, arbitrary filesystem access, URLs, shader source, Vulkan handles, and unbounded allocation requests. Local execution also requires strict loopback binding, origin validation, per-launch credentials, bounded connections, and predictable shutdown. Finally, we needed to keep the browser responsive while the native Vulkan application continued running independently of page refreshes, reconnects, or agent availability. Accomplishments that we're proud of OA already provides a transport-independent MCP server with strict JSON parsing, bounded messages, deterministic tool registration, typed arguments, structured results, and adversarial tests. Its training adapter uses the existing oa::TrainingSession safe-point command system rather than mutating model or GPU state directly. The same session can therefore be controlled by native UI actions, MCP, and WebMCP without changing the underlying training semantics. We are particularly proud that OA remains the product: compute and rendering execute through our native Vulkan runtime; one oa::Engine owns GPU resources and scheduling; JavaScript does not emulate or replace the native workload; tool calls expose semantic actions rather than raw implementation handles; the human and agent work with the same live state; WebMCP becomes a reusable OA Network capability rather than challenge-specific glue. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it exposes meaningful application operations instead of reproducing every button in the interface. The strongest human-agent experiences share visible state, history, selection, and results. The agent should be able to act precisely, while the user can immediately inspect what changed and undo or refine it. We also learned that control traffic and bulk data need separate paths. JSON and WebMCP are appropriate for commands, metrics, provenance, and resource identifiers—not tensors, model files, video frames, or GPU memory. Most importantly, a generic bridge between a validated native tool registry and WebMCP is more valuable than writing isolated JavaScript handlers for every demonstration. What's next for oa::Network - WebMCP for native Vulkan applications Our first milestone is the complete tiny-language-model demonstration: live Vulkan training, metrics, pause and resume, evaluation, checkpoint reload, generation, and WebMCP control through one shared browser workspace. If time permits, the second demonstration will add prompt-to-motion generation, native 3D preview, timeline inspection, deterministic edits, and export through OA’s ALM and rendering stack. After the challenge, we plan to: qualify the bridge under sanitizers and adversarial protocol tests; add installed-package and fresh-browser testing; expand reusable TypeScript bindings without moving compute into the browser; support additional OA vision, audio, video, and 3D applications; benchmark the complete native-to-browser control path; add authenticated remote deployment while preserving the secure local default.  NEXUS-GEMINI: Autonomous Strategic Intelligence & Governed Performance Management Framework 

 Comprehensive Architectural Specification, Empirical Validation, and Master Implementation Report 

 

 Executive Summary 

 Modern enterprise performance management and digital forensic incident triage suffer from structural inefficiencies, cognitive bias, and fragmented execution loops. Organizations deploy millions of dollars into business intelligence (BI) dashboards, Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems, and multi-cloud telemetry fabrics. However, the human cognitive latency required to analyze complex multivariate datasets, synthesize strategic interventions, simulate downstream impacts, and execute remediation workflows creates a catastrophic gap between observation and action. 

 NEXUS-GEMINI bridges this chasm. Built as an agent-native, mathematically grounded, and strictly governed autonomous strategic intelligence platform, NEXUS-GEMINI unifies: 

 
 The 11-Layer Strategic Intelligence Architecture : Operationalizing organization-wide telemetry across financial, operational, technological, and tactical vectors into actionable decision tensors. 
 Dynamic Digital Twin State Simulation : Modeling the organization as a continuous state-space dynamical system governed by the transition function $D_{t+1} = F(D_t, A_t, E_t)$. 
 The Autonomous Action Score ($A_s$) & Multi-Tiered Governance Gate : A rigorous, tamper-evident mathematical gating mechanism that balances model confidence, empirical evidence quality, downside operational risk, and policy compliance before triggering autonomous actuators. 
 Standard WebMCP & SIFT Tool Fabric : Exposing 14+ type-safe, sandboxed, and tamper-resistant tools directly to autonomous agents via document.modelContext.registerTool() and custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) server endpoints. 
 Econometric & Empirical Validation Lab : Providing multivariate OLS regression modeling, statistical power analysis ($1-\beta = 0.99$), and paired sample hypothesis testing confirming an 89.4% velocity improvement and zero evidence spoliation . 
 

 

 1. What Inspired the Project 

 In high-stakes enterprise management and cyber incident response, decision-makers are overwhelmed by massive telemetry streams while simultaneously starved of causal clarity. Current solutions fall into two flawed extremes: 

 
 Passive Dashboards : Modern dashboards (Tableau, PowerBI, Datadog) display static historical figures. They describe what happened , but cannot diagnose why it happened , simulate what will happen if we act , or execute corrective actions . 
 Ungoverned Agentic Playgrounds : Generic LLM agent frameworks grant models unconstrained shell access ( execute_shell_cmd ), creating dangerous risks of evidence spoliation, runaway loops, and unverified hallucinations. 
 

 NEXUS-GEMINI was inspired by the conviction that autonomous agents must be architecturally constrained by rigorous mathematical models, empirical verification, and immutable governance gates . We set out to build an operating system for autonomous enterprise decision-making that thinks like a senior management scientist and digital forensics incident response (DFIR) lead. 

 

 2. What We Learned 

 Throughout the design, mathematical formulation, and full-stack implementation of NEXUS-GEMINI, our core engineering findings include: 

 
 Architectural Guardrails Over Prompt-Based Guardrails : Relying on system prompts (e.g., "Do not delete files" ) is intrinsically unsafe. True evidence integrity and enterprise safety require architectural enforcement : sandboxed MCP servers exposing typed, read-only methods ( get_amcache() , extract_mft_timeline() ), leaving no path for destructive execution. 
 Mathematical Formalization of Autonomy : Autonomy cannot be a binary toggle. By formulating the Autonomous Action Score ($A_s$) :
 A s = w 1 ⋅ C + w 2 ⋅ E + w 3 ⋅ ( 1 − R ) + w 4 ⋅ P 
where $\sum w_i = 1$, we establish a transparent, calibrated threshold separating autonomous execution (Tier 1, $A_s \ge 0.85$), human-in-the-loop executive sign-off (Tier 2, $0.55 \le A_s < 0.85$), and mandatory board review/rejection (Tier 3, $A_s < 0.55$). 
 Continuous Digital Twin State Modeling : Framing strategic operations as a state vector $D_t \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with intervention matrix $A_t \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and exogenous environmental noise $E_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$ enables Monte Carlo simulation and predictive trajectory bounds ($95\%$ confidence intervals) before committing enterprise capital. 
 Context Window Optimization via Structured Tool Summarization : Feeding raw disk images or multi-gigabyte CSV logs directly into LLM context windows causes severe degradation. Purpose-built WebMCP tools must aggregate, parse, and structure outputs into dense JSON summaries prior to LLM ingestion. 
 

 

 3. How the Project Was Built & Architectural Blueprint 

 NEXUS-GEMINI is engineered as a full-stack, real-time agentic platform with a modern React 18 + Vite frontend, an Express/Node.js orchestration backend, and the Google Gemini 2.5/3.7 Pro API engine.

 Technical Stack Specifications

 4. Problem Statement & Mathematical Formulation 

 The Latency & Alignment Problem 

 Enterprise operational friction is quantified by the decision latency interval $\Delta T$:
 Δ T = T execution − T observation = t ingest + t parse + t triage + t approval + t actuation 

 In traditional enterprise and incident response setups, $\Delta T \approx 4.8 \text{ hours}$ to $14 \text{ days}$, resulting in compounding financial churn and persistent adversary dwell time.

title: Signpost
pitch: One request. Many sites. Capability resolution for WebMCP agents.
about_excerpt: One request. Many sites. Capability resolution for WebMCP agents. Like Comment Story Updates Where the agent looked. What was allowed or blocked. What actually ran. ChatGPT: sources/multi-provider Exact term authorization Exact term revalidation test: authorized 10:00, proposed 10:30 - BLOCK, with 0 provider calls Signpost explores what happens when a user's compound request becomes a journey across independently operated WebMCP sites. Inspiration WebMCP gives individual websites a way to expose structured capabilities to browser agents. Those capabilities are exposed locally, while a user's compound objective can span several independently owned providers. I wanted to see whether a generic agent could compose that kind of journey without requiring any one provider, resolver, or platform to own it. For the challenge, that meant separating the problem: providers declare what they can do, Signpost resolves where those capabilities are available, and the agent decides which capabilities it needs and in what sequence. Consequential providers retain control over whether their own mutations may execute. The user can therefore begin with the outcome they want rather than a prearranged itinerary across specific sites: "order a coffee, book a basic haircut, and check this palette." What it does Signpost is a stateless capability resolver. An agent asks where a capability can be performed, and Signpost returns matching provider surfaces from declarations published by those providers. Signpost never receives the user's full objective. It doesn't decompose the request, maintain a session, choose the next step, or own an itinerary. The agent remains responsible for deciding what capabilities it needs and what to do next. For providers, this preserves a different boundary: they declare their own capabilities at their own origins rather than surrendering ownership of those capabilities to the system composing the journey. For the challenge, I built three independently deployed WebMCP reference providers: Deckhouse Coffee: order coffee Chair & Comb: find and book an appointment Hex Registry: check a hex value against a palette In the live demo, ChatGPT receives one request spanning all three. It determines the capabilities it needs, resolves them through Signpost, navigates to each provider, discovers its WebMCP tools, and completes the journey. For consequential actions, the agent can propose an action but cannot grant itself authority to execute it. Deckhouse Coffee and Chair & Comb display the exact material terms for user authorization at the provider. The pending invocation waits, then resumes and revalidates those terms immediately before execution. Only a valid, matching, single-use authorization permits the provider mutation. Signpost also keeps evidence separate from agent narration. Participating surfaces record authorization decisions, provider calls, and provider results so the evidence view can show what actually happened without becoming part of the agent's planning state. How I built it Participating providers publish small capability declarations describing what can be done at their origin. Signpost fetches those declarations and exposes one WebMCP tool: resolve_surface({ capability }) Matching is deliberately transparent: lexical retrieval with limited fuzzy matching, rather than another model in the loop. The result tells the agent where a capability is available, but never what it should do next. Each reference provider is an independent WebMCP surface and knows nothing about the others. Consequential providers place authorization and execution control at their own mutation boundary. The execution seam reuses @zioladev/execution-control@0.1.0 , a small package I published before the challenge. Its rule is intentionally narrow: only allow permits execution; block and indeterminate do not. The exact-term authorization flow, await/resume integration, reference providers, trusted-activation guard, evidence capture, and multi-provider Signpost flow were built during the challenge. I also included a deterministic drift test. It authorizes one set of material terms, presents different terms at execution, and verifies that the execution boundary returns BLOCK with zero provider calls. Challenges and what I learned The hardest challenge was not building too much into Signpost . Once an agent begins moving across several sites, it is tempting to give the resolver a session, itinerary, cursor, or concept of "next." Those features make orchestration easier, but they also change what Signpost is. I moved those responsibilities back to the generic agent, so the resolver remained stateless and journey blind. Cross-origin execution made that boundary practical rather than theoretical. Each provider had to stand independently on its own origin, while the agent could return to Signpost whenever it needed to locate another capability. The consequential flows evolved during the challenge as well. My first authorization design returned a "needs authorization" result and required the agent to retry after approval. I replaced it with await/resume: the original invocation now waits for authorization and then revalidates immediately before execution. That removed an unnecessary human-to-agent signaling round trip and narrowed the interval between authorization and use. That improvement made deliberate term drift difficult to demonstrate naturally in the live flow. Rather than weaken the runtime to manufacture a better demo, I moved that failure case into a deterministic test against the same execution boundary. A much smaller bug reinforced why I wanted the resolver to stay inspectable. An early provider description used words such as "ordered" while explaining what the provider didn't do. The lexical resolver matched it to an order query anyway. It was doing exactly what its transparent scoring rules said it should do. The failure was easy to understand and correct without introducing an opaque ranking layer. The larger lesson was that these responsibilities do not have to collapse into one agent system. A generic agent can choose the journey without becoming the capability registry, the source of execution authority, or the sole narrator of what happened. What's next Signpost is a reference implementation, not an attempt to prescribe how web-scale capability discovery must work. The broader question is what infrastructure an agent-operable web needs when agents begin moving across independently owned sites to complete a compound objective. Signpost explores one possible separation: The agent owns why and sequence. Signpost answers where. Providers own what. Consequential providers control whether a mutation may execute. Evidence records what happened. title: Restock Room
pitch: An agent-ready retail workspace that turns a stock alert into a reversible draft, then leaves approval to the operator.
about_excerpt:
An agent-ready retail workspace that turns a stock alert into a reversible draft, then leaves approval to the operator.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Retail teams do not need an agent that silently buys stock. They need help turning messy operational signals into a clear, reviewable next step. A shelf can be below its reorder point, compatible alternatives can exist, and the decision still belongs to the person responsible for stock and spend. 

 Restock Room explores that handoff. It gives an agent a narrow, explicit set of capabilities for finding evidence and preparing a proposal, while keeping the normal workspace understandable and the final approval visibly human. 

 What it does 

 Restock Room starts with visible low-stock alerts and a visible replenishment policy. A browser agent can read the alert evidence and policy, search the visible synthetic catalog for the affected item and alternatives, and create a replenishment draft or a policy-aware two-alert plan. The operator then reviews every proposed line in the same UI and approves or rejects it. 

 The draft or plan is intentionally the end of the agent's authority. The multi-alert plan enforces the visible 75% signal-confidence threshold, two-line limit, and $1,800 budget. Approval is a local, auditable UI action only: it never contacts a supplier, creates a cart, submits an order, or handles a payment. All catalog and inventory records in the demo are synthetic. 

 Why this is a strong WebMCP use case 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer workflows from a page's layout and text, which is brittle for operational work. Restock Room exposes the meaningful actions as structured tools, with stable names, input schemas, and safe outcomes. The agent can work with the same stock alert and catalog information the operator sees instead of guessing which controls or records matter. 

 That produces a better joint experience: the agent reduces the research and proposal work, while the human retains context, discretion, and final control. The normal UI remains fully usable even if WebMCP is unavailable, so agent support enhances the workspace instead of replacing it. 

 How we built it 

 The React and TypeScript app registers seven client-side WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser exposes the API: 

 
 
 Tool 
 Safety boundary 
 
 
 
 get_stock_alert 
 Read-only view of one visible alert and its evidence. 
 
 
 search_catalog 
 Read-only synthetic catalog search and alternative lookup. 
 
 
 create_replenishment_draft 
 Creates a reversible in-app draft; it cannot purchase or submit an order. 
 
 
 get_replenishment_draft 
 Read-only view of the draft and human approval state. 
 
 
 get_restock_policy 
 Read-only view of the visible budget, confidence threshold, line limit, and human-approval rule. 
 
 
 create_replenishment_plan 
 Creates a reversible two-alert plan only when it fits the visible policy; it cannot purchase or submit an order. 
 
 
 get_replenishment_plan 
 Read-only view of plan budget use and each line’s human decision. 
 
 

 The read-only tools use readOnlyHint , inputs are bounded with object schemas, and no tool exposes untrusted or user-generated content. The deployed static app also sets origin-isolation and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) headers for the WebMCP environment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hard product decision was restraint. It is easy to make a replenishment demo look impressive by letting an agent complete a purchase, but that conceals the real risks. We narrowed the tool surface to what an operator can inspect, reason about, and safely reverse. 

 We also designed the UI and the tool contract together. Every agent-visible result must make sense to a person looking at the workspace, and every material action must leave a visible trace. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 
 A complete alert-to-draft-to-approval workflow and a multi-alert policy plan rather than isolated tool calls. 
 A small WebMCP contract that clearly separates read-only lookup from reversible state changes. 
 A human-first fallback experience and an explicit audit trail. 
 A public HTTPS deployment that is ready for judges to test in a WebMCP-enabled browser. 
 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native product design is less about exposing every button and more about naming the few actions that carry real intent. A structured tool can make an agent more reliable, but the product must still say who owns the decision and what the tool is not allowed to do. 

 What's next for Restock Room 

 The next iteration would connect to real inventory feeds behind explicit authorization, add role-aware approval policies, and preserve a durable audit history. Any supplier or purchase integration would remain a separate, explicit human-approved step rather than an extension of the draft-creation tool.

title: Second Cursor: Moving Day
pitch: AI has entered the web. Second Cursor gives it a visible hand—and keeps the human in control.
about_excerpt: AI has entered the web. Second Cursor gives it a visible hand—and keeps the human in control. Like Comment Story Updates The Second Cursor interaction stays legible on mobile, including Agent status and human decisions. Human and Agent share one live room: visible intent, protected choices, and an explicit handoff. One workspace. Two cursors. A first step toward giving AI a visible hand on the web. The web was built for one cursor AI agents change that assumption. They introduce a second actor that can inspect, decide, and operate—but most interfaces still hide that work behind a chat box. We see the request and, later, the result. We do not see what the agent is targeting, what it is allowed to change, why it is waiting, or when control has returned to us. Second Cursor is a first step toward giving AI a visible hand on the web. One workspace. Two cursors. The white cursor belongs to the human. The blue cursor belongs to the agent. Both work on the same live surface, and the interface makes collaboration legible: target, intent, progress, constraints, changes, and handoff. Why a moving room? Moving Day turns an abstract interaction model into something everyone understands. A person and an agent arrange a room together. The agent can: inspect the live room and its constraints; point out a problem without changing anything; move or rotate unlocked furniture; ask the human to choose between equally valid options; finish with a visible summary of what changed. Every operation happens through a structured WebMCP tool and appears directly in the interface. The blue cursor travels to the object it is about to affect and explains why. Actionable transparency, not chain-of-thought Second Cursor does not expose or imitate private model reasoning. It reveals the information a person needs to supervise real work: the agent's target, intended action, resulting change, active constraints, waiting state, and control handoff. This is transparency at the interaction layer—the place where trust becomes a product behavior instead of a promise. Human authority is built into the surface The agent is capable, but it is not the owner. Lock an object and the agent must preserve it. Grab an item during an operation and the agent yields. When two placements are both valid but depend on taste, the agent asks instead of guessing. The human owns preference and final authority. The agent contributes attention, structured action, and speed. Why WebMCP? WebMCP lets a web page describe meaningful capabilities to compatible agents. That changes more than automation; it changes the basic grammar of the web. A page is no longer only a place where a person clicks. It can become a shared world where humans and agents act together. Second Cursor uses six real tools registered through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) : inspect_room , point_out_issue , move_item , rotate_item , request_choice , and finish_layout . The tools use bounded JSON schemas, stable furniture IDs, live page state, human locks, room constraints, explicit handoffs, and abort signals. No proprietary server-side model is required: the intelligence comes from the visiting WebMCP-compatible agent, while the page supplies capabilities, constraints, and visible feedback. What becomes possible Traditional software gives one person one cursor. Second Cursor imagines software where an agent can guide you, work for you, or work beside you—without becoming an invisible operator. The Moving Day prototype is intentionally simple, but the model can extend to design tools, spreadsheets, dashboards, editors, planning canvases, and any shared workspace where people need to understand and govern agent actions in real time. Built and verified The product is built with React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, and WebMCP, and hosted on ChatGPT Sites. It includes a scripted fallback so judges can experience the collaboration even when their current browser does not expose WebMCP. OpenAI Codex supported product research, concept refinement, implementation, schema design, automated testing, browser QA, deployment, demo production, and submission packaging. The public deployment was tested in ChatGPT's in-app browser: all six tools were discovered, and a live inspect_room call returned the current furniture, human locks, room bounds, and constraints. The automated suite passes 3/3 tests and the production build succeeds. AI has entered the web. Second Cursor makes its hand visible—and keeps the human in control. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: GomiMCP
pitch: Municipal waste rules that AI agents can understand and act on—without guessing, while humans retain control of final decisions.
about_excerpt: Municipal waste rules that AI agents can understand and act on—without guessing, while humans retain control of final decisions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Japan has highly organized waste-disposal systems, but the rules differ between municipalities. The same object may be classified differently depending on the city, quantity, size, material, or safety risk. People also rarely use exact official category names. They say things like: “I have ten of those transparent things sold at convenience stores for rainy days, something I put on the floor to sleep on, and a portable battery for charging my phone.” An AI agent can understand what the user probably means, but it should not invent municipal rules or automatically complete a potentially unsafe action. GomiMCP separates those responsibilities: The municipality declares the rules. The agent interprets the user’s language. The human makes the final decision. What it does GomiMCP is a static WebMCP-powered interface that exposes structured municipal waste rules directly from a webpage. The page registers three WebMCP tools: resolve_item converts ordinary or indirect wording into a canonical waste item. get_disposal_rule returns the municipality’s declared rule for that item. prepare_bulky_pickup prepares an eligible bulky-waste request without finalizing it. In the demo, the agent interprets one indirect Japanese request as ten umbrellas, one futon, and one mobile power bank. It makes eight real WebMCP calls: resolve_item ×3 get_disposal_rule ×3 prepare_bulky_pickup ×2 Under Aoba City’s fictional test rules, ten umbrellas and the futon are classified as bulky waste. GomiMCP prepares both requests and displays a Human Confirmation Gate totaling 800 yen. The mobile power bank is classified as high-risk. Automated preparation is refused, and the result is marked manual_review_required . The agent can prepare eligible requests, but it cannot press the final confirmation button. Nothing is booked until a human explicitly confirms it. How we built it GomiMCP is a static JavaScript application deployed with GitHub Pages. Its tools are registered using document.modelContext.registerTool() . Each tool provides a name, natural-language description, JSON input schema, execution logic, and safety annotations. The implementation separates: Item aliases and canonical identifiers Municipality-specific classifications Conditional rules such as quantity thresholds Fees and reservation requirements Risk levels and automation permissions Human-confirmation requirements Rule provenance and version information The LIVE WEBMCP TRACE displays only actual tool calls made through the page, making the interaction visible and auditable. No backend, database, authentication system, payment integration, or real municipality booking is used. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was deciding where language interpretation should end and authoritative decision-making should begin. Natural language is flexible, while municipal rules must be precise. Allowing a language model to invent a disposal category would be unsafe. Passing an entire ambiguous sentence directly into a rule engine would also be unreliable. We solved this with a staged flow: The agent interprets each description as one ordinary item concept. GomiMCP resolves that concept to a canonical item. The page applies the selected municipality’s declared rules. Risk policies determine whether automation must stop. Consequential actions stop at a visible Human Confirmation Gate. Another challenge was proving that the tools were actually called. The LIVE WEBMCP TRACE records real page-level tool activity rather than displaying a simulated agent response. Accomplishments that we're proud of We successfully demonstrated: Semantic interpretation of indirect Japanese descriptions Eight real WebMCP tool calls Deterministic results based on municipality and quantity Automatic refusal for a high-risk mobile battery Preparation of two eligible bulky-waste requests A mandatory human-confirmation boundary A visible and auditable trace of every tool call A complete product experience running as a static website We are especially proud that the demo shows a useful division of responsibility: the agent understands the user, the page owns the rules, and the human retains control of the final action. What we learned AI does not need to own every decision to be useful. The model is best used for understanding human intent. The authoritative source should still own the rule, the safety constraint, and the final action boundary. WebMCP makes this division practical. It allows an ordinary webpage to expose structured capabilities to an agent while preserving the page’s existing logic, state, and user interface. We also learned that observability matters. Showing the real tool-call trace makes the system easier to test, explain, and trust. What's next for GomiMCP The current version uses fictional municipalities and test rules derived from official municipal open-data structures. It must not be used as real-world disposal advice. Future work includes: Importing and validating real municipality-maintained rules Expanding rule provenance and version tracking Supporting more item conditions, such as dimensions and remaining contents Adding multilingual municipality-maintained descriptions Providing reusable schemas for additional municipalities Exploring Remote MCP and SDK integrations Testing the same contracts across more WebMCP-aware agents and browsers Our longer-term goal is simple: municipalities should be able to declare their rules once and make them safely usable by people, websites, and AI agents. title: Velaire — WebMCP Agreements for Service Businesses
pitch: Two independent agents negotiate through a live service website while humans control every consequential decision—with versioned offers, immutable receipts, and accountable change orders.
about_excerpt: Two independent agents negotiate through a live service website while humans control every consequential decision—with versioned offers, immutable receipts, and accountable change orders. Like Comment Story Updates System architecture: two independent ChatGPT agents share one revisioned ServiceCase while humans retain final authority. Live sequence: request, evidence, offer, counter, revision, booking and acknowledgment across separate agent sessions. Owner journey: scan the queue, read the case, stage terms, visibly send, wait for the customer and propose changed work. Customer journey: qualify, verify, open a case, negotiate, compare versions and prepare a human-confirmed booking. WebMCP observability exposes result codes, latency, revision effects, recovery states and zero autonomous commitments. Promise diff: offer V1, customer counter, accepted V2 and later changed work stay visible against the frozen receipt. Safety and trust gates cover emergencies, privacy, state, revisions, offers, human approval, asynchronous waits and audit. Structured tool results become useful map, route, market-price, project-timeline and agreement artifacts for people. WebMCP tool surface for discovery, evidence, negotiation, booking, routing, project planning, change control and audit. Evidence-aware discovery uses provenance, freshness, synthetic labels and untrusted-content hints before recommending a next step. Native WebMCP replaces brittle click automation with declared intent, typed inputs, explicit effects and valid next actions. Agreement state machine: valid states, revision checks and visible human gates control every consequential transition. Recorded proof: both sides finish on revision 9, a $320 authorized total and the same append-only decision trail. Recorded proof: the customer agent opens a request and the independent owner agent retrieves the same case and constraints. Recorded proof: a +$145 change order stays pending beside the locked $175 booking until the customer decides. Inspiration Service businesses already have websites, but most of those sites expose pages and contact forms rather than the structured truth an AI agent needs to complete a real customer journey. Pricing, availability, exclusions, messages, approvals, and later change orders are scattered across interfaces. An agent can discover a business yet still over-promise, act on stale terms, or mistake a private draft for an accepted agreement. We built Velaire to test a more useful WebMCP pattern: can an ordinary service website become a trustworthy agreement room for a customer's agent, an owner's agent, and the two humans who retain authority? What it does Velaire is a WebMCP-native reference implementation for service businesses, demonstrated through a fictional HVAC company. A customer speaks naturally to ChatGPT; the live website publishes typed capabilities that let the agent check service fit, policies, business evidence, pricing, and safety before opening a structured service case. A separate owner ChatGPT finds that same case through the owner route. The agents are independent and never role-play both parties in one conversation. They communicate through one revisioned ServiceCase that remains authoritative for messages, offers, counters, bookings, receipts, and changed work. The owner agent may prepare an offer, but it stays private until the owner presses Send. The customer agent may compare versions and prepare a booking, but only the customer can confirm it. That confirmation freezes an immutable receipt. If work changes later, Velaire compares the proposed charge against the exact accepted snapshot instead of silently rewriting history. Demo journey The customer asks for same-day help with an AC blowing warm air. ChatGPT checks eligibility, pricing evidence, availability, credentials, and safety. It opens a case with a $180 ceiling and explicit no-surprise-fee constraints. A separate owner agent retrieves the live request and prepares a $195 offer. The owner visibly sends the offer. The customer counters at $175 with no travel or after-hours fee. The owner sends offer version two. The customer agent compares both versions field by field. The agent prepares the booking; the customer confirms it, creating an immutable $175 receipt. The owner proposes a +$145 capacitor change order. Velaire shows the added scope, $320 total, and time impact against the original promise. The customer approves the change, the owner acknowledges it, and both agents independently read revision 9 with no pending decision. No real payment is taken, and every person, address, credential, review, price, and transaction shown is synthetic demonstration data. The WebMCP tool surface Customer discovery and trust velaire_check_service_fit checks need, postcode, urgency, budget, safety, and service eligibility. velaire_get_business_evidence returns source cards for credentials, pricing, availability, cancellation, warranty, and reviews. velaire_get_market_price_context and velaire_compare_quote_context provide transparent pricing context without presenting synthetic estimates as live market truth. Service, policy, site-search, contact, and agent-help tools make the ordinary website understandable without scraping its buttons. Shared customer–owner workflow velaire_open_service_case creates the authoritative record. velaire_get_service_case returns its current revision, messages, offers, decisions, and valid next actions. velaire_submit_case_message adds a bounded question or counteroffer and rejects stale revisions. velaire_wait_for_owner_reply and velaire_wait_for_customer_reply represent waiting honestly, with timeout and cancellation recovery. velaire_set_service_location, velaire_plan_service_route, and velaire_get_case_visuals return map, route, timeline, and visual artifacts. Owner workflow velaire_list_service_cases and velaire_get_owner_case expose the owner queue and exact case state. velaire_stage_owner_reply, velaire_stage_service_offer, and velaire_stage_change_order keep drafts private until a visible human Send action. Agreement protection and audit velaire_compare_offer_versions compares price, timing, deposit, warranty, scope, exclusions, and expiry deterministically. velaire_prepare_booking stages one exact offer version; it cannot confirm it. velaire_get_booking_receipt returns the full accepted snapshot rather than a mutable offer reference. velaire_compare_change_order checks later work against the accepted promise. velaire_audit_invoice_against_receipt detects invoice drift. velaire_get_webmcp_health exposes tool-call success, latency, revisions, read/action distribution, and recovery states. How we built it Velaire uses React, strict TypeScript, and Vite, deployed as a static application on Vercel. It registers native imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). The human UI and every WebMCP handler dispatch through the same pure TypeScript command gateway and reducer, preventing agent actions from bypassing the rules shown to humans. The demo persists state in localStorage, synchronizes tabs with BroadcastChannel and browser events, uses optimistic revision checks for every write, and records an append-only audit trail. Tool inputs use strict JSON Schema and runtime validation. Route scoping keeps customer and owner capabilities separate. Safety and human authority Emergency phrases such as gas smell, smoke, sparks, fire, or carbon monoxide trigger a safety stop instead of an ordinary quote flow. Agent schemas exclude payment details, direct contact identifiers, and exact home addresses. Agents can inspect, draft, compare, and prepare; humans alone send owner commitments, confirm bookings, approve changed work, and send the final acknowledgment. Challenges The hardest problem was not tool registration. It was preserving meaning across two asynchronous sessions: distinguishing a draft from a sent offer, rejecting stale writes, keeping accepted terms immutable, and treating “awaiting owner” or “awaiting human” as valid workflow states rather than fake success or failure. A second challenge was making the WebMCP layer invisible to ordinary customers. Velaire remains a polished service website; the agent uses the tool surface while the person sees familiar evidence, offer, comparison, booking, map, receipt, and decision interfaces. What we learned WebMCP becomes most valuable when tools expose domain decisions rather than page mechanics. “Click submit” is weaker than “prepare this exact offer version and show the human what will change.” Trust comes from typed outcomes, versioned promises, explicit non-effects, and visible authority boundaries—not simply from adding more actions. What's next The production path is server-side identity, durable cross-device storage, signed owner notifications, real calendar and payment providers behind the same prepare-before-commit gates, and adapters for clinics, agencies, repair companies, and other estimate-

video_transcript_excerpt: This walk through uses the AI voice of a mod Bukhari. The lair is a normal service business website. It's live page also gives a customer's chat GPT a structured way to understand the business and take safe action without scraping buttons or guessing from page text. The customer says the air conditioner is blowing warm air and asks for same-day help. Chat GPT checks service area, pricing, availability, credentials, and safety, then opens a case. The customer never needs a tool name. The owner's separate chat GPT checks the live queue and finds that case. Two independent agents in two independent sessions now communicate through one authoritative service record. The owner's agent prepares a response, but the draft stays private until the owner presses send. The first offer is $195 with a 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. window and a $49 deposit. The customer counters at 175 with no travel or after-hours fee. The owner sees that revision and sends a new offer. Now the customer's agent compares both versions field by field. It confirms the $20 reduction and checks that the schedule, deposit, warranty, scope, and exclusions have not quietly become worse. Chat GPT prepares the booking, but cannot accept it. The terms stay visibly pending until the customer confirms them on the page. That human action creates an immutable receipt for the accepted $175 agreement. No payment is taken. Next, the owner discovers a weak capacitor and proposes a $145 change order. The agreement is not overwritten. The customer sees added scope, total, and schedule impact against the accepted snapshot, then chooses whether to approve it. After approval, the authorized total is $320. The owner sends a final acknowledgement and both sides independently read the same revision with no pending decision. What you just saw is a chain of purpose-built web MCP tools. On the customer side, service fit and business evidence tools checked eligibility, pricing, source cards, and safety. Case and reply waiting tools carried the conversation without scraping the page. On the owner side, Q reply, offer, and change order tools kept every draft private until the owner pressed send. Comparison, booking preparation, receipt, map, route, and market price tools then gave the customer verifiable artifacts instead of a vague "Okay." The audit and health tools expose every call, revision, outcome, and latency. More importantly, the missing layer we address is not another chatbot. It is safe, asynchronous, two-party agreement infrastructure for service websites. Structured negotiation, explicit human consent, immutable receipts, and later charges compared against the promise that was actually accepted. HVAC is the reference implementation, but the same pattern can serve any service business.

title: tobidas
pitch: Pop-up book-style web builder
about_excerpt: Pop-up book-style web builder Like Comment Story Updates tobidas — Pop-up book-style web builder GIF Exports a single HTML file containing asset images, audio, and video. Production is possible while switching between the editing and playback screens. It is not limited to works for children; free expression is possible. Inspiration Advancements in AI technology have made it possible to create increasingly complex and beautiful graphics. I realized that I could finally bring to life the kind of pop-up book visuals I had loved since childhood. Excited by the prospect of creating something even more imaginative and fantastical than the pop-up books I used to craft from calendar cardboard as a child, I decided to give it a try right away. What it does Tobidas is a web page builder inspired by pop-up books. Tobidas means "pop-up" in Japanese. It allows users to create web pages with a pop-up book aesthetic, combining visual elements with images, audio, and video. Projects can be exported as a single, self-contained HTML file containing all necessary image, audio, and video assets. How I built it I built tobidas as an online, browser-based builder that keeps project data and imported media in the user’s browser instead of uploading them to a server. I used React, TypeScript, and React Three Fiber to create the interactive 3D pop-up book canvas. Book projects are represented as structured data containing spreads, pages, elements, assets, timelines, and camera settings. For WebMCP, I register structured tools when the browser exposes document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext . These tools can read project state, inspect spreads and assets, place and edit elements, update timelines and cameras, assign audio, navigate between spreads, and use undo/redo. I designed the standard builder UI and WebMCP to use the same state-management, validation, and command paths. This allows people and agents to work on the same project with the same behavior, undo history, and autosave system. WebMCP does not directly modify the DOM or bypass the builder. I included the player used to preview and export finished works in the public build, which I deployed as a static application on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges I ran into I was committed to maintaining a "static delivery model" where the user-side agent could build the project directly within the browser. My goal was to enable sophisticated visual expression via a single URL, without requiring users to clone the Tobidas repository. One of my biggest challenges was figuring out how to provide the fine-grained controls required by the builder while keeping this model intact. Relying solely on direct DOM manipulation made agent interactions unstable and often resulted in long wait times and unreliable operations. Furthermore, previous implementations that used a dedicated DOM manipulation interface for AI—in addition to the standard human-facing interface—created a maintenance burden due to the need to manage two separate systems. Accomplishments that I'm proud of By integrating WebMCP, I was able to provide agents with highly reproducible and reliable control capabilities without significantly altering the human-facing UI. The dedicated AI DOM manipulation interface was completely eliminated, allowing the human UI to serve seamlessly for collaboration with agents. In short, this realized a production experience where agents handle complex operations—maintaining a high degree of creative freedom—while humans can intervene as needed via the UI for detailed visual checks and fine-tuning. Furthermore, the WebMCP tool list doubles as a feature catalog for "Tobidas." This has improved both explainability and maintainability, enabling agents and developers to understand the application's capabilities without relying solely on visual UI information. What I learned While AI and other tools can greatly enhance creativity, they aren't a cure-all. Although WebMCP was incredibly powerful and contributed to the evolution of tobidas , I also encountered areas within the ecosystem ripe for improvement, such as browser compatibility issues and varying levels of support across different agents. In an era where almost anything can be created, I have come to realize that the most critical decision for a developer is to constantly think for themselves: what to prioritize, what to express, and how to compete using the resources currently at hand. What's next for tobidas There is still plenty of room to expand the expressive capabilities of tobidas . I also found that a single prompt to an agent is often not enough to produce a truly satisfying result. I will continue exploring new interaction designs and integrations with external tools, with the goal of enabling people and agents to create higher-quality work with fewer instructions.
