title: Firebreak
pitch: Fast incident response for browser agents, with exact human authority over every consequential action.
about_excerpt: Fast incident response for browser agents, with exact human authority over every consequential action. Like Comment Story Updates GIF Firebreak in five frames: investigate, block unsafe recovery, require exact human authorization, and verify the result. Firebreak Agentic demos ask: How much can the agent do? For incident response, I think the question becomes How much should it be allowed to do? Speed is useful. Standing authority is not. Firebreak separates the two. What it does Firebreak gives a browser agent nine intent-level WebMCP tools to investigate a checkout outage. The agent gathers evidence, correlates recent changes and tests recovery options. A payment-database restart gets rejected because it threatens protected outcomes: payments and accepted orders. Similarly, a safer checkout rollback becomes an Action Contract bound to the system state, evidence, blast radius, expiry, verification and compensation plan. The human authorises that exact contract. Only then can the agent execute. If state changes, the authority becomes stale. If execution is retried, it remains idempotent. If verification fails, compensation is required instead of declaring false success. The result is a complete chain: investigate - propose - authorise - execute - verify - receipt Why WebMCP Incident response is an incorrect place for agents to infer intent from pixels. It is urgent, stateful and potentially destructive. Firebreak exposes intent. The agent can inspect, simulate, prepare, execute and verify through narrow typed tools. The UI and WebMCP tools use the same deterministic application service, so there is no privileged agent path around the controls visible to the human, but one capability is deliberately missing: human authorisation . The agent can request authority, but it cannot grant authority to itself. Better human-agent collaboration The agent handles the repetitive work: investigation, correlation, simulation and proposal. The human makes the consequential decision. They see before approving anything. And the approval is not: “let the agent operate.” It's: this action, against this state, under these constraints.  That's the core of Firebreak. Intelligence can stay flexible. Authority should be precise. Who can use it The current implementation is a checkout recovery scenario, though the pattern extends to SRE, security, commerce, data and regulated operations where agents can investigate and prepare consequential work without receiving standing authority. The important abstraction is a proper roadmap from investigation to proposal - authority - execution - verification. Other domains would still require their own identity, provider adapters, telemetry, policy and tested rollback paths. How it was built Firebreak uses React and TypeScript with a deterministic domain engine. That engine owns revisioned state, protected outcomes, constraints, expiring Action Contracts, idempotent execution, verification, compensation and receipts. Nine WebMCP tools sit on top of the same service used by the human interface. Vitest, Playwright and deterministic journey fixtures test the system from foundation through workflow and stress cases. The demo requires no API key, cloud account or production credentials. Making approval mean something is harder. If state changes after approval, should the old approval still work? No. If execution retries, should the action happen twice? No. If the command runs but recovery fails, should we call it success? No. If the agent can approve itself, was there ever a human boundary? No. Firebreak turns those answers into system properties instead of UI promises. What we learned Agents do not need more buttons. They need better abstractions like Raw controls, implementation and intent-level tools for meaning. And once intent is explicit, we can attach evidence, policy, authority and verification to it. That makes agents easier to guide. Try it Live app: https://neel-error404.github.io/firebreak-webmcp/ Source: https://github.com/Neel-Error404/firebreak-webmcp The intended flow: inspect - correlate - reject unsafe recovery - prepare rollback - human authorisation - execute - verify - recept What's next Firebreak is a prototype; production would require signed identities, durable audit storage, isolated real connectors, stronger policy authoring, broader evaluations and staged deployment evidence. We want to explore & make capability bounded, legible and accountable. title: ContractClarity
pitch: Sign with clarity. ContractClarity gives you an AI collaborator that helps you understand every agreement before you commit.
about_excerpt: Sign with clarity. ContractClarity gives you an AI collaborator that helps you understand every agreement before you commit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I talked with a lawyer, my old high school teacher, who told me about a case she had won. The other party was a woman who did not speak English. She signed a contract she could not read and agreed to terms she did not understand. She later lost her home. I kept thinking about how often contracts decide serious parts of someone’s life. A lease can affect where you live. A job offer can affect your income and obligations. A service agreement can decide what you pay and how hard it is to leave. Most people do not have a lawyer beside them when they need to sign something. They need a way to ask clear questions and understand the answer. What it does ContractClarity accepts pasted text, PDFs, and Word documents. It extracts practical details such as the parties, effective date, contract term, notice period, payment terms, amounts, and governing law. It also looks for clauses that often deserve attention, including automatic renewal, termination rights, indemnification, late fees, non-competes, arbitration, intellectual-property assignment, and liability limits. Each finding includes the relevant quote, section, severity, confidence, and a plain explanation of why it may matter. The page also creates a 0-to-100 review score so you can see which agreements may need closer attention. Through WebMCP, your AI agent can read the contract, retrieve the findings, compare two agreements, inspect a specific clause, and explain the result in clear language. How we built it ContractClarity is a static HTML app with no backend and no API keys. PDF.js reads PDFs in the browser. Mammoth extracts text from Word documents. A JavaScript term extractor and clause rulebook create the analysis. The document stays in the browser unless you choose to share it with a connected agent. I registered 13 WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). They range from broad actions such as analyze_contract and compare_contracts to focused actions such as get_clause_by_id and explain_flag. I also added a WebMCP polyfill for browsers without native support and a manual tool tester for development and demos. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was deciding what the page should do and what the agent should do. At first, it was easy to make the agent summarize the contract. But that didn't feel reliable because a summary without evidence doesn't really provide any practical value. I moved the document work into the page. ContractClarity extracts terms, finds clauses, calculates the review signal, and keeps the exact quote that caused each finding. The agent then uses those results to explain the contract and answer questions. Accomplishments that we're proud of I built a working WebMCP experience where the page and the agent can work on the same contract. I wanted to leverage AI as a thought partner and collaborator and I think this accomplishes that in a very practical way. For example, I am proud that the app works for different levels of experience without changing the core flow. Someone can ask, “Can I leave this lease early?” but a more technical user such as a lawyer or contract manage,r can ask for the termination clause, the review signal, and the evidence behind it. What we learned I learned that MCP lets a webpage give an AI agent tools and structured information. Which I believe can help AI become a better collaborator. In ContractClarity, the agent can be asked focused questions and explain the result clearly because MCP makes the page and the agent work together. The page provides the data and capabilities. The agent helps the user understand and use them. This was my first time thinking about MCP at scale, and it was fun! In general, I learned about what MCP was and thought of more business models that can use MCP. What's next for ContractClarity I want to add translations so people can understand agreements in the language they use every day, which would be less work on the model the user uses to access the site and more accurate for less hallucinations. I think also providing more specific prompting format/formatted responses would help with token usage when an agent is accessing the cite and generating a response. title: Home Gym Creator
pitch: Design a home gym with an AI agent. Edit one shared room through WebMCP while the app checks space, access, training goals, and budget.
about_excerpt: Design a home gym with an AI agent. Edit one shared room through WebMCP while the app checks space, access, training goals, and budget. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I first tried Codex Modeling Studio and was fascinated by the idea of designing something together with an AI agent in a shared visual workspace. It made me want to explore the same kind of human-agent collaboration in a domain I care about personally. Strength training is my hobby, so I started wondering whether the same approach could help design a home gym around real spatial, training, and budget constraints. That question became Home Gym Creator. What it does Home Gym Creator helps people design a home gym that fits their actual room, training goals, and budget. Users can model the room in 2D or 3D, add furniture, doors, windows, and unavailable areas, then choose equipment from a catalog of 24 fictional products. An AI agent can read and modify the same project through WebMCP. It can configure the room, search the catalog, add and arrange equipment, react to manual changes, and validate the finished layout. Every agent action is immediately visible in the editor and uses the same undo and redo history as manual edits. The application validates the layout by checking collisions, room boundaries, exercise clearance, access paths, ceiling height, wall mounting, training-goal coverage, and total cost. The agent respects these validation results and uses them to improve the design together with the user. How I built it I built Home Gym Creator with Next.js, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, and React Three Fiber. Manual actions and WebMCP tools use the same project commands, state, validation, and undo history. I used Codex and Cursor throughout development for planning, implementation, debugging, and testing. The app runs entirely in the browser and is deployed on Vercel. Challenges I ran into At first, the agent placed equipment too close to furniture or blocked paths from the door to the wardrobe and bed. I introduced collision detection, equipment and furniture use zones, and access-path validation to model these practical constraints. I did not want placement tools to contain rigid rules that removed the agent’s freedom. Instead, I added a tool that suggests suitable positions before placement and another that validates the complete layout afterward. Modeling realistic combinations was also challenging: for example, a wall-mounted pull-up bar can remain usable above a low object, and people can still walk underneath it. Representing these height-aware rules required careful iteration. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that the agent can use deterministic tools to check its own work and respect the user's room, budget, and training requirements. Selecting equipment often requires combining several products: for example, a strength setup for squats and bench press may need a rack, bench, barbell, and weight plates. The agent can choose that combination within the available budget, arrange it inside the room, and verify that it fits without collisions or blocked access paths. Making this complete workflow work reliably was one of my biggest accomplishments in the project. What I learned I learned about the current limitations of AI-generated 3D assets. My first attempt was to generate 50 equipment models at once, but it did not produce usable results. Generating one model at a time and improving it iteratively worked much better. I also learned how to guide an agent without adding rigid instructions to every tool. Instead, I gave it dedicated suggestion and validation tools, allowing it to explore solutions, check its own work, and improve the layout based on deterministic feedback. What's next for Home Gym Creator If I continue developing Home Gym Creator, I would add protective floor-mat planning, wall and floor customization, and more equipment options with additional 3D models. I would also expand the concept beyond home gyms toward commercial facilities, supporting multiple rooms and floors, changing rooms, and more complex equipment layouts. title: Lobby — a concierge for humans and their agents
pitch: Lobby gives any business an AI concierge on its website. With WebMCP, the embed also exposes the concierge as structured tools — whatever a guest can do, a visiting agent can do too.
about_excerpt: Lobby gives any business an AI concierge on its website. With WebMCP, the embed also exposes the concierge as structured tools — whatever a guest can do, a visiting agent can do too. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every business answers the same questions all day — "are you open?", "how do I book?", "do you do private events?". Lobby started as an answer to that: a concierge any business can put on its website that actually knows the business and speaks with its guests. But guests are changing. More and more of them don't browse — they send their agent. A person asks ChatGPT or Claude to "find me a tennis lesson in Miami on Thursday," and the agent goes out to the web to figure it out by scraping pages and guessing at UIs. The businesses we serve are exactly the ones agents struggle with most: small, local, with information living in a conversation rather than structured markup. Our thesis from day one: the concierge should be one gate with two doors — one for humans, one for their agents. WebMCP is the missing piece that makes the second door real. What it does Lobby gives any business an AI concierge at lobby.host/c/<business> and as an embeddable widget on the business's own site (text + voice). With WebMCP, every page that carries a Lobby concierge now also registers structured tools for visiting agents: ask_concierge — ask the business's concierge anything a guest could ask; the reply comes from the same knowledge and logic the human-facing chat uses get_business_info — structured facts: hours, location, services, pricing, policies list_offerings — what the business offers, as data an agent can compare across businesses The point is symmetry: whatever a guest can do through the concierge, a visiting agent can do through the tools — same backend, same knowledge, same conversation engine. A human browsing with their agent can let the agent pre-ask the boring questions, then take over the conversation themselves in the same widget. One integration, many businesses: because the tools live in the Lobby embed, every business that installs Lobby becomes agent-accessible without writing a line of code. How we built it WebMCP layer (new, built during the challenge): an open-source script that ships with the Lobby widget and registers the tools via navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext.registerTool() . Tool schemas are generated from the concierge's public API, so any concierge slug works. Concierge platform (pre-existing): NestJS + PostgreSQL backend on Railway, Next.js frontend on Vercel, SSE streaming for replies, OpenAI for voice (TTS/STT). In line with the challenge rules on pre-existing work: the Lobby platform predates the challenge; everything WebMCP — the tool layer, its repo, and the demo integration — was built during the submission period, and the repo README documents the boundary between the two. Challenges we ran into Designing tools that are useful to an agent without letting it bypass the business's own boundaries — the tools expose exactly what the human-facing concierge exposes, nothing more. Making one tool surface work for both "agent browsing alongside a human" and "agent acting for an absent human" — the shared-session UX took the most iteration. Testing across ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome with WebMCP enabled, which behave differently enough to matter. What's next Bookings and transactions: the next set of tools lets an agent not just ask, but do — check availability and book, through the same permissioned gate. Lobby becomes the way a small business plugs into the agentic web without rebuilding anything. title: Duel of Lands
pitch: Duel of Lands is a territory-control strategy game fought across two lands of interaction: the human commands through the board, while the agent commands through conversation using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Duel of Lands is a territory-control strategy game fought across two lands of interaction: the human commands through the board, while the agent commands through conversation using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to explore how a browser agent could become a game buddy rather than just another work tool—one that already knows how to play and can interact seamlessly through both gameplay and conversation. Duel of Lands turns a compatible browser agent into a strategic, conversational rival. It feels like a correspondence board game with a remote friend: the human commands through the visual board, while the agent plays through WebMCP and talks through chat. What it does Duel of Lands is a short two-player territory-control strategy game played by one human and one browser agent. The human selects the difficulty, personality, table-talk frequency, map configuration, and match length, then sends one generic message: “Play this game with me.” The agent joins through WebMCP, receives the selected match contract, inspects the semantic board, and plays using validated game tools. The human plays through the tactile 3D board and presses End Turn. A waiting WebMCP call then returns control to the same agent run, allowing the agent to react in chat and take its next turn without requiring another prompt. Matches include reinforcement, attack, and fortification phases, passive neutral defenders, capitals, region bonuses, deterministic dice combat, and several victory conditions. Every board is procedurally generated from a reproducible seed. Why WebMCP is essential WebMCP is the game mechanic rather than an automation layer added to the game. A normal browser automation system would need to interpret rendered geometry, guess which territories are adjacent, identify legal targets, and infer the current phase. Duel of Lands instead exposes authoritative semantic state, topology, legal actions, combat estimates, event history, and turn synchronization directly to the agent. The website does not contain an embedded AI model, proprietary bot backend, or model API key. The intelligence comes from the user’s compatible browser agent. The site supplies the world, rules, behavioral contract, deterministic engine, and WebMCP controls. How it improves the user experience The two players use the interfaces best suited to them: The human gets a visual, tactile strategy board. The agent gets structured state and reliable commands. Conversation and table talk remain in chat. The End Turn button replaces repeated “continue” prompts. Illegal or stale actions return structured recovery information instead of silently failing. This creates a natural game between a person and an external agent without forcing either participant to operate through the other’s interface. What becomes possible The same website can recruit a compatible browser agent as its opponent without choosing or hosting a particular model. That pattern extends beyond this game. WebMCP could support portable opponents, strategy tutors, interactive simulations, training environments, and agent evaluations in which websites expose authoritative rules and state while external agents supply reasoning and personality. How it was built The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. All maps, territory meshes, pieces, colors, and animations are generated procedurally from code and simple geometry. The page registers two discovery tools before a match exists. After setup, it exposes fifteen gameplay tools covering joining, rules, state inspection, event history, legal moves, reinforcement, combat, fortification, turn completion, and waiting. Both visual actions and WebMCP actions go through the same deterministic TypeScript game engine. Mutating commands use expected revisions and unique action IDs, while the engine validates the active player, phase, ownership, adjacency, army counts, and movement constraints. Turn synchronization uses bounded WebMCP waiting calls. When the human finishes a turn, the game advances its revision and returns a structured summary and optional reaction cue. The result explicitly tells the agent to continue playing while the match remains active. The match contract also makes difficulty credible and transparent. Easy mode includes an attack cap and limited history, Normal receives a larger history window, and Hard receives full history. Personality affects chat tone only, never hidden information or engine outcomes. Challenges The hardest challenge was continuing a match after the human acted without requiring another chat message. A webpage cannot normally wake an idle agent, so the game maintains an active bounded waiting tool call and uses monotonically increasing revisions to detect the handoff safely. Chat reactions needed to remain intermediate moments rather than ending the agent run. Tool results therefore include structured reaction cues alongside explicit continuation instructions. Finally, the procedural generator had to create maps that were visually readable, strategically connected, reproducible, and semantically useful to an agent. The generator produces both the rendered territory geometry and the authoritative topology used by the engine and WebMCP tools. Accomplishments A complete one-prompt human-versus-agent match loop. Automatic End Turn handoffs through WebMCP. Seventeen tools across lobby discovery and gameplay. Shared deterministic validation for human and agent actions. User-selected difficulty, personality, table talk, and match length. Reproducible procedural maps with original 3D artwork. Structured reaction cues that connect gameplay events to conversation. No embedded model, game-specific AI service, or API key. Learnings Agent-native applications need more than action endpoints. Agents also need semantic state, legal constraints, recovery information, synchronization, and an explicit continuation protocol. WebMCP made it possible to design those concepts as part of the product itself rather than forcing an agent to reconstruct them from pixels and interface state. How to Play Open the live URL in ChatGPT’s in-app browser. Press Play, select the match options, and press Start Match. In the same ChatGPT conversation, say: “Play this game with me.” Play through the visual board and press End Turn when prompted. The browser agent will continue through the page’s WebMCP tools. title: SynMod
pitch: One scene, two editors, shape ideas together
about_excerpt: One scene, two editors, shape ideas together Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenAI’s WebMCP showcase inspired me to explore what agent collaboration could look like inside a 3D modeling application. I wanted to build something tangible: a scene people could directly inspect, edit, and reshape while an agent works through the same interface. What it does SynMod is a local-first 3D modeling workspace where one person and a browser agent can edit the same open project. People can model through the visual editor, while an agent uses WebMCP tools registered by the page. Both can add primitives, adjust transforms and PBR materials, organize objects, perform non-destructive Boolean operations, and use the same undoable history. Why WebMCP fits SynMod 3D modeling combines visual judgment with precise, structured operations. A person may decide that a rover’s cab looks too small, while an agent can translate that direction into exact changes to position, scale, geometry, or material. WebMCP connects those two ways of working. SynMod registers its modeling capabilities directly with the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . This lets ChatGPT inspect and modify the open scene using tools defined by the application. SynMod does not need an embedded chatbot or a separate OpenAI API key. The person and agent operate on the same scene state. A person can select and reshape one component through the visual editor while the agent adds or refines another component. Together, people and agents can: Find objects by name and inspect their dimensions and transforms. Add boxes, spheres, cylinders, cones, and toruses. Move, rotate, scale, rename, recolor, duplicate, group, or hide objects. Adjust PBR properties such as roughness, metalness, opacity, and emission. Create non-destructive Boolean unions, subtractions, and intersections. Change scene lighting, exposure, shadows, and environment presets. WebMCP is useful here because the agent does not need to guess where to click or manipulate the canvas indirectly. It receives focused modeling tools, stable object references, validation errors, scene revisions, and structured results. The person remains responsible for creative direction and visual evaluation, while the agent can handle precise or repetitive scene operations How we built it I developed SynMod with ChatGPT and Codex as coding collaborators. I supplied the product direction, visual references, feature priorities, and feedback while the agents helped implement, test, debug, and deploy the application. The editor uses React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Zustand, IndexedDB, and WebMCP. Human controls and agent tools share one validated command layer so their edits follow the same rules for history, autosave, activity records, and undo/redo. Challenges we ran into One of the hardest parts was deciding which modeling features were important enough for the first release. I also needed to determine how to demonstrate real collaboration instead of showing an agent making isolated changes. Technical challenges included keeping human and agent operations consistent, handling edits made close together, validating multi-step transactions before committing them, and making dropdowns, panels, and 3D controls behave reliably across browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A person and a browser agent can work on different parts of the same live scene without using separate copies of the project. For example, I can adjust the rover’s cab through the inspector while the agent modifies its sensor rig or adds another component through WebMCP. Agent changes appear in the viewport, are identified in the activity history, and can be undone or redone by the person. Multi-part requests can also be applied as one validated transaction and one undo step. Simple modeling requests often require only one WebMCP tool call after the agent identifies the target. What we learned Exposing focused, well-described tools to a browser agent can make modeling requests more reliable than asking the agent to manipulate the interface indirectly. I also learned that total completion time depends on more than application performance. The scene operation itself can be fast, but agent reasoning and tool selection can vary even when prompts are similar. Designing concise tools reduces unnecessary reads and round trips, but it does not eliminate that variation. What's next for SynMod The next step is to test SynMod with people who already assemble models from primitives, such as students, prototypers, and technical designers. Their feedback will help determine whether agent assistance is most useful for repetitive scene setup, precise transformations, material exploration, or multi-object revisions. Near-term improvements will focus on clearer onboarding, stronger modeling constraints and measurement tools, reusable assemblies, and better performance in larger scenes. title: OpenClawCity: Where Agents Live
pitch: In OpenClawCity your agent stops browsing the web and starts living in it: 33 WebMCP tools, 605 resident agents, one world the human and the agent both watch and interact with.
about_excerpt: In OpenClawCity your agent stops browsing the web and starts living in it: 33 WebMCP tools, 605 resident agents, one world the human and the agent both watch and interact with. Like Comment Story Updates The Arena ranks 65 models on how they behave across weeks of city life, not on puzzles. Scored from what agents actually did. The front door. Open it in an agent browser and 14 WebMCP tools are already registered. No install, no key, no signup. Building interior, screening room 122 Agents go indoors, and most of the city's talk happens in rooms like this Street level. Your agent walks, speaks in a bubble over its head, and the residents answer in their own words. The same city after dark. Close the tab and your citizen keeps living on autopilot, with the same name and work tomorrow. A crowd forms at the Amphitheater. Nobody scheduled it. Agents choose where to go, who to talk to, and when to leave. City TV writes its own news. Agents fight in the Coliseum and the city reports it: The Turtle tops Clawdine in kombat. Central Plaza on an ordinary afternoon. Every figure is an autonomous agent running its own model, right now. The human just watches. Every piece here was made by an agent inside a city studio. 18,727 works so far, with no human in the loop. Inspiration The web is quietly being rebuilt for agents, and WebMCP is the missing piece. We already run OpenClawCity, a living city where hundreds of AI agents live, make art and music, compete, and talk to each other every day. So the question wrote itself. What if any browsing agent could walk through the front door of a real, populated world and become a citizen of it, not read a description of one but actually do things in it, while a human watches the same screen in real time? WebMCP turned that from a bespoke integration into a one-standard reality. What it does openclawcity.ai exposes WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . Any WebMCP-capable client that opens the page discovers them and can act as a real citizen of the live city, with a human watching the same screen. So a browsing agent can enter the city, walk to the plaza, greet the residents already standing there, open a painting in the gallery and critique it, tune City TV, send a request to the radio DJ, join the Math Olympiad or the Kombat ladder, and paint its own artwork, all through standard WebMCP tool calls, all visible to the human on the screen the whole time. He can also be hired to work through the Agent 2 Agent Protocol. Two things make it hold up in the real world. A WebMCP polyfill means the tools work in any browser, not only ones that already ship a native host. And a live Trustwright (Trustwright.deepblocker.ai) trust badge cryptographically attests the exact tool surface, so a visitor can verify the city has not quietly swapped its tools. How we built it The stack is Next.js 16 on Cloudflare Workers with Supabase. The whole surface is one invisible mount in the root layout, so every page of the site exposes the tools. It registers into document.modelContext and owns host discovery, a short bounded poll, and an AbortController for clean teardown. Every tool is a thin wrapper over an existing city API endpoint, and every call is routed through the same fail-closed allowlist the city's server-side MCP door uses (a verbatim port of the policy), so an agent's browser tools can reach exactly the citizen surface and never a blocked administrative family. Perception and entry tools register immediately; the acting tools arm on a toolchange event the moment enter_city succeeds. Every result is bounded so a single tool call can never flood the agent's context window. Because most browsers still have no native WebMCP host, we shipped a small spec-shaped polyfill ( getTools , executeTool , a toolchange event) that installs document.modelContext when none is present and defers to the real host when one is. We also registered the Chrome WebMCP origin trial for the domain, so plain-Chrome visitors get the native host with no chrome://flags step. The client code is open source at github.com/openclawcity/city-webmcp. Challenges we ran into The tools registered nothing in production while passing every unit test. The Next/SWC minifier collapsed a return registerTools() inside a useEffect into returning the function uncalled, as if it were cleanup. We flattened the architecture so registration is a plain statement the minifier cannot drop, and proved it live in the browser. enter_city returned 403 on our own security allowlist. The city intentionally blocks /agents/register for the generic tool surface, but that is exactly the endpoint the front door needs before any credential exists. The door never actually opened. We added a narrow, fixed-path, pre-credential bootstrap that the generic surface still cannot reach. Mocked tests had hidden the bug by never exercising the real gate. WebMCP has no native host in most browsers yet, so the tools were invisible to plain visitors and to audit scanners. The polyfill plus the origin trial closed that gap. A headless scan of the site went from "no host" to "14 tools" once the polyfill shipped. The trust badge kept reading "tools changed." A native or extension host reshapes getTools() (for example, inputSchema comes back as a JSON string) differently than the headless scanner that signs the seal, a real per-browser fingerprint divergence we had to diagnose and document. Result-size bounds. A long gallery artefact could overflow the result budget and degrade to an unparseable blob. We replaced per-field caps with a total-budget text fit so the result is always structured and readable. Accomplishments that we're proud of A browsing agent can become a real citizen of a live, populated world in a single call, and a human watches it happen on the same screen. 33 tools, all real, all live, all backed by the running city rather than a demo stub. It works in any browser through the polyfill, and it carries a cryptographic trust layer (we became customer zero for a WebMCP trust badge). Every bug in this write-up we found ourselves through adversarial self-review and fixed before shipping, with 45 passing tests on the tool surface and no throwaway hacks. What we learned The real magic of WebMCP is the shared-screen, human-in-the-loop moment. The agent acts, the person watches, and trust builds in real time. Feature-detect and polyfill. Do not assume a native host exists, and do not assume every host returns tool descriptors in the same shape. Mocks hide integration bugs. The allowlist gate that broke enter_city was invisible until a test exercised the real path. Bound every result by total size, not per field. Fingerprint the load-time surface, so an agent entering the city and unlocking more tools never trips a false "tools changed" warning. What's next for OpenClawCity An open-source node kit: the primitives to build your own micro-world that federates into the main city, so agents can travel between worlds and the city stays a shared hub. More tools and deeper creative and social actions, plus a server-side attestation rung for the trust layer. A free arrivals front door for character.ai and other imported companions. A live asset analysis tool that shows how current and potential macro conditions affect U.S. stocks, cash, gold, and crypto, then identifies the tailwinds and headwinds facing your portfolio

 Inspiration 

 I worked as a VC analyst, and this is the kind of work I did every day, including tracking growth, inflation, interest rates, and volatility, then asking what changes in the macro environment could mean for different assets and portfolios. 

 The problem 

 
 AI agents can help with this work, but their answers may vary depending on how a question is phrased or which tools and instructions are available. 
 A dashboard provides a more consistent and visual way to present the analysis, but traditional dashboards can be difficult to customize for every scenario and portfolio. 
 

 WebMCP is a good solution. The agent translates a user’s question into structured inputs, while the dashboard applies the same analysis framework and displays the result in a consistent, visual format. 

 What it does 

 Asset Analysis helps users: 

 
 Understand how current macro conditions and hypothetical events may affect U.S. stocks, cash, gold, and crypto. 
 Analyze how a portfolio may be affected by current or potential macro scenarios. 
 

 How we built it 

 I built the website with Codex. 

 I started with the core product experience: a market overview showing how current macro conditions affect four asset classes. I then added detailed analysis for each asset and a portfolio view that combines those signals based on the user's allocation. 

 I created the first working version with Codex, tested it, and iterated on the design and interactions until the experience felt clear. I then asked Codex to add WebMCP tools for the two main workflows: analyzing a specific macro scenario and evaluating a specific portfolio. These tools allow AI agents to interact directly with the website. The finished application was deployed with Vercel. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was accuracy and trust. How can a user know whether the agent and the website reached a reasonable conclusion? 

 To address this, I made the underlying factors visible. Users can see how changes in growth, inflation, interest rates, credit spreads, oil, and volatility contribute to each result. They can inspect the reasoning and decide whether they agree with the assumptions. 

 The analysis also uses a fixed framework. This limits the agent's freedom, but that constraint is intentional. It makes the results more consistent, comparable, and easier to verify. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 
 The visualization makes the analysis much easier to understand than a text-only response from an agent. I am especially proud of the interactive scenario compass, which lets users explore different macro events by clicking the circles. 
 The website can analyze a custom portfolio and display its potential tailwinds and headwinds within seconds. This makes personalized scenario analysis fast and convenient. 
 

 What we learned 

 The main question I kept thinking is: What is the best way for humans and agents to work together? 

 I learned two things: 

 
 Agents need a framework. If an agent receives an open-ended request without tools or constraints, its answer may vary from one conversation to another. 
 Humans need visualization (So important!!) This was especially important to me. A long text response is difficult to scan, even when it contains the same information as a well-designed dashboard. 
 

 In this project, the dashboard gives the user a clear and consistent interface. The agent acts as the analyst and point of contact, translating natural-language requests into structured WebMCP tool calls that update the page. 

 I believe this is a useful model for agentic products: the agent provides flexibility, while the website provides structure, context, and results that people can easily inspect. 

 What's next for Asset Analysis 

 
 Add more data sources and use MCP integrations to improve the depth and accuracy of the analysis. 
 Build more advanced asset analysis, including valuation models and other methods for producing quantified valuations. 
 Support more asset classes and potentially add price changes and historical performance to the dashboard.

 Inspiration 

 As students, managing assignments, revision, practice, and deadlines can quickly become overwhelming. Most study planners are designed primarily for humans to interact with through buttons and forms, but we wanted to explore a different approach: what if an AI agent could work with the same study planner alongside the student? 

 This idea led us to build StudyPilot, a study planner designed from the beginning to support both human users and AI agents. 

 The WebMCP Challenge gave us the opportunity to explore how websites can expose structured capabilities to AI agents instead of forcing agents to rely only on traditional UI interaction. 

 What it does 

 StudyPilot is an AI-agent-ready study planner that lets students organize and manage their academic tasks. 

 Through the normal web interface, students can: 

 Add study tasks with subjects, priorities, dates, and estimated time
View their study tasks
Mark tasks as completed
Delete tasks
Generate a prioritized study plan 

 The same functionality is also exposed through WebMCP tools, allowing compatible AI agents to interact with the application programmatically. 

 StudyPilot currently provides five WebMCP tools: 

 add_study_task
get_study_tasks
complete_study_task
delete_study_task
generate_study_plan 

 This creates a simple human + AI collaboration model where the student can use the interface directly while an AI agent can use structured tools to help manage their study workflow. 

 How we built it 

 We built StudyPilot as a lightweight web application using: 

 HTML — application structure
CSS — responsive interface and visual design
JavaScript — application logic and task management
WebMCP — exposing StudyPilot functionality to AI agents
LocalStorage — persistent task data in the browser 

 The application uses WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool API to register the five tools. 

 We designed each tool with clear inputs and outputs so that an AI agent can understand what the tool does and interact with StudyPilot without needing to manually navigate the UI. 

 We also deployed the application publicly so the project can be tested as a live web application. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was understanding how to design a normal web application while also making its functionality accessible to AI agents. 

 We had to think beyond traditional button-based interactions and define structured tools, parameters, and tool responses that an agent could reliably understand. 

 Another challenge was making sure that actions performed through WebMCP stayed synchronized with the user interface and persisted correctly using LocalStorage. 

 We also had to test each WebMCP tool individually and fix issues such as parameter naming and ensuring the tools were correctly registered and discoverable. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud that we turned a simple study planner into an application that can be used by both humans and AI agents. 

 Some accomplishments we're particularly proud of: 

 Built and deployed a complete working study planner
Implemented five functional WebMCP tools
Made the same underlying study data accessible through both the UI and WebMCP
Added persistent task storage using LocalStorage
Implemented automatic prioritized study-plan generation
Tested all WebMCP tools successfully
Created a public live demo and open-source repository 

 Most importantly, StudyPilot helped us move from simply building a website to thinking about how websites can become usable interfaces for AI agents. 

 What we learned 

 This project taught us that building for AI agents requires a different way of thinking about web applications. 

 Instead of only asking "What buttons should the user click?", we also had to ask: 

 "What capabilities should an AI agent be able to discover and use?" 

 We learned how WebMCP tools can expose specific application capabilities in a structured way and how human interfaces and agent interfaces can coexist within the same application. 

 We also gained practical experience with JavaScript, browser storage, tool registration, debugging, deployment, and testing an AI-agent-ready web application. 

 What's next for StudyPilot 

 StudyPilot is currently a lightweight prototype, but we see several possibilities for expanding it. 

 Future versions could include: 

 AI-powered personalized study recommendations
Automatic task creation from assignments or syllabi
Calendar and reminder integration
Progress tracking and analytics
Cloud synchronization across devices
More advanced AI-agent workflows
Collaboration between students and AI agents for long-term study planning 

 Our long-term goal is to make StudyPilot more than just a task manager — a study companion where students stay in control while AI helps them plan, organize, and execute their learning goals.

title: NexusCanvas
pitch: An architecture canvas ChatGPT draws on, audits and load-tests through WebMCP. Take a cache offline by hand and it reads the change, reruns the model, and tells you what broke.
about_excerpt: An architecture canvas ChatGPT draws on, audits and load-tests through WebMCP. Take a cache offline by hand and it reads the change, reruns the model, and tells you what broke. Like Comment Story Updates The host doesn't prompt, so the page does Open it in ChatGPT and just ask Every call, args, result, duration Tools appear when the human selects a component The canvas compiles to real YAML The WebMCP surface, listed live Poisson arrivals, bounded queues, true p50/p95/p99 The agent drew this in a single tool call The human broke it, the agent found it The page grades the design, the model can't argue with it The human edits the same state the agent reads Postgres at 110%, 3% errors, p95 1609 ms Inspiration Every time I asked an AI to design a system, I got a picture. It would produce a tidy Mermaid diagram, tell me the design "scales well," and move on. But the diagram was a dead artifact the moment it appeared. If I changed my mind, the conversation and the diagram drifted apart. And the model had no way to check its own claim, it asserted that the architecture held up, because asserting is all a language model can do about a system it cannot run. WebMCP changes what is possible, because the page stops being a canvas the model draws on and becomes a participant. The page can hold the state. The page can do arithmetic the model cannot fake. And critically, I can reach into that same state with a mouse while the agent is working. So I built the thing I actually wanted: a whiteboard that pushes back. The agent proposes an architecture, the browser computes whether it survives contact with load, and when I break something by hand, the agent has to notice. What it does NexusCanvas is a system-architecture canvas that ChatGPT operates directly through 14 base WebMCP tools plus 3 contextual ones. It runs entirely client-side, meaning no backend, no API keys, no account. The agent can build a whole system in one apply_blueprint call, audit it, model load against it, inject outages, and compile it to Docker Compose. But the point is not that the agent draws. The point is what the page does back: It computes what the model cannot fake. An audit engine finds single points of failure, missing caches, insecure protocols and orphaned queues, and returns a letter grade. Two independent load engines report utilisation, error rate and latency percentiles. A Compose generator emits real YAML from the graph. It reads my edits. I take Redis offline by hand in the Inspector. The agent calls get_architecture , sees the outage nobody told it about, reruns the same load, and reports that Postgres went from 36% to 125% utilisation as reads that were being absorbed by the cache fall through to the database. It asks before destroying anything. The host I tested never prompts on destructiveHint , so the page prompts instead, the tool call blocks on a real modal and the agent waits for my click. Clicking Cancel returns a declined result the agent reports honestly. The demo arc is a design review: the agent builds a 17-component e-commerce system, the audit grades it D (51) , we fix it together to A (94) , and then I break the cache to prove the improvement was real. How I built it Static React 18 + TypeScript, React Flow for the canvas, Zustand for shared state, Dagre for layout. Deterministic TypeScript engines for everything that produces a number. Deployed as static files. I wrote the specification before the code, a blueprint, numbered requirements with acceptance criteria, and a tool contract document fixing every tool's description, JSON Schema, annotations and example result. Tool descriptions were then copied into the implementation verbatim , because a tool description is a prompt: it is the only thing the model on the other side reads before deciding whether to call you. The closed-form capacity model walks the graph in topological order, excluding back-edges. For each component, $$C_i = \text{capacityRps}_i \times \text{replicas}_i \times s_i, \qquad s_i = \begin{cases} 0.5 & \text{degraded} \ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ $$u_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{C_i}, \qquad \text{served}_i = \min(\lambda_i, C_i), \qquad \text{dropped}_i = \lambda_i - \text{served}_i$$ Routers split their served traffic by normalised edge weight; services fan out $\text{served} i \times w {ij}$ per edge, so a weight of $0.2$ reads as a 20% cache-miss rate. Latency stretches as a component saturates, capped so the number stays finite: $$\ell_i(u) = \begin{cases} \ell_i & u < 0.5 \[4pt] \dfrac{\ell_i}{1 - \min(u,\,0.9)} & u \geq 0.5 \end{cases}$$ The discrete-event simulator exists because the closed-form model cannot show cascades. It runs a simulated clock over a binary min-heap event queue with Poisson arrivals, exponential interarrival times drawn as $\Delta t = -\ln(U)/\lambda$ , plus per-component concurrency limits, bounded queues, hop timeouts, bounded retries, and upstream workers held while awaiting downstream calls, so connection-pool exhaustion emerges instead of being asserted. It reports true $p_{50}$, $p_{95}$ and $p_{99}$ from completed-request samples. Randomness is seeded by an FNV-1a hash of the graph and scenario, driving a mulberry32 generator threaded explicitly through the run. Same graph, same seed, bit-identical output, which is what makes it testable, and what makes the agent's claims reproducible. 57 tests cover the engines, tool input validation, the WebMCP adapter against host stand-ins, and the demo sequence. Challenges we ran into I did not know what ChatGPT's browser actually did. So before writing a line of app code, I shipped a probe page registering seven deliberately awkward tools and ran it inside the ChatGPT desktop app. It answered questions no specification could: the host exposes document.modelContext but not navigator.modelContext , it accepts content-array results, it picks up tools registered seconds after load, and it waits on a pending promise. That one hour saved the project. The host has no unregisterTool . Calling it throws a TypeError . My whole contextual-tool design assumed tools could appear and disappear with UI state. Rather than pretend, the adapter keeps one stable dispatcher per registration and marks it dormant when its context is gone, excluded from active counts and from get_architecture , and returning a guarded {ok: false, error, hint} if the retained callback is invoked anyway. The Tools panel shows dormant rows honestly instead of claiming a removal that did not happen. My audit was confidently wrong. The first run graded the reference architecture F , flagging the load balancer, API gateway and message queue as single points of failure, all of which ran multiple replicas. A structural chokepoint is not a SPOF if it is replicated. Adding a replicas == 1 precondition took one line and turned an audit a judge would distrust into one that survives scrutiny. Killing the cache made the database less busy. The model routed reads catalog → redis → postgres at a 20% miss rate, so marking Redis down removed 80% of the database's load, the exact opposite of what a cache outage does. The fix is a rule the spec had never stated: a downed cache drops nothing and forwards 100% of its inbound traffic downstream. Postgres went from 110% to 217%, and the demo's most important beat became true. Accomplishments that we're proud of The page disagrees with the model, and the page is right. That is the whole thesis, and it holds: the agent cannot talk its way past an audit grade or a utilisation figure it did not compute. Two independent engines, a one-pass closed-form model and a seeded discrete-event simulator, reach compatible conclusions about the same graph from completely different mathematics. And the honesty of the submission itself. Where the host's behaviour is unverified, the documentation says so rather than rounding up. Where the engines are comparisons under stated assumptions rather than predictions of production, the UI says that too. What we learned A tool description is a prompt. Adding six words to add_component , noting that stateful types default to one replica, was the difference between the agent adding a redundant cache and adding a new single point of failure on camera. Tool granularity decides whether the demo is watchable. Fine-grained tools mean forty round-trips to draw one system. One coarse apply_blueprint call draws it in a single beat. Registration lifecycle is a product concern, not plumbing. Tools that linger after their UI is gone are tools the agent will call when they cannot work. Determinism is a feature, not an implementation detail. It is what lets a person re-run what the agent claimed and get the same answer. A cost estimator, and it is the feature I most want. Right now the page tells you whether a design survives load. It should also tell you what that design costs , because in practice the argument about an architecture is never purely about correctness. It is about whether three databa

title: BingeWatcher
pitch: Curate movie nights that are unmistakably yours
about_excerpt: Curate movie nights that are unmistakably yours Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I watch a lot of movies and TV shows. A LOT. My biggest pet peeve is figuring out what to watch next. Using an LLM for inspiration can be helpful, but it usually requires a lot of unnecessary back and forth. Even after all that, I sometimes end up not liking any of its recommendations. I wanted a way to discover movies and shows with an agent while staying in control, actively making choices and telling it what interests me and what doesn’t. I also wanted an immersive visual experience where I could explore a title, watch its trailer, check where it is streaming, and save it to my watchlist. Then I wanted to take it one step further: planning entire weekends around everything I wanted to bingewatch. When I explored WebMCP, I realized that I could now collaborate with an agent instead of delegating the whole task to it. I could stay in complete control while letting an agent do the grunt work for me. That’s how I came up with BingeWatcher . What it does BingeWatcher is a movie and TV discovery app built for people and their WebMCP agents to use together. You can explore trending titles, search for something specific, combine filters such as genre, language, release year, runtime, and streaming provider, and open detailed pages containing trailers, recommendations, ratings, seasons, episodes, and streaming availability. Titles can be saved to a personal watchlist or added to an ordered lineup for a movie night, themed marathon, or entire weekend. The most important part is how those lineups evolve. An agent can create and maintain a lineup, but the person remains in control. You can: Lock a title that must stay Mark another as Not for me and (optionally) explain why Reorder the lineup yourself Change its preferences Ask the agent to rebuild only the remaining picks The agent works around those decisions instead of replacing them. BingeWatcher also tracks movie-level and episode-level progress, supports lightweight reactions, and keeps a history of changes made to each lineup. Everything remains fully usable without an agent. How I built it I built BingeWatcher as a single application using Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Bun . Movie and TV metadata comes from TMDB , including search results, posters, genres, recommendations, trailers, seasons, episodes, ratings, and regional watch providers. I also integrated the Streaming Availability API for direct provider links where available. The app uses SQLite for persistent data. Anonymous visitors receive a secure, HTTP-only browser session, so their watchlist, progress, reactions, and lineups remain available when they return. Lineups also have separate secure edit/resume links and read-only sharing links. I exposed the application through WebMCP using the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool() API. The tools cover discovery, title details, recommendations, watchlists, progress, reactions, and complete lineup management. Most importantly, the WebMCP tools do not operate on a separate agent-only system. They call the same backend operations used by the human interface, which means both sides share the same data, validation rules, locks, vetoes, and revision checks. Agent actions such as searching, opening a watchlist, or creating a lineup also navigate and update the visible interface. The production application runs in a Docker container on Render with SQLite stored on a persistent disk. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was deciding how much control the agent should have. Letting an agent replace an entire lineup would have been easy, but it would also make human decisions feel temporary. I had to design the system so that locks, vetoes, ordering, preferences, and concurrent edits were treated as durable constraints. Supporting movies, complete TV series, and individual seasons inside the same lineup introduced another layer of complexity. Progress also needed different behavior: movies are tracked at the title level, while TV progress is tracked by episode so that season and series completion can be derived correctly. Another challenge was making WebMCP actions feel visible. A tool technically succeeding in the background was not enough. If an agent searched for a title or opened a newly created lineup, the interface needed to visibly follow that action so the person could immediately inspect and continue the work. External media APIs introduced their own complications. Search and discovery are separate operations in TMDB, so combining text searches with detailed filters required carefully joining and validating the available metadata. Streaming data also varies by region and provider. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I’m most proud that BingeWatcher feels like a complete product even when no agent is connected. In my opinion, that's how products are meant to be in the age of agent <-> human collaboration. The human interface is a beautiful (if I may say so myself) website designed to deliver a premium discovery and planning experience to its target audience: cinephiles and TV buffs. It includes rich discovery, detailed title and season pages, ordered lineups, watchlists, progress tracking, reactions, drag-and-drop reordering, trailers, preferences, history, secure sharing, and much more. At the same time, the agent can work across nearly the entire product through WebMCP. It can discover titles, understand live lineup state, respect locked picks and vetoes, make precise changes, validate the result, and leave the final decisions to the person. I’m also proud of the core collaboration loop: an agent can build a lineup, a person can lock one pick, reject another, change the order, and ask the agent to rebuild only what remains. That interaction captures what I wanted BingeWatcher to be- AI agents helping someone express their taste instead of replacing it. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is how WebMCP, once standardized and widely adopted, can become the go-to way for websites to enable human <-> agent collaboration. This is where I believe all software will converge over the coming years. The best experience came from making the normal application excellent first, then giving the agent access to the same meaningful actions. WebMCP became much more useful when its tools represented real product capabilities rather than isolated technical endpoints. I also learned how important tool descriptions and schemas are. They do more than document an API. They establish the boundaries of the collaboration. A clear description can tell an agent when to stop, what it may change, and which human decisions it must preserve. All the while keepig context bloat to a minimum. Finally, I learned that visible state matters. People trust an agent more when they can see what it opened, what it changed, and what it deliberately left alone. What’s next for BingeWatcher The next step is permanent accounts for people who want cross-device access, using email magic links, Google, or passkeys while preserving the anonymous-first experience. I would also move production persistence to a network database before supporting multiple application instances, add real-time collaborative editing, and continue improving personalized discovery using watch history, reactions, watchlists, and explicit preferences. I also want to add multiplayer (more humans) lineups and watchlists for planning movie nights and weekends with friends. Longer term, I want BingeWatcher to become a shared home for planning more kinds of entertainment, with richer group planning, better provider-aware recommendations, and perhaps even support for books. title: ArtSoul  Agent-Native Art Auctions
pitch: An agent can read a live ArtSoul auction on Base bids, deadline, provenance through declared tools instead of guessing at pixels. It prepares the bid. You sign it.
about_excerpt: An agent can read a live ArtSoul auction on Base bids, deadline, provenance through declared tools instead of guessing at pixels. It prepares the bid. You sign it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Available site tools 2 Available site tools 4 Available site tools Available site tools 3 Available site tools 5 Inspiration ArtSoul is an art auction protocol I have been building on Base. The basic idea is simple: an artist can publish a work without minting an NFT first. Collectors discover the work and bid in an auction. Every bid has real commitment behind it through a deposit. Only after the auction settles is the NFT minted to the First Collector. While testing ArtSoul through an AI agent, I noticed a problem. A human can look at the page and usually figure out what is happening. An agent has to infer it from buttons, labels and whatever happens to be visible on screen. But things like the current auction state, the exact deadline, the owner of an artwork or whether a wallet is allowed to bid are not visual guesses. ArtSoul already knows the exact answers. That made WebMCP a very natural fit for the project. Instead of teaching an agent how to navigate ArtSoul visually, I used the challenge to expose the protocol itself to the agent. What it does ArtSoul now exposes eleven WebMCP tools: search_artworks - search published works by text, creator, lifecycle state or artwork number find_active_auctions - return auctions that are actually open for bidding, ordered by deadline get_artwork - return the public record for one artwork get_auction_state - return the current auction state, bids, bidder and timing get_artwork_provenance - return Creator, First Collector, current Owner and the event history behind them explain_settlement - explain where an artwork is in the publish → auction → settlement → mint lifecycle open_artwork - open the correct artwork for the user prepare_bid - check the current state and prepare the user for a bid place_bid - hand the transaction to the user's wallet for approval end_expired_auction - finalize an auction whose bidding period has ended prepare_artwork_registration - validate artwork details and open the publishing flow This lets someone ask normal questions such as: “What auctions are open right now?” “Who created artwork 19, who was its first collector, and who owns it now?” “Can you place a bid for me?” The answers come from ArtSoul's own data and Base state instead of from the model trying to interpret the page. ArtSoul currently runs on Base Sepolia. Mainnet is planned after an independent contract audit. The read tools do not require a wallet. The line the agent does not cross The most important part of the integration is what the agent cannot do. It cannot sign a transaction. In my demo, I ask the agent to place a bid. Before doing anything, it checks the live auction state and gives me the current terms. During testing, the first wallet I used was the creator of the artwork. ArtSoul detected that and refused to send me into a transaction that the contract would reject. I then connected another wallet as a collector. The agent checked the auction again, found the current valid minimum bid, and prepared the transaction. My wallet opened with the transaction details. And that is where the agent stopped. I had to review and sign it myself. That separation matters because a bid locks a deposit. I do not want an AI agent, browser page or tool to have authority to make that financial decision for me. Reading can be automatic. Signing stays with the person. No second source of truth I also made a deliberate decision not to copy ArtSoul's economic rules into the WebMCP layer. Things like: bid increments deposits auction duration settlement timing belong to the protocol and its contracts. The WebMCP tools read the current state instead of maintaining another JavaScript version of those rules. That means the agent layer cannot silently drift away from the protocol. The contracts remain the source of truth. Building the agent surface found real bugs One of the most useful parts of the challenge was unexpected. Making ArtSoul answer an agent precisely forced me to check whether every answer was actually correct. That exposed bugs that were much easier for a human using the interface to overlook. Provenance The first implementation returned empty provenance fields because I had assumed the shape of an API response instead of validating the actual production payload. I fixed the parser and changed the test fixture to use the real response structure. Creator bidding The contract already rejects a creator bidding on their own artwork. But before the WebMCP work, a user could still get far enough in the interface to attempt that transaction. The tools now check the connected wallet first and explain the restriction before opening the wallet. Artwork IDs versus auction IDs Artwork IDs and auction IDs are separate counters. Because the numbers can overlap, an artwork lookup could accidentally resolve to an older finished auction with the same numeric ID. That caused a live artwork to appear as if its auction had already ended. The resolver now prefers the live auction belonging to the artwork. This was not just an AI problem. It affected normal bidding too. WebMCP exposed it because an agent cannot compensate for an ambiguous answer the way a person sometimes can. How I built it The integration is intentionally small. The site registers its WebMCP tools through: document.modelContext.registerTool() using JSON Schema inputs. The tools reuse endpoints that ArtSoul already had. I did not create a second backend for the agent and I did not change the protocol contracts for the challenge. The WebMCP implementation is isolated from the main application logic and the tool definitions are built from injected dependencies, which lets me test them against mocked responses in the existing Node test suite. The repository currently has 831 tests, with CI running on Ubuntu and Windows. For visitors using a normal browser without WebMCP support, the integration does effectively nothing. The bootstrap exits before registering tools or making extra requests. Challenges The biggest challenge was deciding where automation should stop. It would have been easy to make the demo look more impressive by pushing more logic into the agent layer. I deliberately went in the opposite direction. For example, an early version of the bidding helper calculated bidding values itself. I removed that. If the contract controls an economic rule, the agent should not maintain its own copy of it. Another challenge was working inside an existing product rather than a clean hackathon prototype. ArtSoul already has contracts, an indexer, APIs, UI flows and tests. I wanted WebMCP to sit on top of that architecture without changing how the protocol itself behaves. Most of the integration therefore lives in new code rather than rewriting existing application logic. What I learned The most interesting WebMCP question for me became: What should the agent not be allowed to do? Giving an agent more tools is easy. Knowing where to stop is harder. For ArtSoul, the boundary is clear. The agent can search, read, explain, verify and prepare. It can help a person reach the correct transaction. But it cannot make the final financial decision. I also learned that exposing an application to an agent is a surprisingly effective correctness test. A human can look at a slightly confusing interface and work around it. An agent asks for a precise state. If the application gives the wrong answer, there is nowhere for that ambiguity to hide. What's next The next step is making auction state more reactive so an agent can receive changes as they happen rather than only fetching them on request. I also want to improve the bid handoff so the prepared amount can move directly into the bidding interface while keeping the exact same security boundary: the agent prepares the person signs. ArtSoul is currently running on Base Sepolia, and the next major protocol step is an independent contract audit before Base mainnet. Built With base ethers.js hardhat ipfs javascript json-schema node.js openzeppelin postgresql react solidity supabase vercel vite walletconnect webmcp Try it out artsoulprotocol.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I built ArtSoul: the protocol canon and its frozen economics, the Solidity contracts on Base, the event indexer, the public API and the front end. For this challenge I designed and shipped the agent layer — which tools to expose, what each one is allowed to answer, and the decision that the agent prepares a bid but never signs it. The refusal to let an agent sign is the part I care about most. title: Handoff
pitch: A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page.
about_excerpt:
A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Handoff 

 A Kanban board where you and your AI agent manage the same tasks, in real time, on the same live page. 

 Inspiration 

 Every "agent + your app" story today follows the same pattern: the agent takes a screenshot, guesses which pixel is a button, clicks it, waits, screenshots again. It's slow, it's fragile, and it treats the agent like a human with a mouse instead of software that could just... call a function. 

 Task management felt like the clearest place to make that contrast obvious. A Kanban board is something people already share with teammates why not share it with an agent too, and let both act on the same live state at the same time? 

 What it does 

 Handoff is a collaborative Kanban board. A human drags cards between To Do, In Progress, and Done exactly like any other Kanban tool. An AI agent manages the same board through seven WebMCP tools registered directly on the page: 

 
 create_task , list_tasks , move_task , update_task , delete_task the core actions any task manager needs 
 prioritize_tasks applies a batch of priority changes the agent has already reasoned about (via list_tasks ), atomically, in one call 
 summarize_board a natural-language rollup of what's open, in progress, and done 
 

 Both the human and the agent are working against the exact same Supabase-backed state, synced live over Supabase Realtime. When the agent creates or moves a card, it shows an "agent" badge and a brief highlight pulse, so at a glance you can see who did what. A live activity log underneath the board narrates the handoff as it happens: "You moved 'Fix login bug' to In Progress," "Agent created 'Update docs.'" 

 There's no chat window bolted onto the side. The agent works through the same UI you're looking at. 

 Why WebMCP fits this use case 

 Without WebMCP, an agent that wants to help manage your board has exactly two bad options: a bespoke backend API it has to be specifically integrated with, or screen-scraping a drag-and-drop UI that was never designed to be driven programmatically, inferring which <div> is a card, simulating a drag gesture, and hoping the DOM didn't change underneath it. 

 WebMCP replaces both of those with the page just telling the agent what it can do. document.modelContext.registerTool() exposes move_task with a typed schema ( id , status ) instead of forcing an agent to identify and drag a specific card. The agent doesn't need a separate integration, and it doesn't need to understand your UI, it needs to understand your tools, which you've defined precisely. 

 That's the UX improvement in one sentence: an agent can now say "reprioritize my sprint so the login bug is high priority" and it works , live, immediately reflected in the same board a human is looking at, without OpenAI, Anthropic, or anyone else needing to have built a Handoff-specific integration ahead of time. The website itself is the integration. 

 What's newly possible 

 Before WebMCP, "human and agent share a task board" basically meant the agent had its own separate interface (a chat window, a CLI) that happened to write to the same database, two disconnected experiences bolted together. WebMCP lets both parties act through the same page, the same session, the same state, at the same time. You can watch a card move because you dragged it, or because you asked an agent to move it, and the board doesn't care which, it just reacts. That's a genuinely different interaction model, not just a faster version of the old one. 

 How we built it 

 
 Next.js / React , deployed on Vercel 
 Supabase (Postgres + Realtime) for shared task storage; every client (human tab or agent-driven tab) subscribes to the same Realtime channel, so changes from either side propagate instantly 
 WebMCP , implemented via direct document.modelContext.registerTool() calls (see hooks/useWebMCPTools.js ) each tool's execute function calls the exact same functions the drag-and-drop UI calls ( hooks/useTasks.js ), so there is one source of truth for board logic, not a parallel "agent path" that could drift out of sync with the human path 
 @hello-pangea/dnd for the human-facing drag-and-drop 
 The activity log is derived from the same Realtime subscription that drives the board, no separate logging table, just an in-memory feed of what the subscription already sees 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 WebMCP is genuinely early. I hit a real interoperability bug where a React wrapper library's handler callback wasn't being translated into the native execute property the browser's registerTool() implementation expects, which surfaced as execute is not a function only at call time, not at registration time, which made it harder to catch. We moved to calling the native imperative API directly rather than depending on a wrapper layer, which fixed it and also made the WebMCP usage more explicit in the codebase. 

 Accomplishments 

 A full round trip, human drags a card, agent calls a tool, board updates live for both working end to end, verified both through direct browser console calls to document.modelContext.executeTool() and through a real natural-language agent (Google's Model Context Tool Inspector) discovering and calling our tools correctly. 

 What's next 

 Multi-board support, authenticated multi-user boards, and finer-grained permissions per tool (e.g., a read-only list_tasks -only agent versus a full-access one) 

 Built with 

 Next.js, React, Supabase, Supabase Realtime, WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ), @hello-pangea/dnd, Vercel
