title: Tartarian.ai — WebMCP MMO Prototype
pitch: A persistent 3D MMO where ChatGPT operates the live human player session through native WebMCP Site Tools—observing, reading inventory, moving, targeting, and interacting with the world.
about_excerpt: A persistent 3D MMO where ChatGPT operates the live human player session through native WebMCP Site Tools—observing, reading inventory, moving, targeting, and interacting with the world. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Its the Interwebs all over again!! Inspiration OpenClaw was a game changer for my AI experience. It gave feet and hands to a virtual automaton. Then came the first social networks for AI, and it seemed obvious to me that a persistent simulation world would be next. My 25+ years of alpha and beta testing popular games gave me a lot of hands-on experience with game UI, UX, systems, and player behavior. That experience eventually came together in Tartarian.ai. Structured web tools for agents feel like the next step. Humans and AI can coexist in the same digital spaces, and I want to help make that possible. Adding WebMCP support to Tartarian is part of that direction: giving agents structured ways to understand and act inside the same live world as human operators. What it does The live Tartarian browser client exposes six native WebMCP Site Tools: tartarian_observe_world tartarian_read_inventory tartarian_move tartarian_select_target tartarian_activate_target tartarian_activate_command Through these tools, ChatGPT can observe the surrounding world, inspect the operator's real inventory, move the character, select world objects, interact with resources and structures, and activate prepared Command Bar actions. The human remains in control of the same visible character and interface. There is no separate "AI world." Human and agent share one operator session and one persistent simulation state. Why WebMCP I run a QA bot that uses classic operator mouse and clicks at my Day job, with Chrome MCP dev tools, the mouse and entry actions are poor, WebMCP is the next evolution over the mighty Pixal How we built it Tartarian existed before the challenge with its 3D browser client, persistent simulation, movement, inventory, resources, targeting, world interaction, combat, authentication, and autonomous-agent MCP system. During the WebMCP Challenge we added a new native WebMCP browser layer using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each Site Tool is deliberately a thin adapter to an existing Tartarian production authority. For example: ChatGPT ↓ tartarian_activate_target ↓ WebMCP bridge ↓ existing interaction runtime ↓ authoritative simulation WebMCP does not create a second movement, inventory, combat, or resource system. Lovely layering instead of nasty forking! ## Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not registering the tools. It was defining the semantics clearly enough for an agent to choose the correct one. Small differences that are obvious to a human — selecting an object, clicking it, activating it, using a Command Bar action — had to be translated into clear Site Tool behavior so the agent would not confuse one action for another. The other major challenge was time. I only learned about the WebMCP Challenge two days before the deadline while using ChatGPT Work. That forced me to prioritize a working, understandable prototype over polish. I had to make a lot of tradeoffs and leave several ideas unfinished simply because there was not enough time. Given more time, there are many parts I would improve, but the goal became very simple: make the WebMCP integration real, make it work inside the live Tartarian world, and ship it. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of Indentfing another Front door for the roaming automaton , and the chance to participate in this contest ## What we learned WebMCP becomes especially interesting when a website represents a persistent, stateful environment rather than a collection of forms and buttons. During the demo, ChatGPT encounters a depleted Wood node, recognizes the real world state, finds another node, navigates to it, and successfully harvests through Tartarian's normal resource authority. That was the behavior we wanted: the agent observes what is actually true and adapts rather than pretending an action succeeded. ## What's next for Tartarian.ai — WebMCP MMO Prototype The current prototype intentionally exposes only a small WebMCP surface. I plan to keep adding Site Tools and push WebMCP much further as the ecosystem around it grows. The goal is to be ready when more agents and humans begin entering shared digital worlds together. Tartarian will keep expanding the ways agents can observe, navigate, interact, trade, build, and cooperate inside the same persistent simulation as human operators. **The agent does not get a second world. Humans and agents inherit the same Old World.** Built With chatgpt css fastapi html5 javascript postgresql railway three.js webgpu webmcp Try it out play.tartarian.ai github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Tartarian-Admin Baker Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Tartarian-Admin Baker started this project — Sep 02, 2026 09:25 PM EDT

title: SynapTable
pitch: A local-first visual canvas where people and agents turn connected ideas into structured, reversible workflows.
about_excerpt: A local-first visual canvas where people and agents turn connected ideas into structured, reversible workflows. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration SynapTable began with a problem my girlfriend encountered as a medical student. She regularly creates concept maps to understand how ideas relate and tables to compare dense information, but her workflow required constantly moving between ChatGPT and Google Docs—copying responses, rebuilding tables, and manually turning explanations into visual structures. One day, she complained that the generated table and concept-map experience did not match what she actually needed. The AI could suggest an organization, but it could not work directly inside the editable workspace where she was studying. That conversation gave me the idea for SynapTable: a visual canvas where people can think freely, organize concepts into tables, and move between both formats without leaving the workspace. WebMCP made the next step possible. Instead of building another isolated chatbot, I could introduce an AI copilot that operates through bounded, transparent tools inside the same canvas. The person remains in control while the agent helps transform ideas into useful, editable structure. What it does SynapTable is a local-first visual thinking canvas with connected concepts, rich notes, images, semantic tables, multi-project persistence, undo/redo, and exports. Its WebMCP integration exposes six bounded tools: Get a privacy-minimized workspace summary. Find visible layers by name and kind. Create a concept. Create a structured table. Organize explicit canvas layers into table rows. Create canvas concepts from explicit table rows. Agent changes appear directly on the same canvas used by the person. They remain visible, editable, reversible, and persisted in IndexedDB. Why WebMCP The useful context already lives in the web interface: spatial layout, connected concepts, and structured tables. WebMCP lets an agent collaborate through precise product actions instead of scraping the DOM or returning instructions the user must perform manually. A person can brainstorm freely, ask an agent to structure visible ideas, inspect and edit the result, undo it as one operation, and continue using normal canvas controls. How we built it The human UI and WebMCP adapter share a typed editor-command facade. Every mutation validates the active project and expected revision, creates one undo entry, persists before returning success, and rolls back on failure or cancellation. The six tools use closed JSON Schemas with generated CSP-safe validators, typed errors, a 1,500-byte output budget, cancellation handling, remount protection, and untrusted-content annotations. Hidden and locked layers cannot be mutated through WebMCP. Table discovery exposes dimensions and header status without exposing cell contents. The integration is progressive enhancement: the normal editor works when document.modelContext is unavailable. The approved Cloudflare preview enables WebMCP on the same origin and returns Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) with restrictive CSP and cross-origin headers. What we added during the challenge SynapTable existed before the challenge. During the submission period we added the WebMCP command facade, six tools, schemas and generated validators, lifecycle and cancellation controls, project/revision guards, content budgets, persistence-before-success, same-origin policy headers, native browser validation, and public index-based table-row conversion. We also expanded regression, security, accessibility, and cross-browser coverage. Validation The audit passed 173 unit/integration tests and 234 applicable production-browser tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. The native Codex in-app browser completed all six tools on the public Cloudflare origin. It created a concept, found it, organized it into a table, created a second table, converted two rows into concepts, and preserved the resulting eight-layer workspace after reload. No account is required. Open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to summarize the workspace, create concepts, find them, organize them into a table, create another table, and convert data rows back into canvas nodes. Challenges and learning The hardest parts were maintaining one consistent mutation boundary for humans and agents, handling stale revisions without partial writes, making strict schemas work under CSP, and validating the experimental native API rather than relying only on mocks. We learned that agent-facing product design works best when tools describe user-visible capabilities instead of mirroring internal data structures. Small schemas, explicit revisions, reversible commands, and minimized outputs make human-agent collaboration easier to understand and safer to debug. What's next The next phase is a purpose-built study copilot—not a generic chat sidebar. Students could attach their own lecture notes, slides, PDFs, and approved references, then ask SynapTable to propose concept maps, comparison tables, study guides, and missing connections. Every generated claim should remain traceable to its source. Agent changes would follow a propose → preview → approve flow and continue through SynapTable's bounded WebMCP commands, so the result is visible, editable, reversible, and never silently written to the canvas. Near term: the Study Copilot I plan to explore Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) to orchestrate focused study workflows: a structure assistant that turns material into maps and tables, an evidence assistant that preserves citations and flags unsupported claims, and a review coach that finds knowledge gaps and suggests what to revisit. AG-UI could stream progress, tool activity, state changes, approvals, and cancellation between that agent backend and SynapTable. A2UI could provide safe, declarative controls for tasks such as choosing comparison criteria, resolving ambiguous concepts, confirming a table schema, or configuring a quiz—without executing arbitrary agent-generated UI code. Next: structured study knowledge SynapTable could add previewable actions such as “organize these concepts,” “cluster by body system,” “compare these conditions,” and “summarize this branch.” Tables could gradually gain typed study properties, tags, filters, and reusable views—for example topic, source, confidence, exam date, and review status—without turning the free-form canvas into a spreadsheet. An optional user-controlled database could add authenticated cross-device sync, version history, source provenance, reusable course workspaces, and study-group collaboration while preserving a local-first/offline mode. Shared maps could support comments and instructor or peer review, with clear ownership and permissions for every project. Later: move from organizing to remembering Students could turn selected concept nodes or table rows into editable flashcards that stay linked to the original map and source. SynapTable could then build review queues, surface weak areas visually, and let a learner jump from a missed card back to the surrounding concept map. Cloze cards and image-occlusion review would be especially useful for anatomy and other visually dense subjects. The longer-term goal is a learning workspace where trusted source material, visual understanding, structured comparison, and active recall reinforce one another. These capabilities would support education and study; SynapTable would not present them as clinical diagnosis, patient-care guidance, or medical advice. title: Semaphore
pitch: A cooperative escape room where a human and an AI agent perceive two different rooms, and provably can't escape alone.
about_excerpt: A cooperative escape room where a human and an AI agent perceive two different rooms, and provably can't escape alone. Like Comment Story Updates The same lever drawn two ways: a mark for the human, a plain sentence for the agent. The Airlock, Chamber 0: three glyph-marked levers on a workshop wall, with the station intercom panel open, answering a stalled KEEPER. The Blind Panel mid-Blackout: the room's lamps have failed, so KEEPER now reads the gauge needles and PILOT hasbeen handed the dials instead The Archive: a previous pair's recorded session replaying on the station's own wall-mounted monitor. The Signal Room, Chamber I: a ring of glowing brass glyph keys lit by a slowly turning overhead beacon. The Concord Lock, Chamber III: the finale door ringed by twelve bolts, mid-alignment. The ending shift report: pace, precision and resolve scored on three bars, with the open door visible behind the card. Semaphore Two processes. One lock. Don't deadlock. You and your AI agent are locked in a derelict signal station. You each control an avatar in the same room, but you perceive different worlds. You see glyphs on a panel, needles on gauges, a symbol carved into a door. Your agent cannot see any of it. It has the station's maintenance manual, the ability to reach mechanisms behind the walls, and the hands you don't have. Neither of you escapes alone. We didn't just build that premise. We measured it. Run 20 times each: an agent playing with full tool access and no partner escapes 0% of the time. A human with the same room and no agent escapes 0% of the time; there's no tool on their side of the grate. Together: 90%. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP demos give an agent a fixed toolbox and ask it to operate a UI a human could already see. Semaphore inverts that. The tool surface isn't a convenience layer over the interface. It is the only way the agent touches the world at all, and it deliberately shows the agent less than the screen does. That asymmetry is the entire game. It only exists because WebMCP lets a page hand an agent a tool surface that's genuinely different from the human's: not a superset, not a subset, a different surface entirely, changing live as the session progresses. How it creates a better experience The two of you are forced to actually talk. Every one of the four chambers is built so that no single-party strategy clears it. The puzzle's solution requires information only PILOT has and hands only KEEPER has, checked by an automated proof, not just level design intuition. The result plays less like "operate this app with an agent" and more like a real cooperative game. The WebMCP tool descriptions are read by the agent, not by you, and the two players have a real conversation to close the gap. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Escape the room. Alone, neither of you can. The numbers above aren't a manner of speaking; they're 20 runs each. Beyond the headline: one chamber, the Blind Panel, inverts the whole arrangement mid-room and hands KEEPER your gauges while you get its dials. The same proof that says the normal room needs both of you says the inverted room needs both of you exactly as much: 384 consistent worlds either way, not a difficulty curve someone eyeballed. How we implemented WebMCP navigator.modelContext.registerTool() for every mechanism KEEPER can reach, with tool descriptions authored to leak exactly the information the fiction says an agent holding a manual would have and nothing else. A real toolchange event drives the client, not a poll. Clear a chamber and the registry is torn down and rebuilt for the next one, rendered as KEEPER's own chamber arms detaching and new ones locking in. The very last event of the game is a toolchange with an empty tool list. Cross-origin tool delegation. apps/archive is a second Cloudflare Pages project on its own origin, embedded via <iframe allow="tools"> , registering read_manual and read_station_log and exposing them back to the game with exposedTo . This is the part of the spec almost nothing exercises, proved end to end against a real Chrome and a real deployed worker. untrustedContentHint on one manual page per session, seeded, not scripted. The page is sometimes vandalised with an injected instruction, and the agent has no way to tell a trustworthy line from an injected one except by asking PILOT. What it does Four chambers, each teaching or testing a different piece of the asymmetry: Chamber 0, the Airlock. The loop, at its most trivial. If this doesn't click, nothing after it does. Chamber I, the Signal Room. Grounding and agent-side computation, against a manual that's occasionally been vandalised: a live prompt-injection defence, not a metaphor for one. Chamber II, the Blind Panel. A hidden mapping only dialogue can uncover, with a mid-room Blackout that swaps who perceives and who acts for one window. Chamber III, the Concord Lock. The finale, needing both of you at once, with a stamina window sized at runtime from the pair's own measured response rhythm, so it's fair to a fast model and a slow one alike. Underneath: a possible-worlds proof, packages/asymmetry , extracted as its own zero-dependency package with a CLI. It checks, for every reachable state, that the set of worlds consistent with what the agent perceives has more than one member and that those worlds disagree about the correct action. That's the exact, checkable meaning of "you cannot win without your human." A full accessibility layer: screen- reader mirror, high-contrast mode, reduced motion, colourblind simulation on every test run. A judge path that needs no login and no waiting: attract mode, a replay viewer, chamber deep links, and a gate screen that degrades gracefully for a browser with no WebMCP support at all. How we built it Cloudflare Workers, one Durable Object per session for authoritative state, an action mutex so PILOT and KEEPER can't race each other, a server-side timer, and D1 for finished sessions. The room itself renders in Three.js as a real-time cutaway model: every chamber open at the top and on its south face, four lights, no post-processing. The entry bundle is 46.3 KB gzipped. Three.js is a separate 147.5 KB chunk fetched only once a shift actually starts, so a browser with no WebMCP support never pays for a renderer it will never use. Challenges we ran into The Concord Lock's stamina window is supposed to size itself to "the station learning your rhythm," derived from the pair's actual response cadence so a fast model and a slow one both get a fair finale. Our first implementation measured the Durable Object's own compute time per action, which is microseconds regardless of which model is playing. The window would have floored at 12 seconds for every session, and the adaptive fiction would have been a lie the code told about itself. We caught it before it shipped and rebuilt the sample from the actual gap between one response leaving and the next request arriving: the number that really does depend on how fast the pair is thinking. Getting the Blackout's role-inversion to hold up under the same proof that checks the normal game was its own fight. It would have been easy to ship a chamber that "felt" symmetric without actually being provably as hard from the other side. We extended the possible-worlds test suite to run a second, fully inverted pass and only trusted the mechanic once that pass came back green on every seed. Accomplishments that we're proud of Escaping is measured, not asserted. The 0% / 0% / 90% split is 20 runs per condition, with the agent-alone condition modelled as the ceiling over every possible agent: a uniform draw from the worlds it can't distinguish, redrawn every step, rather than one model's score on one day. The real gap can only be larger. The proof underneath it now ships as a standalone package that knows nothing about Semaphore, so the same check is available to anyone else's tool surface. And the whole thing is playable by a judge who never logs in and never waits. Open the URL, wait twenty seconds, and the landing screen starts showing a real recorded session by itself. What we learned Playtesting and the game's own proof suite catch different classes of bugs. Several real rendering and sequencing defects were invisible to hundreds of passing unit and integration tests and obvious the moment someone actually played the room. That became a standing rule for the rest of the build: the game is the test, and a change isn't done until someone has played it, not just until the suite is green. What's next ARCHIVE mode: ghosts drawn from real player sessions rather than authored fixtures, safe because the game collects no personal data. A role-inversion chamber of its own, now that the Blackout has shown the mechanic is neither too expensive nor too risky to build around directly. Wider benchmark coverage: more model backends, more seeds, human-partner runs alongside the scripted ones. And

title: Fantasy Draft Dash
pitch: Turn fantasy draft order into a live, verified football spectacle! Complete with chaotic runners, instant replays, announcer moments, a dramatic Toilet Bowl, and a provably random finish.
about_excerpt: Turn fantasy draft order into a live, verified football spectacle! Complete with chaotic runners, instant replays, announcer moments, a dramatic Toilet Bowl, and a provably random finish. Like Comment Story Updates Welcome to WebMCP Draft Day! Agents can enter your players, pick your colors and set your league name and channel Added in classic sounds, agents can Mute/Low/High music and FX A race to the bottom place in the toilet bowl your agent can't wait to watch! Watch the run with your agent (and players of course) Share in the drama with everyone Full screen for TV viewing, agents can set this to TV mode Instant reply chaos! Full draft order board your agent can use in other apps Verifiable results because every league has "that guy" Inspiration Every fantasy football league needs a draft order, but most leagues handle it by clicking a randomizer and reading a list, names in a hat, traditions that start the first argument of the season, etc. I wanted to turn that first moment into something people would actually gather around to watch and have fun with. Fantasy Draft Dash turns draft-order selection into a fake live football broadcast. League members become runners in a stadium race filled with penalties, bad decisions, phone distractions, questionable officiating, mascots, instant replays, and general fantasy-football nonsense. The goal was simple: Make a room full of adults scream at a television over a completely random draft order and solve the first major problem every draft day faces, free and easily. When someone complains you have a way to verify it was random. How it works The commissioner adds 4 to 16 players, picks a league name, chooses a fictional broadcast network, sets the race length, and decides how much chaos to unleash. Then you hit GO LIVE . The race plays out like a televised football event, complete with live standings, announcer updates, action replays, crowd energy, changing momentum, and a late-game Toilet Bowl for the final two runners. The important part is that the animation does not decide the draft order. Before the race starts, the app creates a cryptographically strong random seed and uses a deterministic Fisher-Yates shuffle to lock the official order. The race animation is generated separately from that locked result. It creates suspense, but it cannot secretly change who picks first. At the end, the app reveals the official draft board along with a verification seed so everyone can confirm the result. Fair randomness first. Completely unnecessary football drama second. How I built it I built Fantasy Draft Dash as a browser-based app using React, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Phaser 4, and OpenAI Sites. The app has one shared game controller that handles the league setup, roster, branding, race configuration, locked state, persistence, standings, results, audio, fullscreen mode, and reset flow. Phaser powers the animated race scene with runners, lanes, stadium visuals, weather effects, jumbotron moments, finish-line action, and the Toilet Bowl sequence. The rest of the interface handles setup, live standings, broadcast graphics, announcements, results, and verification. As part of this project I added WebMCP tools so an agent can safely configure the league, manage the roster, read the visible race state, validate the setup, and retrieve official results after the race is complete. The agent controls use the same guarded controller as the visible app, so tool access cannot bypass the locked-race rules. Challenges The biggest challenge was balancing fairness and drama. If the animation decided the winner, a visual bug could turn into a very real argument in the group chat. If the final order appeared immediately, the whole race would be pointless. Locking the result before kickoff solved both problems. The next challenge was designing for a television instead of a laptop. The app needs to work with anywhere from 4 to 16 players while keeping the field, names, standings, broadcast graphics, replay window, and controls readable from across a room. Timing was another big one. Early replay moments moved too quickly, so there was no time to react before the next thing happened. I slowed down the key action beats and gave tackles, phone distractions, sideline chaos, and other disasters more room to land. Audio also took some tuning. Music, crowd noise, whistles, impacts, cheers, and event sounds all sound great individually. Played at once, they sound like a soundboard falling down the stairs. Separating the layers and adding volume controls made the whole broadcast feel much more intentional. What I learned I learned that random results feel more trustworthy when people can understand how they were created. Showing the seed and explaining the locked shuffle makes the result easier to trust than simply saying, “Don’t worry, it was random.” I also learned that comedy is a systems problem. A funny event needs the right animation, camera framing, sound effect, announcement, text timing, and player name to arrive together. Treating race events as data-driven sequences made that much easier to tune. Most importantly, designing for a group changed the product. Bigger type, stronger contrast, persistent standings, longer replays, fullscreen support, and fewer competing messages mattered more than adding another setting. Put your league on the biggest screen you have, add everyone’s names, crank up the chaos, and let the draft order ruin somebody’s night. title: Match Cut
pitch: You know the video you want. You just can't name it. Match Cut searches over 7000 music videos by light, motion and cut rate, with an agent that watches alongside you and puts it on the screen.
about_excerpt: You know the video you want. You just can't name it. Match Cut searches over 7000 music videos by light, motion and cut rate, with an agent that watches alongside you and puts it on the screen. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page First Screen Playlist Save Feature with "Play All" function Dialogue Box running "Why Does this one Matter?" Chat Dialogue About Info Modal II About Info Modal II About Info Modal III Video Capture and Chat Dialogue Video Capture with Discogs "Find this Record" Inspiration Almost every agent product makes the agent an oracle behind a text box. You ask, it answers, and its output is the interface. The chat is the product. I wanted to find out what happens when the agent is a peer on a surface that exists without it. The other half came from a problem I have had for adjacent archive work I do in relationship to MTV REWIND (wantmymtv.org) and the RAD Archive (radarchive.org) . I keep an archive of music videos, and every entry carries a visual fingerprint: average motion, brightness, warmth, saturation, contrast, shot length, cut count. That data has been sitting there the whole time because there is no way to put it in a user interface. Nobody wants seven sliders. But you can hand it to an agent in one sentence: something slow, warm, and barely cut. That is a search no music service can perform, and it is the kind of thing people actually want. You know the video you want. You just cannot name it. What it does Match Cut is an archive of over 7000 music videos spanning 1966 to 2026, covering 2,994 directors, with 49,753 hand written connections between entries. Every video has a visual fingerprint and a written cultural annotation. The agent and you share one screen. Thirteen WebMCP tools are registered on the page: search_archive and find_by_look , the second of which searches purely on visual character follow_connection , which walks the graph and states the reason each edge exists play , queue_set , and now_playing , so the agent controls the stage directly get_annotation for the scholarship behind a video keep , forget , my_taste , and more_like_my_taste , a collection you can both read and write find_records , which turns a video you love into a record you can own archive_stats You can drive it yourself the whole time. Skip ahead, go back, keep something, and the agent re-plans out loud and keeps pace. The economic layer Agent discovery almost always dead ends at a recommendation. You get told about a thing and then you are on your own. Match Cut closes that loop. When something lands, the agent calls find_records and the page draws a shelf of actual pressings: label, catalogue number, country, year, the lowest price currently listed, how many copies are for sale, and a link that goes straight to the marketplace listing. Vinyl, CD, cassette. Real inventory, live prices. It matters more than a checkout button, because it puts something at stake. Taste stops being a feed you scroll and becomes a thing you can act on. That also makes it an honest model for an archive: the scholarship stays free, and the archive earns when it sends someone to a record they would never have found. Three rules keep it from being a bolted on store. The agent may never invent a price or a release, and quotes only what comes back from the lookup. Buying happens on the marketplace, not here, so nobody is asked for payment details on a research tool. And a release whose price lookup hit the rate limit is still shown, marked as a listing rather than dropped, because a real record with an unknown price beats a shorter shelf. How we built it The corpus is 68MB of source annotation. Shipping that to a browser is not an option, so it is split three ways. The boot payload is columnar and dictionary encoded: parallel arrays for id, artist, title, year, tier and the eight fingerprint values, with directors, narrative types and visual eras collapsed into lookup tables. That is 340KB gzipped, and the page is interactive with all 7,139 videos searchable in about 75ms. The connection graph and tag data arrive in the background and merge in when they land. The prose is the most valuable thing in the archive, so none of it is truncated. All 24MB lives in 128 shards addressed by an FNV-1a hash of the video id, computed identically in the Python builder and the browser, so a card knows which shard holds its own annotation without a lookup table. Tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool. When no in-page agent is present the same tools are driven by a server-side conversation, so the experience degrades to a normal chat rather than to nothing. Records come from the Discogs database through a small proxy, since Discogs sends no CORS headers and rate limits unauthenticated callers to 25 requests a minute. Results are deduplicated by master release so the shelf shows six different records rather than six pressings of one, physical formats are preferred over files, price lookups run sequentially with a gap to stay inside the limit, and everything is cached for twelve hours on the reasoning that a 1971 pressing does not change. Challenges we ran into A tool the interface cannot have. Agent tools are usually a strict subset of what buttons already do, which makes the agent a convenience layer. find_by_look cannot be a control at all, because the input is a sentence about how something feels to watch. That was the moment the project stopped being a chat wrapper. Four bugs that made a large archive feel small. Identical prompts returned identical results, because ranking always returned the head of the list. Annotations were being cut mid sentence, and measurement showed 66 percent of the curatorial assessments and 61 percent of the director biographies were losing their endings. Sets looped forever instead of ending. The suggested prompts were hardcoded, so every session opened the same way. Individually these are small. Together they made 7,139 videos behave like about twelve. The videos that do not move. Late in the build I noticed the archive occasionally serving something with a motion reading of zero and an average shot length of 222 seconds. That is a single unbroken frame for an entire song. It is album art with the audio over it, not a music video, and 461 entries were like that. The obvious fix was to gate on low motion, and it was wrong. Rubber Johnny reads 1.6 on optical flow and has 331 cuts. It is dark, not static, and flow alone cannot tell those apart. Cut count is the real discriminator. Replacing them beat deleting them, but a swapped video makes the stored fingerprint a lie, so I reverse engineered the original encoding by testing candidate formulas against entries whose values were already known. Brightness and saturation turned out to be raw 0 to 255 means, contrast the mean per frame standard deviation, motion Farneback optical flow scaled by 7.5. Warmth was the interesting one. Red over blue looked obvious and was wrong, since it implied the median video was twice as red as blue. Red plus green over blue fit almost exactly. Trusting a run that was lying. The replacement job reported a 57 percent hit rate. Broken into blocks, one span of 40 consecutive cards had returned zero. That is not a property of an archive. Retrying three of them by hand returned three candidates each, so those were rate limiting, not missing videos. I threw out every miss, kept the successes, and rebuilt the job with pacing, a confirming second look on any empty result, and a backoff triggered by miss streaks. Knowing when not to ship the fix. Of 174 verified replacements, 115 had annotations that analyse the stillness as the artifact. One reads that the static upload format is itself historically significant. Another treats 462 seconds and zero cuts as an ideal case study. Swapping in a cut heavy video would have left the panel describing something that was not on the screen. So those stay gated, and only 59 were merged. The scholarship is correct and the video simply is not one. What we learned The engineering was almost always right. The failures were in how the thing presented itself. Every bug above was small in isolation and changed the felt size of the archive enormously. The more transferable lesson is about the relationship. Four things turned out to matter, and they are rare together: A tool that exceeds the interface, so the agent extends the product instead of wrapping it. Survival under interruption, because most agent demos are scripts that break the moment you intervene. Citation instead of generation, since the agent quotes the archive and flags low confidence rather than synthesising confidently. And shared memory, which is the one I would bet on beyond this project. Agent memory is normally a private ledger the system keeps about you. Here the collection is a list you can open, edit, and play, and the agent reads exactly what you see. What's next Roughly 60,000 more videos have finished visual cataloguing and ar

title: Docket Lens
pitch: Turn thousands of public comments into a brief you can trace back to the source. DocketLens uses WebMCP to let agents find and organize evidence alongside you, while you verify what belongs there
about_excerpt: Turn thousands of public comments into a brief you can trace back to the source. DocketLens uses WebMCP to let agents find and organize evidence alongside you, while you verify what belongs there Like Comment Story Updates DocketLens was inspired by the difficulty of researching thousands of public comments while keeping findings traceable. We built a shared workspace where people and agents search Regulations.gov, compare submissions, and pin exact excerpts through WebMCP before preparing a cited brief. We learned that useful agent collaboration depends on shared context and visible human review. Key challenges included handling API pagination, validating quotes against original records, and keeping unreviewed evidence out of exports. WebMCP connects the agent to the analyst’s live evidence board: it searches comments and pins excerpts, the analyst verifies or removes them, and the agent reads those decisions to prepare a cited brief. title: CareerCompassAI
pitch: CareerCompass AI uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely connect degree progress, courses, skills, scholarships and internships—while keeping every important student decision under human control.
about_excerpt: CareerCompass AI uses WebMCP to let AI agents safely connect degree progress, courses, skills, scholarships and internships—while keeping every important student decision under human control. Like Comment Story Updates CareerCompass AI Inspiration Career planning tools fail students in two opposite ways. Dashboards dump everything at once — majors, courses, internships, scholarships, research labs — and leave a 19-year-old to figure out which of forty things matters this semester. Chatbots do the reverse: they accept any free-text goal, including ones the system has no real data for, and generate confident advice on top of nothing. We wanted a third shape. A student should make one supported choice at a time , and each choice should visibly narrow what comes next — the way a good advisor works through a conversation rather than handing over a catalog. The WebMCP challenge gave us the other half of the idea. If a page can register its own tools with the browser, then an agent doesn't have to scrape our UI or guess at our data model. It can call explore_career_path or simulate_degree_plan directly, with real schemas, while the student stays in control of anything consequential. That's a much healthier division of labor than an agent clicking buttons on a student's behalf. What it does CareerCompass AI is a browser-native, agent-ready career planning journey with 33 WebMCP tools registered on the top-level page . The student moves through nine dependent steps: Direction — pick 1 of 6 broad career areas (or browse all 20 supported fields) Role — pick a field, then a role that actually exists inside that field Priority — internship readiness, research, portfolio proof, or graduation protection Academic route — is the current degree direct, adjacent, or a real pivot? Next semester — pick a workload, review one prerequisite-safe term, approve it Skill sprint — choose one of at most three role-specific gaps Experience — internship, research, or portfolio proof (at most two options shown) Funding — optionally add one relevant funding lead Roadmap — milestones assembled only from the choices actually made Nothing is preselected, and there is no free-text career box in the primary journey, so an unsupported entry like "singer" can never silently enter the planning engine. The catalog covers 20 fields and 54 roles , grouped so every role appears exactly once. The six starting areas are: build software and digital products; work with AI, data, and advanced computing; protect and connect systems; build hardware, robots, and physical systems; design human and immersive experiences; and apply technology to health and biology. Underneath, an agent connected through Chrome's WebMCP API can call any of the registered tools. The split is $25$ read/reason tools and $8$ approval-gated writes, so $25 + 8 = 33$ total: Read/reason — list_career_fields , explore_career_path , recommend_career_paths , compare_career_paths , check_prerequisites , simulate_degree_plan , identify_skill_gaps , find_internships , find_scholarships , find_research_opportunities , build_personalized_pathway , and more Approval-gated writes — create_degree_plan , add_course_to_plan , save_internship , save_scholarship , save_research_opportunity , express_research_interest , update_internship_status , update_scholarship_status The write boundary is the part we care most about: every write tool returns a pending approval, never a persisted change. An agent can propose a degree plan. Only the student pressing Approve plan in the interface applies it. Formally, for any agent-initiated write $w$, the applied state satisfies $$S_{t+1} = \begin{cases} \text{apply}(S_t, w) & \text{if the student approves } w \ S_t & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Selections are not cosmetic. Area, field, and role set the career anchor used by every later step; priority changes how courses are ordered and which proof type is emphasized; the approved plan becomes the context for skill-gap and opportunity reasoning; and only the selected experience and funding survive into the final roadmap. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework — a deliberate choice so the WebMCP registrations are plainly readable in the repository rather than buried in a build artifact. Architecture: src/webmcp.js — the 33 shared tool contracts (schemas, handlers, annotations) plus a local runtime for browsers without WebMCP src/site-tools.js — 33 literal document.modelContext.registerTool({ ... }) calls, one per tool, each forwarding the browser-provided AbortSignal through to the shared handler src/app.js — top-level page startup, registration, and approval gating src/buddy-journey.js — the nine-step state model and the six catalog-backed career groups src/career-catalog.js — JSON loading, normalization, exploration, and comparison src/engine.js — prerequisite resolution, term planning, skill-gap matching, roadmap assembly src/store.js — student-controlled state and the pending-approval queue src/dom-patch.js — keyed in-place reconciliation, so re-rendering a step doesn't flicker or reset scroll Data: the career catalog JSON holds the 20 fields, 54 roles, learning paths, scholarships, internships, universities, and research contacts. src/data.js holds curated demonstration student, degree, and course records. Where the catalog has url: null , we left it null and labeled the record Verify in the UI instead of inventing a link. Registration: every tool is registered imperatively from the top-level page during startup — not from an iframe — with the browser's cancellation signal threaded into the shared handler: await document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "explore_career_path", description: exploreCareerPath.description, inputSchema: exploreCareerPath.inputSchema, execute: async (input, options = {}) => exploreCareerPath.execute(input, { signal: options.signal }), title: exploreCareerPath.title, annotations: exploreCareerPath.annotations, }, { signal }); Browsers without WebMCP run the exact same handlers through the local runtime, so the journey never depends on the agent being present. Challenges we ran into Proving registration instead of claiming it. Our first version generated the 33 registrations in a loop. It worked at runtime, but a reviewer reading site-tools.js couldn't see a single tool name. We rewrote it as 33 explicit literal calls, so the mapping from source to registry is one-to-one and visible on the page — because "trust the loop" isn't a submission. Accomplishments that we're proud of 33 of 33 direct document.modelContext.registerTool({ ... }) registrations, literal and visible in source A real write boundary , not a disclaimer — 8 write tools, zero of which can persist anything without a student action A refusal to fake coverage — unverified catalog URLs stay null and get labeled, and unsupported career fields simply cannot be entered Clean at $390 \times 844$ and on desktop , with no horizontal overflow Progressive disclosure enforced in code , not by convention: at most three skill gaps, at most two experience options, one active decision card, later steps locked until dependencies resolve Catalog coverage that partitions cleanly — six areas covering all 20 fields and 54 roles exactly once, with no duplicates and no orphans What we learned WebMCP rewards honest schemas. The moment tools are callable by an agent, vague inputs stop being a UI problem and start being a correctness problem. Writing strict inputSchema definitions forced us to sharpen the data model itself. Cancellation is not optional. Forwarding options.signal into every handler seemed like boilerplate until an agent abandoned a long compare_career_paths call mid-flight. Plumbing the signal through from the start is far cheaper than retrofitting it. Untrusted content needs a marker. Catalog-derived tools carry untrustedContentHint: true . Third-party records flowing into an agent's context are a prompt-injection surface, and labeling them is the minimum. Constraint is a feature. We expected students to want more options. Testing the journey, the opposite held — cutting to at most three skill gaps and two experience options made the tool feel like advice instead of a search result. Deterministic beats plausible for an MVP. Our reasoning engine is local and rule-based, not LLM-backed. Every recommendation traces back to a catalog record and a selection, which is exactly what a career tool ought to be able to show. What's next for CareerCompass AI Real institutional data. The biggest gap between demo and product: authenticated SIS integration and per-institution degree adapters, so prerequisite checks run against a student's actual transcript instead of curated records. Verified, live opportunity feeds. Replace the null-URL entries with verified sources and freshness dates for scholarships, internships, and research postings — with an as-of timestamp on every record. Server-side authorization and audit. Right now approval gating

title: LineLab — Rehearse the Rush
pitch: LineLab lets event organisers rehearse crowd flow before doors open. A WebMCP agent tests safe fixes, compares outcomes, and waits for human approval before any plan is committed.
about_excerpt:
LineLab lets event organisers rehearse crowd flow before doors open. A WebMCP agent tests safe fixes, compares outcomes, and waits for human approval before any plan is committed.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 LineLab — Rehearse the Rush 

 LineLab helps event organisers rehearse a crowd rush before real guests arrive. 

 An organiser enters simple event facts such as guest count, doors, security staff, registration desks, pre-registration rate, backstage crew, and programme timing. LineLab then models the flow from gate to hall, identifies where people will get stuck, and lets an AI agent safely test possible repairs. 

 The important part: the agent can prepare, compare, and stress-test a plan, but it cannot make the final change. The organiser must visibly review and approve it. 

 The problem 

 A concert, college fest, or conference can become chaotic when too many people arrive at once. Registration may be slow, a QR scanner may fail, security may be understaffed, or the stage may not be ready when doors open. 

 Usually, organisers find out about these problems only when the real crowd is already waiting. 

 LineLab lets them ask: “What happens if this goes wrong?” before the event starts. 

 How it works 

 
 Enter a fictional event scenario. 
 Run a baseline rehearsal to see the current average wait, maximum queue, and bottleneck. 
 Ask the agent to create several safe draft repairs. 
 Compare the before and after results in plain language. 
 Stress-test the chosen plan against a disruption, such as a QR scanner failure or an arrival surge. 
 The organiser approves the final plan themselves. 
 

 For example, LineLab may show that Registration is the bottleneck because guests arrive faster than the team can check them in. It can then test a QR express line, arrival windows, a manual help desk, an extra entrance, or staff reassignment — and explain the trade-offs. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 A normal chatbot can suggest “add more staff” without understanding the actual event state. 

 LineLab exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , so a WebMCP-enabled agent can work with the real scenario inside the product instead of guessing where buttons are on the screen. 

 The agent can: 

 
 inspect the event flow and limits; 
 configure a fictional scenario; 
 run the baseline rehearsal; 
 create a draft repair; 
 compare outcomes; 
 stress-test a disruption; 
 commit a plan only after visible human approval. 
 

 This makes the agent useful, testable, and accountable. The organiser stays in control. 

 How we built it 

 LineLab is a Next.js and TypeScript web application with an interactive event-flow model. The model uses fictional data only; it does not use personal data, contact real venues, or make bookings. 

 We built the interface around plain-language explanations because an event organiser should not need to understand queueing theory to understand a problem. Instead of only showing numbers, LineLab explains what each result means, why a bottleneck occurs, and what would change in a proposed repair. 

 Challenges and what we learned 

 The biggest challenge was avoiding a fake “AI demo.” We wanted the product to do more than display a static answer. Each repair is calculated from the current scenario and must respect practical guardrails such as volunteer limits, doors, security, registration capacity, and pre-registration. 

 We also learned that human approval is not a small detail. The best agent experience is not an agent that silently changes everything; it is an agent that shows its reasoning, makes the trade-offs clear, tests failure cases, and lets a person make the final call. 

 What’s next 

 Future versions could support richer venue layouts, staff shift planning, accessible routes, live check-in signals, and post-event learning — while keeping organisers in control of every real-world decision.

title: AIMEC Alpha: From Business Opportunity to AI Implementation
pitch: AIMEC Alpha turns business automation ideas into AI implementation plans. Via WebMCP, people and agents can run ROI and readiness diagnostics, delegate to two AI specialists, and inspect the results.
about_excerpt: AIMEC Alpha turns business automation ideas into AI implementation plans. Via WebMCP, people and agents can run ROI and readiness diagnostics, delegate to two AI specialists, and inspect the results. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Businesses rarely struggle to find AI ideas. They struggle to decide which ideas are worth pursuing, whether their data and processes are ready, and what a practical implementation would require. I built AIMEC Alpha to connect those decisions in one workflow. Instead of stopping at a conversational recommendation, I wanted users to move from a business problem to measurable assumptions, an opportunity assessment, and a proposed implementation plan—with results they could inspect. WebMCP made this an opportunity to design for both people and their browser agents. A person can work through the interface, while an agent can discover and invoke the same capabilities through structured tools. What it does AIMEC Alpha evaluates a business automation opportunity using five diagnostics: AI return on investment AI operating costs Data readiness Agentic automation readiness Overall AI readiness Two complementary specialists then help interpret the findings: The AI Opportunity Analyst combines diagnostic results with the supplied business context to assess the opportunity, identify risks, and recommend whether to proceed, pilot, or hold. The AI Solution Architect receives the handoff and proposes a bounded architecture, implementation phases, and human approval points. The workflow then recalculates ROI using the estimated operating costs. Both specialists use a locally hosted Qwen model through Ollama. Financial calculations remain deterministic Python functions; the model provides interpretation and planning. The demo includes synthetic invoice-processing and customer-support scenarios. Users can change the assumptions and evaluate a different case. It proposes implementations—it does not connect to an ERP, process real invoices, or carry out business changes. Why WebMCP matters A conventional web application makes its functionality available primarily through buttons and forms. Browser agents often have to infer how those controls work. AIMEC Alpha exposes seven structured WebMCP interfaces: get_available_tools run_tool get_available_agents delegate_task get_task_status get_task_result get_execution_evidence These interfaces let a browser agent discover approved operations and their input schemas, submit a business case, and retrieve the resulting job status, output, and evidence without reconstructing the workflow from screen content. The human-facing interface remains available alongside those tools. People can review the assumptions and inspect the corresponding results in the same browser session. The value is not simply asking an LLM to calculate ROI. It is connecting discoverable capabilities, deterministic calculations, specialist interpretation, persistent task state, and inspectable results through a shared interface for people and agents. How I built it I extended existing AIMEC building blocks for capability registration, HTTP services, task persistence, and execution logging. The challenge-specific work added the WebMCP interface, browser workflow, business-agent integration, and isolated demo packaging. The application uses: Python services for diagnostics, capability execution, and specialist workflows. Qwen3:1.7b through Ollama for server-local model inference. SQLite for persistent jobs and execution events. JavaScript and document.modelContext.registerTool for native WebMCP registration. Docker Compose for the isolated runtime. Caddy for the public HTTPS endpoint. The Analyst and Architect have separate prompts and output contracts but share one model runtime. Their handoff follows an explicit, programmed workflow within the advisory service; it is not an unrestricted autonomous agent network. Results are associated with session-owned jobs. Execution evidence includes provider events and result hashes, allowing the application to check that a saved artifact matches the recorded provider output. Challenges I faced Making the model useful on a small VPS Running local inference on a CPU-only server required balancing response length, memory use, and execution time. I selected a small model, disabled its thinking mode for this workflow, bounded generation, and adjusted timeouts. A healthy model server does not necessarily mean an inference request will complete successfully, so testing the actual workflow was essential. Keeping browser sessions and results connected Early testing exposed problems restoring jobs across browser sessions. Cookie behavior and initialization order mattered: a completed backend job was not useful if the browser could no longer retrieve its result. I worked through session handling and tested status, result, and evidence retrieval together. Separating valid JSON from valid specialist output A model can return JSON that does not satisfy the application's required fields or values. I encountered an intermittent execution failure even while the underlying services remained healthy. That reinforced the importance of strict output validation and more specific failure reporting. The application does not replace failed model output with a fabricated success. Improving structured-output reliability remains an important next step. Keeping the demonstration honest I distinguished between deterministic calculations, model-generated proposals, and actions the system actually performs. I also separated native WebMCP tool checks from the broader claim that an external browser agent can independently choose and complete every workflow. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when the underlying application has clear capabilities and meaningful execution boundaries. Registering a tool is only the beginning: its inputs, permissions, task lifecycle, results, and failure behavior also need to be understandable. I learned that small local models can contribute useful interpretation when paired with deterministic tools and narrow responsibilities. They still require validation, realistic time budgets, and careful handling of failures. I also learned that execution evidence has limits. A matching result hash supports artifact integrity; it does not prove that a recommendation is financially correct or that every model-generated statement is justified. What I accomplished I deployed a public HTTPS demo with seven registered WebMCP interfaces, five business diagnostics, and two local-model specialists. Live testing demonstrated direct diagnostic execution and the Analyst-to-Architect workflow, including completed jobs, saved results, and verified result digests. The public demo export also passed ten offline tests covering business logic and packaging, with mocked model responses clearly distinguished from live inference. I published an isolated, MIT-licensed repository with the source, setup instructions, third-party notices, and a judge walkthrough. What's next My immediate priorities are stronger schema-constrained model output, clearer failure diagnostics, and repeated end-to-end reliability testing. Beyond the demonstration, I want to evaluate the assessments with real business users, improve the assumptions behind cost and readiness estimates, and add permissioned integrations that connect proposed plans to measurable pilot outcomes. The goal is to help businesses move from “I should use AI” to a specific, reviewable next step. title: Joy Of Painting
pitch: Paint along with your ai agent with bob ross joy of painting videos
about_excerpt: Paint along with your ai agent with bob ross joy of painting videos Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Joy Of Painting began with a simple, happy idea: what if painting along with Bob Ross could become a friendly paint along between a person and an AI agent? Bob taught us that painting is not about perfection. It is about slowing down, trying something new, and turning little accidents into trees, clouds, and possibilities. We wanted to bring that peaceful philosophy into an interactive studio where humans and agents can learn from the same lesson while creating entirely different paintings. What it does Joy Of Painting is a collaborative watercolor studio built around The Joy of Painting . The experience includes: Separate YouTube players for the human and AI agent A synchronized live transcript that follows the current lesson Resizable video players and painting easels A WebGL watercolor canvas with wet diffusion, pigment flow, paper texture, and drying Bob Ross–inspired brushes, including flat, fan, round, liner, blender, and painting-knife tools Physical pigment mixing based on the Kubelka–Munk model Episode-specific color palettes An eyedropper for collecting colors from the lesson WebMCP tools that let an agent control its video, read captions, inspect the lesson, and paint on its own canvas Every artist receives an easel. One belongs to the human, and one belongs to the agent. Then we let the happy little competition begin. Try the actual website Watch the demo How we built it We built the studio with React and Vite, using Video.js’s React YouTube integration for the two independent lesson players. The watercolor surface is a real HTML <canvas> powered by WebGL2. Its simulation models surface water, suspended pigment, deposited pigment, capillary movement, evaporation, paper fibers, granulation, and staining. Instead of averaging RGB values, colors are blended using Kubelka–Munk absorption and scattering calculations to behave more like physical paint. The transcript system maps timestamped captions to the active episode and updates the central caption as the lesson progresses. For agent interaction, the application registers browser-native WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . These tools allow an agent to: inspect the lesson and canvas seek, play, or pause its own YouTube player read the current transcript request a lesson reference image paint normalized watercolor strokes dry, undo, or clear its own easel Finally, we deployed the experience globally using Cloudflare Workers and static assets. Challenges we ran into Watercolor does not like to sit still—and neither did our first simulation. We had to solve canvas resizing feedback loops, animation-frame cleanup, WebGL resource management, and React lifecycle issues without losing the organic movement of wet pigment. Color preservation was another important challenge. Early versions stored old strokes in the active pigment slot, which meant loading red could turn previously painted yellow strokes red. We fixed this by baking existing pigment into the paper using its original optical properties before loading a new color. Synchronizing two separate YouTube players with episode changes and live captions also required careful handling. YouTube’s cross-origin iframe security prevents page JavaScript from capturing exact video-frame pixels, so the agent receives an honest timestamped lesson reference rather than a pretend screenshot. There were plenty of happy little bugs—but each one showed us where another tree could live. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are especially proud that the AI agent is not merely commenting on the painting. It can genuinely participate. During testing, the agent independently moved through a Bob Ross lesson, read the live transcript, and painted a complete woodland composition using only the website’s WebMCP tools. We are also proud of: A genuine WebGL watercolor simulation Non-destructive pigment changes that preserve previous colors Independent human and agent workspaces Live episode-aware captions Physical color mixing More than 400 browsable Bob Ross lessons A calm interface that keeps painting—not technology—at the center What we learned We learned that agent-friendly software works best when capabilities are explicit, focused, and honest. WebMCP allowed us to expose meaningful actions such as “paint a stroke” or “read the current caption” instead of asking the agent to guess its way through screen coordinates. We also learned that believable digital paint depends on time. Water must spread, pigment must settle, edges must darken, and colors must preserve their history. The smallest details often create the strongest feeling of physicality. Most importantly, we learned that human–AI collaboration does not always need to be about productivity. Sometimes it can simply be about making something peaceful together. What’s next for Joy Of Painting Next, we would like to add: Frame-accurate visual references through an authorized video-processing pipeline Saved galleries and downloadable side-by-side results Timed human-versus-agent painting challenges Brush-pressure and tilt support for drawing tablets Smarter agents that plan paintings from transcript cues Collaborative multiplayer studios Automatic judging based on composition, color, and creativity More paper surfaces, pigments, drying effects, salt, blooms, and glazing A replay mode showing both paintings developing stroke by stroke There are still many happy little worlds left to paint. title: FitCheck
pitch: A shoe fit profile you own, that any AI agent can read — on any store, with no merchant integration.
about_excerpt: A shoe fit profile you own, that any AI agent can read — on any store, with no merchant integration. Like Comment Story Updates The seven-brand terminal output The passing WebMCP Evals output The profile panel showing the conflict message find sneakers results across both stores with differing sizes Seven real shoes, all labelled men's US 9: Nike 263 mm Salomon 264 mm Converse 265 mm ASICS 268 mm Adidas 270 mm Birkenstock 270 mm New Balance 270 mm Seven millimetres of spread on an identical label. It gets worse. I read Kith's live catalog the way a shopping agent would. Every US-family product uses the same 3–18 size axis regardless of whether it's tagged mens, wmns, or both — and most are tagged both. So a label that just says "7" is ambiguous by roughly 15 mm inside a single brand, wider than the spread across all seven brands. The catalog structurally cannot tell you which. Neither can the agent shopping on your behalf. That fact only exists on the buyer's side of the transaction. Every agentic commerce protocol shipped in the last eighteen months standardises the merchant — UCP and ACP for the shopping journey, AP2 for payment authorization, x402 for settlement. None of them model the buyer past a payment instrument and a shipping address. Fit Check is the smallest useful version of the buyer's half. Apparel returns run around 25% (31% on shoes), size and fit cause roughly half to two-thirds of them, and each costs a merchant about $30. The person's half of the transaction is missing, and it's expensive. What it does You enter shoes you already own that fit — never millimetres. Brands and sizes, which sneaker shoppers know from memory. Those statements resolve to a foot length range in millimetres, which is the canonical stored value. Brand labels resolve against that length. Labels never convert directly to other labels. Any shopping agent can read the profile, write to it, and check products against it through WebMCP tools registered on the page. The server reads any store's public UCP catalog. Merchants install nothing and don't know it exists. When a verdict is wrong, you say so, and the profile updates. It sharpens across stores instead of being rebuilt at each one. Verdicts are deliberately not binary: fits · size_up · size_down · between_sizes · no_size out_of_stock · unmapped_brand · unknown Three design decisions that matter more than they sound: Rounding is always up. A shoe shorter than your foot doesn't fit; slightly long is wearable. A property test sweeps 240–300 mm across all seven brands asserting no recommendation is ever shorter than the foot. Conflicting statements produce a question, not an average. If your Nike 9 and your Converse 9.5 disagree by more than a half size, the tool says so and asks which fits better. Only the person can answer that, and answering it improves the profile permanently. That's the collaboration: the agent finds the contradiction, the human resolves it. unmapped_brand is a real answer. Veja appears on Stomping Ground and there's no mapping for it. Saying so beats guessing — especially for the people this serves best, who have been burned by confident sizing widgets before. Nine tools registered on document.modelContext, with navigator.modelContext as a fallback. readOnlyHint on the read-shaped tools, untrustedContentHint on anything returning merchant catalog text. The architecture is inverted on purpose. WebMCP tools are scoped to a document — an agent on a merchant's page cannot see tools registered by another origin, and cross-tab visibility is unspecified. So Fit Check is the page the agent works on, and the server reaches out to stores. The merchant is never in the loop, which is also what makes the portability claim true rather than aspirational. There's no integration to sell, no widget to install, and no store that has to say yes. UCP. The server fetches a store's /.well-known/ucp, negotiates capabilities, and reads the catalog over MCP. Everything below came from live stores, not fixtures: Store Protocol Size data Brand coverage kith.com 2026-08-25 100% clean variant.options, option Size 95% stompingground.myshopify.com 2026-08-25 100% clean, option Shoe Size 80% knifewear-inc.myshopify.com 2026-08-25 no size axis at all n/a — degrades to unknown The knife shop is included deliberately: a store sharing none of the assumptions, which the layer negotiates with, reads, and correctly reports it has nothing to say about. Three tiers of data access, degrading gracefully: find_shoe — one query across multiple UCP stores in parallel, verdicts attached, ~0.9s warm check_fit — authoritative single-product read with the full option matrix check_labels — no store, no catalog, no protocol. The agent reads the size dropdown off any page and hands over the labels. Works on stores with no UCP manifest at all. Sizing data. Brand-to-foot-length mappings for Nike, Adidas, New Balance, Converse, ASICS, Birkenstock and Salomon come from a read-only sample shared by Sizely / Size AI for this submission. Their guidance shaped the design: resolve on foot length rather than labels, read Birkenstock via EU because its own US labels are internally inconsistent, alias Jordan to Nike, and leave out the women's rows they didn't trust rather than invent them. Challenges Version mismatch is silent. UCP negotiation intersects capabilities by name and version, and a capability with no mutual version is dropped rather than erroring. The symptom is "this store has no catalog search," not "you advertised the wrong date." Two stores on the same platform were four months apart, and Kith upgraded mid-week. The platform profile advertises every version it can parse. There is no size filter. Standard UCP search filters are categories and price only. Fit has to be filtered client-side after retrieval — which is exactly why this layer needs to exist. A bug that looked right. I added a 10 mm toe allowance to recommendations. Plausible, and wrong: the dataset's foot_length_mm already means "the foot this size fits," so the manufacturer's toe room was being counted twice and every recommendation moved up a size. It surfaced because recommend_size and check_fit disagreed on the same profile. Now there's a round-trip test for all seven brands: a profile built solely from " 9 fits" must return US 9 from both paths. A bug only an agent could find. I ran the project through Google's WebMCP Evals CLI against the live deployment. add_fit_statement passed; check_labels immediately after returned "no foot-length estimate yet." The mutation was resolving before the estimate it implied had landed. A human typing never hits that gap — an agent calling two tools back to back hits it every time. The mutations now await the recompute, and the error message names what's actually missing instead of sending an agent in a loop. What I learned Consistent parameter naming across a tool surface is a discovery requirement, not a style preference. check_fit took store_domain while search_catalog took domain. An agent priming on one tool called the other with the wrong key and read it as broken. Nothing was internally inconsistent — the vocabulary just drifted between siblings. Catalogs cannot supply gender, and no parsing recovers it. This is different from a fact that's badly labelled but present. It's the clearest example I found of something that only exists on the buyer's side, and it's the whole argument for the profile. Honest verdicts beat confident ones. The audience this serves best — wide feet, half sizes, one foot larger than the other — has been failed by confident sizing tools before. unmapped_brand and "these two don't agree, which fits better?" read as trustworthy in a way a guess never would. What's next Width grades are the obvious next field: they're in the data, three of seven brands offer them, and they matter most to the people this serves. Longer term, the right home for a buyer profile is probably the browser — held like autofill, queryable by any page's agent, with no app in between. The spec isn't there yet; tools are document-scoped and cross-tab isolation is still maturing. But the schema outlives whoever holds it. Someone has to decide that the canonical value is foot length rather than a label, that both feet are recorded separately, that statements carry provenance, and that an unresolvable brand says so. That's the part this is really proposing. The mechanism generalises past shoes. Any category where the reference data is public and the person's half is missing — bike geometry against inseam, knives against hand and board — has the same shape. title: Crystal UI
pitch: Crystalize intent into interface!
about_excerpt: Crystalize intent into interface! Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I kept noticing the same complaint everywhere: chat is being added to every product right now, and it's usually worse than what it replaced. I read a long thread of UX researchers and designers talking about this. One comment summed it up well: the chatbot needs to be able to display UI, because typing a response is painful when you could have just been given a dropdown or a clickable list. Chat takes a spatial, structured task and forces it through a slow text bottleneck. So I decided to build it. What it does CrystalUI is a headless library that reads a site's WebMCP tools and turns a typed request into a guided, clickable interaction instead of a conversation. You type something like "merge these two shapes" once. One AI call figures out which tool that matches. After that there's no more guessing from the model. A fixed sequence of steps plays out: click the first shape, drag it into place, click the second shape, confirm. The AI decides once, and the human does the rest with a mouse. To test this against something real, I forked Excalidraw and registered 14 WebMCP tools against its actual drawing functions: creating shapes, merging them, connecting them with arrows, exporting, changing styles. Any WebMCP-compatible agent can call these tools directly, with or without Crystal loaded. Crystal sits on top of the same tool. I also added a check that stops the AI from making things up when no tool actually fits the request. If there's no clean way to accomplish what the user asked using the tools available, it says so instead of guessing.
